且: The passage begins mid-quotation. 且 is composed of 几 with two horizontal strokes at its foot; the 一 is the ground, depicting something resting on the ground. 丱: The commentary takes this graph as the ancient form of 卵. The Jiujing ziyang says: "The Shuowen writes 卝, which in clerical script became 卵," which shows that the Tang recension of the Shuowen certainly contained 卝. Zhang's citation of the Shuowen's ancient 卵 and deletion of the text is not sound; his meaning should have been that the upper form is the Shuowen's and the lower its clerical derivative, but he mistakenly adduced the ancient variant of a duplicate graph. Even so, it confirms that the Shuowen of Tang times had 卝.

元: The passage begins mid-sentence: "...it is a book of forms. For each seal-script character the meaning is glossed first — as 'beginning' or 'summit'; then the form is explained — as 'from such-and-such' or 'such-and-such is the phonetic'; then the sound is explained — as 'such-and-such a sound' or 'read like so-and-so.' 公: In [Shuowen]: "To divide equally; composed of 八 and 厶, where 八 means 'to turn the back' and 厶 is read like 私 (private)." Han Fei says: "To scheme for oneself is 厶; to turn one's back on 厶 is 公." [Liji, Wangzhi]: "to ennoble a man at court is something shared with the knights"; [Shiji, biography of Zhang Shizhi]: "the law is that which is shared with the whole world."

Xu Kai explains that the miǎn is what is added above: six inches long, narrow and round in front, broad and square above, painted in red and green, with long hanging lappets before and behind; the pendants are the strings of pearls hanging in front, dipping and winding like flowing water, while the silk filling is yellow floss attached to both sides of the cap and tied below with jade plugs, also called ear-ornaments, slender and pointed like a brush tip and inserted at the ears, meaning that one makes no display of cleverness but keeps himself empty to await others. The word miǎn means "to bow": leaning back above and bowing forward, it signifies reverence. [Liji, Yuzao]: "the feudal lords wear the lesser miǎn when they hold audience"; the Liqi adds that the Son of Heaven's miǎn has red and green strings and twelve pendants, the feudal lords nine, the senior grandees seven, and the junior grandees five, adornment being thereby valued.

凑: A place on the water where people gather; alternatively, to assemble. [Jizhong Zhoushu]: "The Duke of Zhou, being about to retire from government, built the great city of Chengzhou in the central lands, making it the great convergence of the world."

几: A low stool to sit or lean on. [Xu Xuan] explains it as what a person rests or sits upon. In [Shijing, Daya]: "Some spread out mats for them, some hand them stools." [Zhouli, Chunguan] lists five kinds of stool—jade, carved, red-lacquered, black-lacquered and plain. [Liu Xin, Xijing Zaji]: "By Han regulation the Son of Heaven had a jade stool, over which in winter a fine brocade was laid, called the brocade stool; all dukes and marquises had stools of bamboo and wood, and in winter fine..." (the quotation breaks off here).
凡: That which sums up and encompasses all. [Yupian]: "not one only." [Guangyun]: "constant; all." [Zhengyun]: "in general, approximately."
凤: A divine bird. [Erya, Shiniao] states that the yǎn is the feng and its female counterpart the huang. Guo Pu's commentary calls it "a bird of auspicious response, about six feet tall." [Shanhaijing] records that on Mount Danxue there is a bird shaped like a crane, five-coloured and patterned, named the feng. [Kongyantu] says: "The feng is the essence of fire, born at Danxue; it perches on no tree but the wutong, eats no fruit but bamboo seeds, drinks no water but sweet springs; its body bears all five colours and its cry matches the five notes; it appears when the way prevails, and when it flies all birds follow it." [Guangya] describes the fenghuang as having a chicken's head, a swallow's chin, a snake's neck, a goose's body, a fish's tail and paired wings, with the five colours marking head as virtue, wing as compliance, back as righteousness, belly as trust and breast as benevolence; the male's cry is jiji and the female's zuzu, while its cries at dusk, dawn, day, on rising and on alighting have their own names. [Shujing, Yiji] says "the fenghuang came and danced in courtesy"; [Liji, Liyun] counts the feng among domestic creatures so that birds do not take fright; and the [Dadai Liji] makes the fenghuang the chief of the three hundred and sixty feathered creatures.
処: Chǔ (処) means to stop, to rest. It is composed of 夊 (slow step) and 几 (stool): obtaining a stool, one comes to a stop. [Yupian] says it is the same as 處.
凫: This passage is commentarial, discussing the wild duck (fú). It notes that under the entry for fú the term shū-fú is adduced, and that although general usage need not distinguish them, the very saying of shū-fú is after all an analytic distinction. It further observes that Xu Shen placed the character not in the bird section but in the 几 (jī) section, a sentence that exemplifies the interrelation of the two sections.

Li Yangbing objected to this form and held that it should be written 函; but were Li's view followed, the character would easily be confused with 臽. 刃: The hard edge of a knife; the graph images the form of a knife having an edge. In [Zhuangzi, Yangshengzhu]: "My knife has been in use for nineteen years and has cut up several thousand oxen, yet its blade looks as if it had just come from the whetstone."

分: To divide, to separate. It is composed of 八 (to divide) and 刀 (knife), for the knife is what separates things. [Yijing, Xici]: "Things are separated according to their kinds."

刘: To kill. [Shujing, Pangang]: "Value our people; do not destroy them utterly." [Shijing, Zhousong]: "They overcame Yin and put a stop to slaughter." [Zuozhuan, Duke Cheng, 13th year]: "They slaughtered and ravaged our borderlands."
则: To mark things off in equal parts. It is composed of 刀 (knife) and 貝 (cowrie), the cowrie having been the ancient currency. [Xu Xuan]: "Zé means a limit; taking and using have their limits, and the knife is what cuts and regulates them."

包: Bāo (包) images a person pregnant. The foetus is within, imaging the child not yet formed. The primal vital force begins at zi (子); zi is what man is born from. Si becomes the child, and after ten months it is born; the male proceeds from si to yin and the female from si to shen, and hence the male's years begin at yin and the female's at shen.

嘗: To taste with the mouth. The character is composed of 旨 (delicious) with 尙 as phonetic. The [Shijing, Xiaoya] has "he tastes whether it is good or not"; the [Hanshu, Jiaosi Zhi] speaks of "the hundred spirits tasting the offerings," and the commentator Yan Shigu explains 嘗 as "to accept and enjoy the sacrifice."
嘘: To blow; to breathe out slowly. The [Yupian] gives "to blow and to breathe out"; the [Shenglei] states that a rapid expulsion of breath is called chuī and a slow one xū, while the [Zhengyun] says that pressing the lips together to expel breath is chuī and expelling breath with the mouth opened wide is xū. Breath blown from the lungs belongs to yin and is therefore cold, while breath breathed up from the cinnabar field belongs to yang and is therefore warm. The [Zhuangzi, Tianyun] asks, "Who is it that breathes out and in?"

噍: To chew, to gnaw. The [Yupian] glosses it as "to chew." The [Hou Hanshu, Yili Zhi] notes that the dove is "a bird that does not choke," and the [Guangyun] gives the variant 咽 while the [Jiyun] gives 䭇 and 饐.

噫: The breath of one who is satiated; to belch. The [Guangyun] gives "to belch." 回: The character is composed of 囗 (an enclosure), with the inner element depicting the form of revolution or turning. Xu Kai observes: "The breath of the whole heaven: heaven and earth support each other, heaven encircles the outside of earth, and yin and yang with the five agents revolve within it."
囟: The crown of the head, the covering of the brain; the fontanelle. The character is pictographic in form. Wei Xiao says: "It is the gate of the crown. While the child is in the mother's womb all its orifices are still closed, and only through the navel does breath enter, the fontanelle serving to let the air pass, for its bones alone have not yet closed; once born, the orifices open and breath enters by mouth and nose while the coccyx releases it, and the fontanelle gradually closes — such is the way of the rising and descending of yin and yang." Medical works say that the centre of the whorl of hair on the crown is the baihui point, one and a half inches in front of it the qianding, and three inches in front the fontanelle proper (囟門).

囷: A round granary. The character is composed of 禾 (grain) inside 囗 (an enclosure). The round one is called 囷 and the square one 京. The [Zhouli, Kaogongji, Jiangren] mentions "round granaries, pits and grain-houses," the commentary explaining that those built above ground are round (囷) or square (倉) while those dug into the earth are pits (窌). The [Shijing, Weifeng] asks, "You neither sow nor reap — how do you take three hundred round granaries of grain?", the commentary glossing 囷 as a round granary.
囹: A prison. The character is composed of 囗 (an enclosure) with 令 as phonetic. Xu Kai explains 囹 as 欞, the name for a railed enclosure or cage. The [Liji, Yueling] says that in mid-spring the officers are commanded to inspect the prisons, the sub-commentary noting that the word means a jail, which the Qin dynasty called 囹圄.
固: Shut in on all sides; firm, secure. The character is composed of 囗 (an enclosure) with 古 as phonetic. Xu Kai notes that the Huainanzi calls the natural defences of the nine provinces "the barriers of the nine provinces." The [Liji, Liyun] speaks of using walls, outer walls, moats and pools as defences; the [Zhouli, Xiaguan, Zhanggu] describes an officer in charge of maintaining the defences of city walls, moats, plantations and canals, the commentary explaining that he is responsible for what the state relies upon for obstruction, all of these being matters of securing. The [Mencius] says that one does not secure a state by the danger of its mountains and streams.
国: A state, a country; the fief of a feudal lord. The character is formed as a compound ideograph. The [Zhouli, Xiaguan, Liangren] states that the officer in charge of the standards for establishing a state divides the state into the nine provinces.
图: To plan and calculate what is difficult. The character is composed of 囗 (an enclosure) and 啚, 啚 conveying the idea of difficulty. Xu Kai explains that in drawing or planning a picture one must first lay out the plan, hence the 囗, and that 啚 has the sense of stinginess and difficulty.
囿: Composed of 囗 (an enclosure) with 有 as phonetic: a park with a wall, or on one account a preserve for birds and beasts. The [Shijing, Daya] has "the king is in the sacred park," the sub-commentary explaining that a 囿 is a bounded area enclosed by built walls in which birds and beasts are kept. The [Zhouli, Diguan, Youren] describes the officer in charge of the prohibitions concerning the beasts that roam the park, the commentary noting that the ancients called it 囿 and the Han called it 苑. On Mencius's reference to King Wen's park, the commentary explains that in antiquity the seasonal hunts took place in the slack seasons of farming as military training, and since the kings did not wish to gallop over cultivated fields and vegetable plots they measured out open, unoccupied land to make a park; the [Chuxueji] adds that 囿 is equivalent to 有 ("to have"), that which has a fence being called 園 and that which has a wall 囿.

圃: A vegetable plot; to grow vegetables. The [Zhouli, Tianguan, Dazai] lists among the nine occupations the second, "gardens and vegetable plots, to nurture plants and trees," the commentary explaining that a plot for growing trees and gourds is called 圃, with a fence around the garden.
圄: To guard, to hold. The [Liji, Yueling] mentions the inspection of the prisons, the commentary explaining 圄 as "to stop," that by which criminals are stopped from entering or leaving a compound. The [Chuxueji] says that 囹 means "to lead" and 圄 "to resist," i.e. to lead in and record the prisoners and to restrain them, while another account has 囹 = "command" and 圄 = "to awake to," since the criminal is made to enter and come to repentance. The [Zuozhuan, Duke Xuan, 4th year] relates that he imprisoned Bo Ying at Liaoyang and killed him.
圆: Round, whole. The [Yunhui] notes that in antiquity 圓 in the sense of "square and round" was always written 圜, and that the present form 圓 is later. The [Yijing, Xici] says that the virtue of the milfoil is round and spiritual while that of the hexagrams is square and wise, and the [Guanzi, Xinshu] that one who can be greatly round embodies the great square; the [Hanfeizi, Shixie] says that in drawing a circle with the left hand and a square with the right one cannot perfect both. Guo Pu's [Rhapsody on the River] describes round pools turning nine times and leaping on high, the commentary explaining that in the deep, swift waters of the gorge the current strikes the bank rocks and forms a circular flow. Yuan Jie's [Song on Hating Roundness] declares: "Better to be square and a menial than round and a minister; better to be square and disgraced than round and illustrious."

圉: The text preserved here is a philological note on prisons: the reading 囹圄 found in the Song edition is rejected. The Yueling says that in mid-spring the officers are commanded to inspect the prisons and in the first month of autumn to repair them, the commentary explaining that the prisons are for confining and detaining, comparable to the separate prisons of the present day. Cai Yong states that 囹 is a jail and 圄 "to stop," that by which people are stopped from going in and out, both being places where criminals are housed; Chong Jing asked to which dynasty's prisons the name 囹圄 belonged — the Zhou calling theirs 圜土, the Yin 羑里 and the Xia 均臺 — and Jiao replied that since the Yueling is a Qin text, 囹圄 is the Qin name for a prison, the Han calling it 若盧 and the Wei 司空. On Cai's view both 囹 and 圄 are places where criminals are housed, and the word "both" implies they need not be one and the same place; hence the enclosure radical says that 囹 is a prison without joining it to 圉, and here 囹圉 is given in inverted order to make the matter clear.
圊: A privy, an earth-closet. Xu Kai explains that the ancients called the privy "clear" (淸) because filth must constantly be cleared away. The [Guangya] glosses 圂 as a privy, and the [Shiming] derives the word from "mixed," since people place themselves mixed together within it.
國: A state, a country; the fief of a feudal lord. The character is formed as a compound ideograph. The [Zhouli, Xiaguan, Liangren] states that the officer in charge of the standards for establishing a state divides the state into the nine provinces.
園: That by which trees are planted; a garden. The [Chuxueji] says that which has a fence is called 園. The [Yijing, Bi] hexagram has "adorned in the hill garden, bundles of silk, small and few," and the [Shijing, Zhengfeng] pleads, "Oh Zhongzi, do not climb over my garden." The commentary explains that a 園 is the enclosure of a 圃, within which trees may be planted.

圜: The body of heaven; whole; encircling. The [Yijing, Shuogua] says that qian is heaven and is the round. The [Shangshu, Yugong] records the soils of the provinces: in Jizhou white loam; in Yanzhou black mould; in Qingzhou white mould; in Xuzhou red clay; in Yangzhou and Jingzhou mud; in Yuzhou loam with mounded black earth below; in Liangzhou blue-black soil; and in Yongzhou yellow loam.
圣: In the region between the Ru and Ying rivers, to exert one's strength on the land was called shèng. 圯: In eastern Chu a bridge was called yí. The [Hanshu, biography of Zhang Liang] relates that Zhang Liang, strolling at leisure in Xiapi, met an old man on the bridge who gave him a book. A note observes that according to the commentary on the Hanshu, Ying Shao took the character as written with the water radical and read it 詳里切 (xiáng-lǐ), meaning "on the Si river," whereas Zhang Mi emended it to the earth radical with the reading yí, and that Song Qi held the old text to have the water radical and Mi's account to be wrong. Since Hu Dan's encomium on the Yi bridge also writes the character with water, and since if it were written with earth it would follow the Shuowen's gloss that a bridge is called yí, Li Bai's line "I came onto the Yi bridge" would absurdly mean "I came onto the bridge bridge." It is therefore proper to accept Ying Shao's view as correct.

塔: A stupa, the Buddhist tower of the Western Regions, of seven, nine or up to thirteen storeys, the five-storeyed form being popularly called a "gimlet." In the third year of the Zhenguan era Emperor Taizong of Tang built the Great Ci'en Monastery south of the palace city at Chang'an and erected a brick stupa to house the Buddhist scriptures that Xuanzang had brought back from the Western Regions, naming it the Goose Pagoda; an Indian tradition explains the name: monks of a certain monastery, following the Lesser Vehicle, partook of the three pure foods — goose, calf and deer — and when they lamented one day that they were short of provisions for the bodhisattva (mahāsattva, in Sanskrit "the greatly generous"), a single goose fell at their words, whereupon the monks declared that it had left them a warning and that its virtue should be proclaimed, and built a stupa to bury it. In the Tang, when Wei Zhao passed the examinations he happened to inscribe his name at the Goose Pagoda of Ci'en Monastery, and the practice afterwards became a tradition; the entry closes with a citation from the Northern Wei record of the seven-storeyed stupa at Changshan, but the source text breaks off there. 塵: The character is composed of three 鹿 (deer) and 土 (earth), expressing the idea that a herd of deer running raises dust. In the regular script the repeated element was reduced, leaving a single 鹿, and the current simplified form 塵, composed of 小 (small) and 土 (earth), is likewise a compound ideograph. Its original meaning is "dust."
塾: A side hall beside the gate. [Liji, Xueji] records that in antiquity, among those who taught, "the district had its 庠 school and the household its shu (塾)"; the [Yili, Guanli] notes that food was laid out in the western shu.
墀: A plastered floor; by ritual the Son of Heaven has a vermilion chi (墀). Xu Kai explains it as the ground at the top of the steps, and the [Dianzhi] notes that under the Han the earth was lacquered with vermilion, whence "vermilion chi," while one laid with jade and stone was called the "jade chi." [Yang Juyuan's poem] has "no means to follow the hundred beasts, dancing in unison on the vermilion chi"; the [Qian Han, Meifu zhuan] speaks of wishing to ascend the hall of patterned stone and mount the path of the red chi; and [Emperor Wu of Han's "Falling Leaves, Mourning the Cicada"] laments that dust has gathered on the jade chi.

境: A boundary. One account treats it as identical with 竟, the sense being that the territory comes to an end here and so terminates. The [Guoyu, Lu yu] says "the words of an outer minister do not cross the border"; the [Shiji, Table of Vassal Kings] says the vassals' territories adjoin, with a note that their lands lie contiguous; and the [Qian Han, Dilizhi] speaks of opening up land and pushing back the frontier. It is interchangeable with 竟.
墅: Land outside the city wall, a country retreat. The [Maoshi Yunzeng] holds that 野 was the ancient form of 墅, and that later writers, having borrowed 野 for the open country, added 土 beneath it to distinguish the two. The [Zhengzi Tong] judges Mao's account plausible but wrong: 野 originally meant open country and rustic, and in antiquity there was no 墅 either as land or as a name; when later households built villas outside their dwellings they borrowed 野 and added the earth radical with a shift of sound to make 墅.

壽: Long life; any length of years is called shou (壽). The [Shangshu, Junshi] has "Heaven's longevity levels and corrects it"; the [Shijing, Daya] has "he made the record for Duke Shao — may the Son of Heaven enjoy ten thousand years"; the [Zuozhuan, Xi 32] speaks of middle longevity, with a note that the upper span is a hundred and twenty years, the middle a hundred, and the lower eighty. 大: Heaven is great, earth is great, and man is also great; the graph depicts the human form. Xu Kai notes that it was originally the ancient form of 人 (person). One reading gives the fanqie 他達, and in the classics and histories 大 is interchangeable with 太 and 泰.
天: The crown or summit; being highest and above, it is composed of 一 (one) and 大 (great). The [Baihu Tong] explains it as "to press down," since it dwells on high and governs below, being what steadies all things, and the [Yijing, Shuogua] says "Qian is Heaven." The [Liji, Liyun] says Heaven holds the yang and suspends the sun and stars; Xunzi observed that Heaven has no substantial form and that all the empty space above the earth is Heaven, while Shao Yong held that beyond the natural there is no separate Heaven. The [Chengzi Yishu] asks whether the blue of the sky is really Heaven's form and whether what is seen from below is not the same, and the [Zhangzi Zhengmeng] says Heaven revolves to the left while what lies within it follows, turning back to the right when it lags; Zhu Xi's [Yulei] treats the "nine heavens" of the Lisao as merely nine layers, the inner ones softer and the outer progressively harder, until the ninth is like a hard shell turning ever more tightly. A note adds that the sky's shape is like the white of an egg, in which seven layers may be discerned, the eighth membrane slightly harder and the ninth a hard shell, and observes that the Western calendrical theory of one layer moving more slowly than the next accounts for the varying speeds of the seven luminaries.

娑: A commentary passage on this character: "It is written 媻; the phonetic gloss of the [Erya] simply gives 娑 as the fanqie 素何 and provides no reading for 婆, which suggests that Lu's [Erya] text read 娑娑. The Lu Song commentary says the sacrificial vessel was adorned with 沙, and Zheng Zhi records Zhang Yi saying that 犧 is read as 沙, 沙 being the phoenix; when asked why the phoenix should be 沙, he answered that the image of the phoenix was carved on the vessel so that its form was 娑娑. In the present classics and commentaries the 娑娑 graphs have all been changed to 婆娑, and even the [Shijing] and [Erya] write 媻娑 together, which is probably not ancient; still, 婆娑 appears not infrequently in old books, and this humble view is recorded to await emendation."

婴: The commentary explains that 嬰 means "to wind around," and that 纓 is interchangeable with 嬰; Lu Ji's poem written on the road to Luoyang has "the world's net winds around my body," and Li's citation of the [Shuowen] for 嬰 as "to wind" rests on an early Tang text that can be trusted. To wind is to entwine: everything entwined is like the 賏 ornament coiled about the neck, and so the graph is composed from 賏. The [Yuejue Shu] speaks of 嬰 with a shield decked with jade discs, the [Sima Fa] of a great officer's 嬰 bow, and the [Shanhai Jing] of 嬰 with a hundred gui and a hundred bi, meaning to array them for a circular sacrifice; again, Mount Yan has many 嬰 stones, that is, stones like jade with figured bands wound about them. In all historical uses, to "嬰 a city and hold it" means to hold it encircled by its walls, and 嬰兒, "infant," is a sound-shifted form of 嫛婗.

宋: To dwell; composed of 宀 (roof) and 木 (wood). Xu Kai explains that wood is what makes a house, providing a dwelling for people.
完: Whole, complete. The [Lunyu] has "if only it were complete"; the [Zhuangzi, Tiandi] says that not letting things frustrate one's purpose is called 完.

宕: To exceed, to be unrestrained; one account says "a cave dwelling," composed of 宀 with an abbreviated 碭 as phonetic. The [Guliang zhuan, Wen 11] says that three brothers of the Long Di roamed unchecked through the central states.

The [Liji, Jifa] records that the house of Yu took Zhuanxu as 祖 and Yao as 宗, the Xia took Zhuanxu as 祖 and Yu as 宗, the Shang took Xie as 祖 and Tang as 宗, and the Zhou took King Wen as 祖 and King Wu as 宗; Jia Yi said that 祖 marks merit and 宗 marks virtue.

The [Zhengzi Tong] notes that the character is also written 桭, citing Yang Xiong's fu and Fu Qian's note that 柍 is the centre and 桭 the roof-beam, but observes that 宸 properly takes its sense from the Northern Asterism, so that the modern use of 宸極 differs from the general word for a roof-beam and the conflation of 宸 and 桭 is wrong.

宾: One who is honoured; the [Yupian] gives "guest." The [Yijing, Guan hexagram] says it is favourable to be a guest of the king; the [Shangshu, Shundian] says he received the guests at the four gates.
宿: To stop; the [Yupian] gives "to halt at night," "to lodge." The [Shijing, Zhousong] has "there are guests who stay one night, there are guests who stay two," a note explaining that one night is 宿 and two nights 信; the [Zhouli, Diguan] provides a lodging every thirty li, each with a wayfarer's room.

寢: To lie down to sleep. The [Shijing, Xiaoya] says "then he rests and then he rises"; the [Lunyu] records that Zai Yu slept during the day.

The [Zhouli, Chunguan, Dazongbo] says that when the king made a great enfeoffment he announced it to the Earth Deity, a note explaining that 封 concerns matters of land.

尺: Ten inches. A man's forearm, with ten moving pulses between the elbow and the wrist, makes the inch-gate (寸口), and ten inches make a foot (尺), a matter of rule and measure; the character is composed of 尸 and 乙, 乙 being what is marked. Under the Zhou system the measures cun, chi, zhi, xun, chang, and ren were all modelled on the human body. The [Jiayu] says that spreading the fingers gives knowledge of the foot and extending the arm gives knowledge of the xun; the [Qian Han, Lüli zhi] says that measures of length, volume, and weight all arise from the pitch-pipe of the Yellow Bell, one millet grain making a fen, ten fen a cun, and ten cun a chi; Cai Yong's [Duduan] records that the Xia made ten cun to the chi, the Yin nine, and the Zhou eight; and the [Zhouli, Sishi] notes that rules and foot-measures were placed in the silk and cloth shops.
尻: The rump; composed of 尸 with 九 as phonetic. The [Yupian] gives "hip" and the [Zengyun] "the end of the spine." The [Liji, Neize] says the hare's rump is removed; the [Zhuangzi, Dasheng] speaks of placing someone's rump on a carved platter; and Qu Yuan's [Tianwen] asks where Kunlun and the Hanging Garden have their base, a note explaining 尻 as the end of the spine and observing that since the mountain is highest there must be somewhere below where its roots rest. The [Jiyun] notes an alternative form.
尾: Small, minute; composed of inverted hair (毛) behind 尸. The [Yupian] notes that birds, beasts, fish, and insects all have one.

屍: The principal in death; composed of 尸 and 死, a compound ideograph. The [Liji, Quli] says that on the couch it is called 屍 and in the coffin 柩; the [Zuozhuan, Wen 3] records that the Earl of Qin crossed the river and burned his boats, then sealed the corpses at Xiao and returned. Xu Kai notes that since dwelling takes 尸, so does moving; 屑屑 means repeatedly bustling about. One account gives "reverent," and "unable to desist."

幞: The entry is truncated at the beginning and opens with the words "also [used in] 巾幞." [Guangyun] says: "The fú-tóu (幞頭, head-wrap) was devised by Emperor Wu of Zhou; he cut a full-width cloth and brought out four feet to make the fú-tóu, and so it was named." [Tangshu, Chefu Zhi] states that "the fú-tóu arose in the Later Zhou, for the convenience of military affairs." [Eryi Shilu] says: "In antiquity three chi of black gauze were used to wrap the head, and this was called the head-cloth; through the three dynasties these were caps, and ranks and commoners alike wrapped their hair with black silk. In the time of Emperor Wu of Zhou, following the ancient three chi, it was cut into the fú-tóu, and Ma Zhou of Tang crossed and untied it." [Zhu Xi, Yulei] notes that "the fú-tóu of the Tang people was at first made only of gauze; later, because the gauze was soft, a wooden mount was cut and placed in front to prop it up." [Bit'an] records that "Emperor Gaozu of Liang first spread lacquer on the gauze and applied iron for the feet." [Songshi, Yufu Zhi] relates that "the fú-tóu, also called the folded-up head-wrap, arose in the Later Zhou, but at first only soft silk hung down at the feet; in Sui times it was first made of paulownia wood, in Tang times gauze first replaced silk, and only the emperor's had its feet turned up while subjects' hung down; in the Five Dynasties it gradually changed to flat and straight. Under the present dynasty's regulations ruler and minister alike wear level feet, and the emperor may wear one turned up. At first a cap of woven rattan and grass served as the lining and gauze as the outer surface, coated with lacquer; later, as lacquer alone was firm, the rattan lining was removed, the front was made as a single fold, and two feet were applied level, made of iron."

忕: The note reads: "忕 means 'to be accustomed to'; thus the early Tang edition contained the seal-graph 忕. Xuanying's book, in juan thirteen, says that 忕 is also written [a form now lost], and it quotes the Zilin: '[that form] means to be accustomed to,' and the Cangjie Pian: '[it] means bright.' Hence the Shuowen wrote 忕 and the Zilin changed it to that form, though the two are really one character; shallow editors used the Zilin to alter the Shuowen. Under 狃 in the dog section it says, 'the nature of dogs is to be accustomed (忕) to things,' which proves that Xu's book did have the seal-graph 忕; instances of 狃 and 忕 in the classics and commentaries are too many to enumerate. Lu Deming gives the fanqie 'shí shì', also 'shì zhì', also 'shí shè'; the Zilin's form gives 'yì shì', fifteenth section. Further note: that character was probably originally written 怈, and the men of Tang, observing a naming taboo, changed many compounds containing 世; the Jiyun and Leipian both treat it and 怈 as variant forms." 悌: The entry opens with a truncated citation: "Kǎi (闓) means 'to open'." The Hongfan discusses the five types of divination cracks, one of which is called yì (圛), the note saying that "yì is a lustrous, bright colour"; the phrase "setting out at evening" above means setting out at nightfall, while this "opening and bright" means travelling as dawn breaks, so that it connects with the passage above. The note adds that 豈弟 (kǎitì) also carries the sense of setting out; Mao's commentary glosses the kǎitì in the Qi Feng poem "Zai Qu" in the same way as elsewhere, but Zheng's commentary does not follow it, and there must be a reason. The Jiyun also gives a fanqie "dài yì", which should be glossed as "to set out"; the present Jiyun still follows Mao's commentary and does not adopt Zheng's, so that this additional reading is superfluous.

掺: The surviving text is a philological note of the kind written by Duan Yucai, imperfectly transmitted, with some graphs lost. It distinguishes 摻, written with the phonetic 參, from 操, written with the phonetic 喿 and glossed "to hold up (奉也)," and explains that the two were confused in vulgar usage and were therefore cited separately. It notes that the present text no longer contains a small-seal graph for 摻, a consequence of the two characters not having been distinguished since the Southern Dynasties, and compares this with similar losses elsewhere in Xu Shen's work — two graphs in the tripod section that resemble each other with one missing, and two in the water section with one lost. It gives the fanqie 所斬切 and places the ancient sound in the seventh rhyme group.

摻: The surviving text is a philological note of the kind written by Duan Yucai, imperfectly transmitted, with some graphs lost. It distinguishes 摻, written with the phonetic 參, from 操, written with the phonetic 喿 and glossed "to hold up (奉也)," and explains that the two were confused in vulgar usage and were therefore cited separately. It notes that the present text no longer contains a small-seal graph for 摻, a consequence of the two characters not having been distinguished since the Southern Dynasties, and compares this with similar losses elsewhere in Xu Shen's work. It gives the fanqie 所斬切 and places the ancient sound in the seventh rhyme group.
摽: [Shuowen]: "The alternative form of 拋, written from 手 with the phonetic 票; it is used generally as 摽." See also the note under 拋. The compiler adds: "According to the Tangyun the fanqie is 符少切, originally in the Xiao rhyme and the rising tone; the Shuowen wrongly placed it in the departing tone. The newly added Guangyun changes it to 頻小切, which should be followed."

攜: The entry opens mid-quotation with the gloss "to lift, to carry in the hand." [Liushu Gu] explains it as "to hold suspended." The [Shujing, Lizheng] speaks of attendants on the left and right who carry and hold, the commentary identifying them as servants who carry and attend; the [Shijing, Daya] has "as though taking, as though carrying," the sub-commentary explaining that when an object lies on the ground one raises it with the hand and carries it. The [Liji, Quli] says that when an elder takes a child's hand to lead it, the child supports the elder's hand with both hands, the commentary explaining "leading by the hand" as drawing someone along as one goes.
攝: The entry opens mid-quotation with the gloss "to draw up and hold." The [Zuo Zhuan, 16th year of Duke Cheng] has "please draw it up and drink." The [Guoyu, Lu Yu] speaks of one who makes a fair name for later ages so that he may long serve as a mirror to the world, and who is therefore able to hold fast without slackening over time. The quotation from the [Qian Hanshu] biography of Zhang Er breaks off unfinished in the source.
攣: The gloss is "to bind, to fasten"; whatever is bound, pulled, or tied together is called luan. The [Yijing, Zhongfu] has "with sincerity, bound fast," the sub-commentary calling this the name for being mutually drawn and tied without break. The [Qian Hanshu] biography of Zou Yang mentions crossing beyond the language of bonds and fetters, and Han Yu's poem on the peace and virtue of the Yuanhe reign speaks of loosening the bonds and cords.
攤: The gloss is "to open out"; alternatively, "to spread out with the hand." The [Shishuo] tells of Wang Rong spreading books over the whole bed. A poem of Du Fu has "all day long, spreading out coins in the high waves."

攫: The gloss is "to seize." The [Zengyun] says "to snatch and take." The [Liji, Ruxing] speaks of birds of prey that seize and strike, the sub-commentary explaining that taking with the feet is called jue while striking with the wings is called bo; alternatively, the word means "to grasp." The [Zhanguo Ce] relates that even if Gongsun Zi were worthy and Xu Zi unworthy, in a fight between the two Xu Zi's dog would still seize Gongsun Zi by the calf and bite him.

The [Qian Hanshu, Tianwen Zhi] says that the distance to the pole is hard to know, and the essential means is the gnomon shadow, for by the gnomon shadow one knows the sun's north-south position. The [Zizitong] says that the gui is what calendrical calculation proceeds from, describing the method: take a height as the body and set up two poles, long and short, as the function; the two poles being equal to the height, measure how much shorter or longer the intervals among the three objects are, and seek the answer by the right triangle, whereupon the length of cold and heat becomes plainly visible. It is written with 咎 because the sun's shadow is subject to discrepancy: the course of heaven has its constant rule, yet cannot but slightly wax and wane, and from this the precession of the equinoxes arises; hence the sun's shadow is established to measure it, which is precisely the method of setting up a gnomon and observing the shadow in the [Zhouli, Kaogong Ji].

桎: The gloss is "a restraint for the feet." Xu says that zhi means to stumble, that is, to be obstructed, and that a restraint on the feet is called zhi while one on the hands is called gu. The citation from the [Zhouli, Qiuguan, Dasikou] breaks off unfinished in the source.
桐: The gloss is "the tong tree, that is, the rong." The [Erya, Shimu] gives "rong: the tong tree." The [Shujing, Yugong] records the solitary tong of the sunny side of Mount Yi, the tradition explaining it as a tong growing by itself on Mount Yi and fit for qin and se strings. The [Shijing, Yongfeng] mentions the yi, tong, zi, and lacquer trees, from which qin and se are made. The commentary on plants and trees distinguishes three kinds, green, white, and red, while Chen Zhu's treatise on the tong lists six: purple tong, white tong, resinous tong, thorn tong, red tong, and the wutong.
桑: The gloss gives it as the leaves eaten by silkworms. Xu says 叒 is read ruo: at sunrise the sun climbs the ruo-tree at Tang valley in the east, and because this is the divine leaf the silkworms eat, 木 is added below 叒 to distinguish it. The "Dianshu" says the mulberry winnow is the essence of a star. The commentary on the [Shijing, Binfeng] explains "seeking the tender mulberry" as the young mulberry and "the graceful woman mulberry" as the sprouting mulberry, while "in the silkworm month they strip the mulberry" means cutting the branches to gather the leaves. The [Liji, Yueling] says that in the last month of spring the warden of the fields is ordered not to fell mulberry or zhe trees, the commentary explaining that this is out of care for the silkworms' food; the [Shiji, Huozhi Zhuan] says that a family in Qi or Lu with a thousand mu of mulberry and hemp is the equal of a marquis of a thousand households.
桓: The gloss is "the marker post of a post-station." Xu says that when marker posts are set up in pairs they are called huan. Under Han law the four corners of the station's marker bore great timbers pierced with square boards, called huan markers, one on each side of the seat of a county. The [Qian Hanshu, biography of Yin Shang] says he was buried east of the huan at the temple gate.
桔: The gloss is "the platycodon, the name of a medicine." The [Zhanguo Ce] says that to seek bupleurum and platycodon in the marshy lowlands is to go many generations without finding a single one.

械: Four explanations are given. First, it means shackles and fetters: Kong Yingda says "xie is jie (to warn), warning and restraining a man so that he cannot move about." Second, it is a general name for implements: the [Liji, Wangzhi] says that implements and weapons have different regulations, the commentary explaining these as the instruments of ritual and music together with weapons and armour. Third, it means "to hold"; fourth, what has a container is a xie and what has none is a qi. The [Zhouli, Sishu] says that every three years a great reckoning is made of the administration of the officials in order to know the number of the people's implements and weapons, the sub-commentary explaining that qi are the instruments of ritual and music while xie are bows, arrows, dagger-axes, spears, lances, and halberds.

樘: A running philological note rather than a plain definition: it argues that the word means 'pillar'. Li Shan's annotation to the 'Changmen Fu' cites the 'Zilin' with the same gloss, and in no place is any slanting member mentioned; only the character 樘 is written variously as 牚 or 撐, and these are merely vulgar forms, while the 'Yupian' likewise says 'Tang is a pillar' without any slant. The note concludes that tang is originally the name of a pillar, as in the 'Lingguang Palace Fu', where branching tangs and forked props lean aslant, tang being paired with storied columns, curved brackets and fungus-shaped capitals, so that the gloss 'pillar' is beyond doubt; tang may be borrowed for 'to prop' just as 柱 may be borrowed for 'to support', whence 'prop' became its standard gloss, and because popular usage holds that propping must be done with slanting timber, a slanting [element] came to be attached to the character.

汗: The entry opens mid-quotation: '...it is the fluid of the human body.' The 'Bencao' quotes Li Shizhen: sweat issues from the heart, being blood within and sweat without, whence the saying that one who robs a man of his sweat has no blood, and one who robs him of blood has no sweat. The [Yijing, Huan] has 'as sweat, the great proclamation'; the [Shiji, Life of Su Qin] 'wiping off sweat like rain'; and the 'Former Han, Life of Liu Xiang' observes that issuing commands is like sweating, for what is out does not return, so that to issue it and take it back is to reverse one's sweat; the 'Wenxin Diaolong' likewise says it comes forth like a cord and is not brought back, like sweat.

The 'Shuijing Zhu' describes the Yi flowing west below Xiapi county and dividing into two streams, one entering the Si southwest of the city's north wall, the other bending east of the city and south of the county to enter the Si likewise, called the Little Yi; on it there is a bridge, regarded by the people of Xu and Si as the place where Zhang Liang met the Old Man of the Yellow Stone. The 'Dili Tongshi' cites Master Zeng: the waters of Xu named Yi are more than one — Li Daoyuan makes one come from Mount Niqiu, flowing northwest past the Yumen gate of Lu, and another come from Mount Guanshi in Wuyang of Mount Tai, both called the Yi.

The [Chuci, Jiuge] has 'on the Yuan there are angelicas, on the Li orchids'.

[Shangshu, Yugong]: 'He guided the Yangzi from Mount Min; eastward a branch forms the Tuo', the commentary citing the Erya, Explaining Waters, that water flowing out from the Yangzi is a tuo and from the Han a qian. The [Shijing Dili Kao] cites Master Cai: in Zhijiang county of Nan commandery there is a Tuo water which flows into the Yangzi rather than issuing from it, while in Huarong county the Xia water issues from the Yangzi at its head and enters the Mian at its tail and is likewise called a tuo — this being the tuo of Jingzhou; the Jiang-tuo of Pi county in Shu commandery lies to the east and enters the great river to the west, and that of Wenjiang county lies to the southwest and enters the river to the east — this being the tuo of Liangzhou. Dai Tong observes that the name tuo is not uniform and that the tuo of Liangzhou is merely the greatest of them.

河: The entry opens mid-quotation: '...the river issues from Mount Kunlun beyond the Dunhuang frontier, and from its source flows down to the sea.' 泊: A philological note rather than a plain definition: it argues that this character is the ancient form of 泊, meaning the look of shallow water, and that the water in question has no name but is described by its shallow appearance, so that it might simply take 洦 as its name. Duan Yucai observes that the current text of Yan's book is corrupt and restores it to this reading; the Shuowen writes 洦 and the clerical script 泊, the two being ancient and modern forms of one character. He adds that the Bo radical entry reads 'pronounced like shallow bo', that shallow water is easily stilled, so that bo also means to moor, that shallow is written as thin, so that bo also serves for thin and thick, and that it is further used for the word meaning calm; the rhyme tables wrongly place bo in the Duo rhyme and 洦 in the Mo rhyme through ignorance of the old sounds. He notes finally that the neighbouring entries are all river names, so that this character ought not to stand in this position, and suspects that a copyist misplaced it among characters resembling 百 and 千.

溱: The passage is a fragment of geographical commentary on the Qin river, arguing that a certain stream has been wrongly called the Zhen. Because the Qin comes from the northeast while the Kuang enters it from the west and the Zhen from the east, the Zhen being what is now the Weng river, and because Ban [Gu] and Xu [Shen] both take the Kuang as the main line, the Qin flowing into the Kuang, the Kuang into the Yu and so to the sea, the smaller Zhen goes unmentioned in Ban and in the Shuijing. It goes on to cite the Fangyu Jiyao, which records the old accounts that the Qin issues southwest of Linwu county in Huguang, passes Qujiang county and flows northwest to join the Wu water and pass through Yingde county, exactly the ancient Qin, which the Shuijing Zhu and the Yuanhe Junxian Zhi also call the Shixing great river.

滁: The passage is Duan Yucai's geographical commentary on the Tu river. He notes that while the sources say the water enters the Sheng, the [Shuijing Zhu] makes it enter the Ruo, Li Daoyuan tracing the Ruo through Yuexi and Dazuo counties to join the Sheng, and concludes that these are different streams flowing into one another and so sharing a common name. The [Shuidao Tigang] identifies the Jinsha river with the ancient Sheng and the Yalong with the ancient Ruo, and describes the Jinsha's long course from the Tibetan lands through Yunnan and Sichuan, so that it is beyond doubt the upper source of the great river. Duan adds that to take the Jinsha as the true source is not the purport of the Yugong's 'from Mount Min he guided the Jiang', the sage naming only the nearer sources, and he admits that he cannot determine where Mumi county or the Tu water now lie.

滎: The passage is a long philological commentary on the character 滎. 潘: The passage is a fragment of philological commentary on the Pan river. It observes that by the rule of the Shuowen and the Zilin the hand-radical character 播 should not be extended to a river name, and concludes that the Zilin rightly writes the graph as 潘, the water lying at Yingyang in agreement with the Shuowen, while Ma, Zheng and Wang in their Shangshu commentaries all write it as 熒播, identifying it with Ying marsh. Xu and Lü, by contrast, make Pan a separate river distinct from Ying, and Zheng's Zhouli commentary, reading 波 as 播, divides Ying, Luo, Bo and Zha into four, so that the false Kong text writes 波 where the Zhouli has 播; Xu's 潘 is thus the correct graph and 播 the borrowed one, though the Pan water can no longer be located.

牚: The commentarial tradition glosses the graph as "a pillar," as when Li Shan's note to the Changmen fu quotes the Zilin: "chēng, a pillar." None of these sources has the word xié (slanting); only the character 樘 is written sometimes as 牚 and sometimes as 撐, both of them vulgar forms. The [Yupian] likewise says 樘 means pillar without any sense of slanting, and it appears that 樘 was originally a pillar's name, as in the Lingguang dian fu's "the branch-pillars crossed and slanted," where the phrase stands parallel to the layered brackets and curved struts. The gloss "pillar" is therefore beyond doubt: 樘 could be borrowed for 䟫 and 歫 just as a pillar can be borrowed for "to prop," and only because ordinary speech supposes that propping must use a slanting piece of wood has the stray word xié become attached. The [Zhengzi tong] enumerates eight kinds of nüè — wind, cold, summer-heat, heat, damp, food, miasma and evil — and describes the chronic form with a mass in the belly as the "mother of malaria," the cold-only as female and heat-only as male, the irregular as ghost-malaria and the hot-without-cold as dan malaria, all arising from phlegm in the middle of the belly and disharmony of spleen and stomach, as set out in the Nüè lun of the Lingshu jing. 疱: A swelling on the face. Xu Xuan says it is a sore on the face, and the [Broad Elegance] glosses it as a disease. The [Zhengzi tong] says that whatever suddenly rises like a water blister on the hands, feet, arms or elbows is called a pào, and the [Huainanzi, Shuolin xun] warns that bursting a small blister may bring out a carbuncle; Han Yu's poem "Eating a Toad" says "though its two thighs are long, what of the blisters on its back?" The [Hanshu, biography of the Lord of Wanshi] records that Qing, ashamed of being unequal to his office, submitted a memorial: "I have been fortunate enough to hold the office of chancellor, but, jaded and dull, I have nothing with which to assist the government." The [Hou Hanshu, Guangwudi ji] says "I take pleasure in this myself, and do not find it wearying." Phono-semantic in an enclosing configuration.

疵: A flaw, a blemish; literally "a sickness." [Yijing, Xici]: "Regret and regretfulness speak of a small blemish." The sub-commentary explains this as a minor defect in a hexagram line. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi, 7th year]: "I take, I seek; I do not make you a blemish or a flaw," glossed as "I do not treat you as a criminal." [Hanshu, Biographies of the Thirteen Kings of Jing]: "Now perchance one has no crime, yet is insulted by subordinates, and the officials blow upon the hair to seek out a flaw (chuimao qiuzi)," the gloss being "a fault."
疸: Jaundice; the yellow sickness. [Neijing]: "When the eyes are yellow and the urine yellow-red, and the patient lies quietly at rest, this is jaundice; when one has eaten and yet feels hungry, it is stomach jaundice." The medical manuals enumerate five kinds of dan: yellow obesity, jaundice, wine jaundice, grain jaundice, and the jaundice of female overexertion.

疽: A chronic abscess; a deep-seated ulcer. The medical books say that an abscess (yong) arises from disharmony of the six bowels, while a ju arises from disorder of the five viscera: when yang is obstructed within yin an abscess forms, and when yin is obstructed within yang a ju forms. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xiang, 19th year] records that Xun Yan suffered from dan-ju, glossed as a malignant sore, the sub-commentary adding that ju is an abscess. [Shiji, Biographies of Sun and Wu]: "When a soldier was afflicted with a ju, [Wu Qi] sucked it for him." [Zhengzi Tong]: "A deep abscess is called ju; the ju is deep and malignant, while the yong is shallow and large."
疾: Illness; also "urgent, swift." Xu [Kai] explains that illness comes on swiftly, and hence the character takes 矢 (arrow), the arrow being swift. [Yijing, Fugua]: "Return is successful; going out and coming in, there is no illness." [Shangshu, Yue Ming]: "If the medicine does not cause dizziness, the illness will not be cured."

Named forms are listed — blemish-abscess, red spreading abscess, hare-bite, the four excesses, virulent abscess, and sloughing abscess — all arising from qi and blood retained and stagnating, so that the nutritive and defensive influences fail to circulate. [Hou Hanshu, Treatise on the Calendar]: "At the Awakening of Insects the gnomon shadow is eight chi two cun; if it arrives before it ought, many suffer from abscess, ju, and swelling of the shins."

痫: An illness. [Yupian]: "the convulsive illness of children." [Zhengzi Tong] holds that epilepsy may arise from wind-heat or from frightful heteropathic influences, and that in every case both vacuity and phlegm are involved. The medical manuals teach that children have five kinds of epilepsy corresponding to the five viscera, each with its own stored humour: in heart epilepsy the cry is like a sheep's, in liver epilepsy like a dog's, in spleen epilepsy like an ox's, in lung epilepsy like a fowl's, and in kidney epilepsy like a pig's; when it strikes, the patient suddenly falls, mouth and eyes are drawn, hands and feet twitch and clench, frothy saliva issues from the mouth, and after the time of a meal he revives. [Hou Hanshu, Biography of Wang Fu]: "If suckling is excessive, it brings on the epileptic illness."

痹: A numbness or paralysis; the surviving text opens mid-sentence, "...arriving, they combine to form bi." "When wind qi predominates it is moving bi, when cold qi predominates it is painful bi, and when damp qi predominates it is fixed bi." The commentary explains that wind is the yang within yin, good at moving and frequently changing, and that what is popularly called "wandering fire" covers such things as migrating joint pains; that yin-cold qi lodging in the muscles, sinews, and bones congeals and blocks them, producing painful bi, that is, gout; and that fixed bi is heavy and does not shift, dampness transforming upward, so that the disease lies in the muscles and not in the sinews and bones. There are heart bi, lung bi, liver bi, kidney bi, intestinal bi, and bladder bi; in general, bi conditions contract on meeting cold and slacken on meeting heat, cold drawing the sinews up and heat relaxing them. Master Cheng said that medical books treat numbness and paralysis of the hands and feet as "without fellow-feeling," and the chapter on disease capability states that bi without fellow-feeling issues as flesh-withering. [Huainanzi, Chuzhen]: "Valley air produces much bi." [Baopuzi, Zhili]: "Sweet flag and dried ginger stop bi and dampness." [Ji Kang, Letter Breaking Off Relations with Shan Juyuan]: "Sitting upright a while, my limbs grow numb and I cannot move," glossed "bi is a damp disease."

痿: Paralysis; a bi-type illness. [Zhengyun] gives "a damp disease," and another account says "the two feet cannot reach one another." [Neijing]: "When the yangming is vacuous the ancestral sinews slacken and the girdle vessel does not draw them, hence the feet wither; one should in each case tonify its nutritive qi, free its transport points, regulate its vacuity and repletion, and harmonize its reversals and smoothness, so that sinews, vessels, bones, and flesh each in its season, receiving the month, are cured." [Shiji, Biography of Han Xin]: "My longing to return is like that of a withered man who cannot forget to rise," glossed "unable to walk." [Hanshu, Annals of Emperor Ai]: Ru Chun says that when the two feet cannot be crossed it is called wei, and Yan Shigu that wei is likewise a bi disease; [Mei Cheng, Seven Stimuli] speaks of going out and coming in by carriage as "the mechanism of lameness and paralysis."

瘧: Malaria; fever and chill alternating. [Yupian]: "a disease of alternating cold and heat." [Shiming]: "Nüe means cruel and harsh; in other diseases there is either cold or heat, but in this one cold comes first and heat after, the two conditions being like cruelty and oppression." [Liji, Yueling]: "In the first month of autumn cold and heat are unregulated, and the people suffer much from malarial illness." [Zhouli, Tiangong, Physician of Illnesses]: "In autumn there are malarial cold illnesses," the sub-commentary explaining that autumn qi gradually wanes while yin qi is at its height, so that fire injures metal and cold and heat are combined. [Zhengzi Tong] enumerates eight kinds — wind, cold, summer-heat, heat, damp, food, miasma, and heteropathic — and notes that chronic malaria with a mass in the abdomen is called the "malaria mother," that cold without fever is female malaria, fever without chill male malaria, attacks without fixed period ghost malaria, cold before fever cold malaria, fever before cold warm malaria, and fever without chill dan malaria, that is, spleen malaria; all arise from phlegm lodging in the middle burner and disharmony of spleen and stomach. See the Malarial Discourse of the Lingshu Jing.
