癯: A modern dictionary entry defines 癯 (qú) as thin, as in 清癯 "spare and clear" and 癯瘦 "gaunt." [note: source text partially corrupted]
癰: A swelling; an abscess. [Guangyun]: "an abscess or boil." [Shiming]: "Yong means 'to block up'; when qi is blocked and congested, it becomes encysted and bursts." [Zhengzi Tong]: "a malignant sore." Named forms are listed — blemish-abscess, red spreading abscess, hare-bite, the four excesses, virulent abscess, and sloughing abscess — all arising from qi and blood retained and stagnating, so that the nutritive and defensive influences fail to circulate. [Hou Hanshu, Treatise on the Calendar]: "At the Awakening of Insects the gnomon shadow is eight chi two cun; if it arrives before it ought, many suffer from abscess, ju, and swelling of the shins."
癱: A phono-semantic character of enclosing structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
癶: The two feet treading apart. [Liushu Benyi]: "The two feet are spread, having something to push aside." The quotation from the Yuanbao Jing that follows is broken off and incomplete.
登: To mount a carriage; the character is composed of 癶 and 豆, depicting the form of mounting a carriage. [Jiyun]: "or written 僜." [Zihui]: "Deng and the deng of 豆豋, the latter written with 月 and 又, are to be distinguished."
白: The colour of the west; when yin is at work, the colour of things is white. The character is composed of 入 (to enter) joined with 二, two being the number of yin. [Shiming]: "Bai means 'to open'; like the colour when water opens [the day]." [Erya, Shitian]: "Autumn is the white storehouse," the sub-commentary explaining that when the qi of autumn is harmonious its colour is white and it gathers and stores. [Zhouli, Dongguan, Kaogongji]: "In the affairs of writing and painting, the west is called white." [Shangshu, Yugong]: "In Jizhou its soil is white loam; in Qingzhou its soil is the white mounded earth."
百: Ten tens; composed of 一 and 白. Ten tens make one hundred, and bai also means "white"; ten hundreds make one guan, and guan means "a strand." Xu [Kai] says that a strand (zhang) is, as one speaks of a zhang of a poem, and that a hundred is likewise a completed number; it is a compound ideograph. [Hanshu, Treatise on Pitch Pipes and the Calendar]: "It is ordered in one, harmonized in ten, lengthened in a hundred, enlarged in a thousand, and extended in ten thousand."
皅: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed on the signific 白 (white) with a phonetic element. [note: source text partially corrupted]
皇: Great; [Fengsutong] gives "Heaven." [Erya, Shitian, sub-commentary]: "To honour and lord over them is to call it august Heaven." [Shangshu, Dayu Mo]: "August Heaven favours and commands."
皋: Composed of 本 and 白. In ritual invocation one says gao, and in mounting to sing one says zou; hence both gao and zou take 本, and 本 means to advance. The quotation from the [Zhouli, Chunguan, Music Master] that follows breaks off.
皎: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, built on the signific 白 (white) with a phonetic element; it denotes a clear, bright whiteness. [note: source text partially corrupted]
皒: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
皓: The Four White-Haired Men of Mount Shang were white-headed old men. [Shiji, Hereditary House of the Marquis of Liu]: "Four men followed the heir, their beards and eyebrows white," and Yan Shigu's gloss explains that this is why they were called the Four Hao.
皕: A compound ideograph of left-right structure, formed by combining several components to express its meaning; it denotes two hundred. [note: source text partially corrupted]
皖: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
皙: A person of white complexion. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Zhao, 26th year]: "there was a gentleman of fair white skin." [Zhouli, Diguan, Grand Minister of Education]: "In the raised and low-lying lands the people are fair and lean."
皚: The whiteness of frost and snow. [Liu Xin of Han, Rhapsody on Fulfilling the Beginning]: "Drifting piles of snow, so white." [Zuo Guipin of Jin, Rhapsody on Parting Thoughts]: "The frost is white and lies along the courtyard." [Du Fu, Poem on Late Clearing]: "The cliffs sink, the valley is drowned, white and dazzling."
皤: The whiteness of old age. [Boya]: "white"; [Yupian]: "plain white." [Yijing, Biangua]: "Adorned and white," the sub-commentary noting that po is the colour of plain white.
皦: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed on the signific 白 (white) with a phonetic element; it denotes a clear, luminous whiteness. [note: source text partially corrupted]
皮: To strip and take the hide of a beast is called pi. The character is composed of 又 (hand) with 爲 abbreviated as the phonetic. [Changjian] objects that 爲 is far removed both in form and sense, and that the character ought to be composed of 又 and 尸. Xu [Kai] says that 又 is the hand, that while alive the hide is called pi, when dressed ge, and when softened wei. [Shangshu, Yugong]: "In Liangzhou the tribute is bears, brown bears, foxes, and wild cats, and woven skins," the commentary explaining it as the skins of four beasts woven with gold and felt. [Zhouli, Tiangong]: "The Keeper of Skins is in charge of gathering skins in autumn and hides in winter, presenting them in spring," glossed "with hair it is pi, with the hair removed it is ge."
皰: A sore that arises on the face. Xu [Kai] says simply "a sore on the face"; [Boya] gives "a disease." [Zhengzi Tong] explains that whatever suddenly rises like a water blister on the hands, feet, arms, or elbows is called pao. [Huainanzi, Shuolin]: "To burst a small blister and bring forth a boil or abscess." [Han Yu, Poem on Eating a Toad]: "Though the two thighs are long, what can be done about the chapped and blistered spine?"
皱: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed with the signific 皮 (skin) together with a phonetic element; it denotes a wrinkle or crease. [note: source text partially corrupted]
皲: The feet cracked. [Leipian] gives "chapped, cracked skin," and also "the hands and feet split and cracked." [Hanshu, Biography of Zhao Chongguo]: "The general's soldiers were cold, their hands and feet chapped and chilblained." [Tangshu, Biography of Li Gan]: "frozen skin chapped and chilblained," glossed "jun means frozen and split." [Jinhu Zikao]: "Jun-zhu, a frostbite sore."
皴: The skin rising in fine ridges; chapped skin. [Yupian] gives "cracked skin." [Liangshu, Annals of Emperor Wu]: "Holding the brush exposed to the cold, my hands became chapped and cracked."
皺: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, built on the signific 皮 (skin) with a phonetic element; it denotes a wrinkle. [note: source text partially corrupted]
皻: A compound ideograph of left-right structure, combining several components to express its meaning; it denotes a chapped or rough skin. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盂: A vessel for cooked grain. [Yangzi, Fangyan]: "Between Song, Chu, and Wei, a bowl (wan) is called a yu." [Shiji, Biographies of the Humorists]: "a single yu of wine." [Han Feizi, Waichu]: "The ruler is like a yu and the people are like water: if the yu is square the water is square, if the yu is round the water is round." [Wenzhongzi, Liyue] speaks of engraving upon plates and yu.
盃: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed on the signific 皿 (vessel) with a phonetic element; it is a variant of 杯, a cup. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盅: A vessel, and the emptiness within it. [Laozi, Daodejing]: "The Dao is empty (zhong), yet use it [and it is never full]," glossed as interchangeable with 沖.
盆: A basin; a bowl. [Guangyun] gives "an earthenware vessel." [Yangzi, Fangyan]: "From the pass westward, an ang is sometimes called a pen." [Liji, Liqi] speaks of serving in a basin, and [Zhouli, Dongguan, Kaogongji] records that "the potter makes basins holding two fu."
盈: A full vessel. [Boya]: "full, replete." [Yijing, Feng Tuan]: "Heaven and earth wax and wane, in accord with the times' increase and decrease." [Shijing, Qifeng]: "The cock has crowed; the court is already full." [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Zhuang, 10th year]: "When they were exhausted and we were full, therefore we defeated them." [Liji, Liyun]: "The moon is born, and in three and five days it waxes, and in three and five it wanes."
益: A compound ideograph of top-bottom structure, combining several components to express its meaning; it denotes increase or overflow. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盎: A basin. [Erya, Shiqi]: "An ang is called a fou," the sub-commentary saying it is an earthenware vessel that can regulate music and hold water or wine. [Yangzi, Fangyan] records that ying and jue are called ang. [Hou Hanshu, Biography of Pang Meng]: "he wore an earthen ang on his head." [Ancient Yuefu, Eastern Gate]: "In the ang there is not a peck in store." [Tanzi Huashu]: "Soup and ang cast into a well — thus is hail transformed."
盏: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed with the signific 皿 (vessel) together with a phonetic element; it denotes a small cup. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盒: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, built on the signific 皿 (vessel) with a phonetic element; it denotes a covered box or container. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盔: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
盖: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed with the signific 皿 (vessel) together with a phonetic element; it denotes a cover or lid. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盘: A tray for holding things. [Zhengzi Tong] describes it as a vessel for holding things, made of wood, or else of tin or bronze. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi, 23rd year]: "Then he presented a tray of cooked food and set it against the wall." [Shiji, Biographies of the Humorists]: "cups and trays in disorder." [Lüshi Chunqiu] speaks of merit and fame inscribed on plates and yu.
盛: Millet and panicked millet placed in vessels, for sacrifice. [Shangshu, Taishi] speaks of sacrificial victims and the grain offerings, the commentary explaining that millet and panicked millet are called zi, and that when placed in a vessel they are called sheng. [Zhouli, Tiangong]: "The Dian Shi leads his subordinates to plough and weed the royal field, in order to supply the sacrificial grain," glossed as the sorts of millet, panicked millet, rice, and grain that may be placed in fu and gui vessels.
盟: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed on the signific 皿 (vessel) with a phonetic element; it denotes the swearing of a covenant. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盡: Empty within a vessel; [Xiao Erya] gives "to stop," [Yupian] "an end," [Guangyun] "to exhaust," and [Jiyun] "all." [Yijing, Xici]: "Writing does not exhaust speech, nor speech exhaust thought." [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Ai, 1st year]: "In removing evil, nothing is better than to make a thorough end." [Guliang Zhuan, Duke Ding, 10th year]: "Confucius ascended step by step and did not finish a single step." [Liji, Quli]: "The gentleman does not exhaust the joy of others"; [Zhongyong]: "The way of heaven and earth may be expressed in a single phrase and be exhausted"; [Shiji, Book of Rites]: "Brightness is the exhaustion of ritual"; and [Xunzi, Zhengming]: "Though desire cannot be fully exhausted, one may approach exhaustion," glossed "to stop at what is fitting."
盤: A tray for holding things. [Zhengzi Tong] describes it as a vessel for holding things, made of wood, or else of tin or bronze. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi, 23rd year]: "Then he presented a tray of cooked food and set it against the wall." [Shiji, Biographies of the Humorists]: "cups and trays in disorder." [Lüshi Chunqiu] speaks of merit and fame inscribed on plates and yu.
盥: To wash the hands. [Zengyun]: "To pour and wash with water in a basin is called guan." [Yijing, Guan Gua]: "He washes his hands but does not offer," glossed "to purify the hands before sacrifice." [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi, 23rd year]: "he held the ewer and poured water for washing." [Liji, Xiangyin and Jiuyi] speak of washing and raising the goblet. [Weishu, Annals of Emperor Wu]: "When about to sacrifice he went to the washing place and put his hands toward the water without washing."
盪: A character traditionally classified as a phonetic loan (jiǎjiè), of top-bottom structure, formed on the signific 皿 (vessel) with a phonetic element; it denotes washing or shaking. [note: source text partially corrupted]
目: The human eye; pictographic, with doubled pupils. [Chunqiu Yuanmingbao] calls it "the envoy of the liver," [Hanshi Waizhuan] "the tally of the heart." [Liji, Jiaotesheng] speaks of it as the clear and bright among the qi. The Shuogua of the Yi says that Li is the eye, glossed as the trigram of the south, governing sight, and hence the eye. [Shangshu, Shundian]: "He made bright the four eyes," glossed as broadening the vision of the four quarters in order to decide the obstructions of the world.
盯: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, built on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes a fixed stare. [note: source text partially corrupted]
盱: To open wide the eyes. [Liushu Gu]: "One who opens his eyes and looks expectantly must be hesitant and not advance." [Yangzi, Fangyan]: "In Yan, Dai, Chaoxian, and the Lie River, the pupil of a black-eyed person is called xu," glossed "to raise the eyes." [Yijing, Yugua]: "Xu and yu — regret," glossed "looking upward." [Hanshu, Biography of Wang Mang] has "xu heng and a stern countenance," the gloss noting that what is above the eyebrows is called the heng, and that xu-heng is to raise the brows and lift the eyes.
盲: The eyes without pupils. [Shiming]: "Blind (mang) means dim (mang) — dim and seeing nothing." [Huainanzi, Taizu]: "The blind have the form of the eye but can see nothing."
直: To see uprightly. [Boya]: "upright"; [Yupian]: "not crooked." [Yijing, Kungua]: "The straight is its uprightness." [Shangshu, Hongfan]: "The kingly way is upright and straight."
相: The apocryphal text of the Yi says: "Of what is observable on earth, nothing is more observable than wood; hence [the character] is composed of 目 and 木." [Zhengzi Tong] adds that "Xiang is popularly written..."; the quotation breaks off.
盹: A modern dictionary entry defines 盹 (dǔn) as a very short sleep, as in 打盹兒 "to doze," 衝盹兒 "to take a nap," and 醒盹兒 "to wake from a doze." [note: source text partially corrupted]
盼: The surviving text opens mid-portion: "...pan, xi, and mian differ in sound and meaning. The Yunbu says pan is sometimes written mian, and the Jiuyao says pan is also the same as xi."
盾: A shield (fa), whereby one guards the body and screens the eyes; pictographic. [Shiming]: "Dun means 'to withdraw'; kneeling behind it, one avoids and hides away." [Shijing, Qinfeng]: "the joining of dragon shields," the commentary saying that a shield is a buckler, that dragons are painted on it, and that they are joined and carried to screen the chariot. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Ding, 8th year]: "the forest keeper flanked them with spear and shield." [Zhouli, Xiaguan]: "The Minister of Arms is in charge of the five shields," glossed as belonging to the category of buckler and shield. [Qiyu]: "Guanzi said: for light offences let them redeem themselves with a decorated shield and one halberd," glossed as stitched hide with patterns like painting. [Guanzi, Youguan]: "In arms the side shield is esteemed," glossed "placed at the side, hence the name." [Songshi, Bingnong]: "Yang Xie presented the spirit shields he had made." [Yuanshi, Annals of Shizu]: "The country of Maba sent tribute of bronze shields."
省: To examine, to inspect. [Erya, Shigu]: "to scrutinize." [Yijing, Guan Gua]: "The former kings thereby inspected the regions, observed the people, and established instruction." [Lunyu]: "I examine myself thrice daily."
眄: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes a sidelong glance. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眇: One eye small. [Shiming]: "When the socket of the eye is sunken and contracted it is called miao; miao means small." [Zhengyun]: "blind in one eye." [Yijing, Lügua]: "The one-eyed can see." [Guliang Zhuan, Duke Cheng, 1st year] records that Xi Ke of Jin was one-eyed.
眈: Looking close at hand while the intent is far off. [Yijing, Yigua]: "The tiger glares down," the exegesis describing it as the appearance of a tiger looking down.
眉: The hair above the eye. [Shiming]: "Mei means 'to charm'; there is grace in it." [Chunqiu Yuanmingbao]: "Heaven has the Sheti star, man has two eyebrows, and they are the outward..."; the text breaks off.
看: To gaze at; [Boya] gives "to look." [Wuzhi, Biography of Zhou Fang] speaks of watching for a gap.
眍: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
眔: The eyes reaching to one another; originally written 眔, composed of 目 with 隶 abbreviated, and all characters such as 鰥 and 懷 follow it.
眙: To look straight at. Xu [Kai] says "to look without shifting." [Shiji, Biographies of the Humorists]: "the eyes stare without restraint."
眚: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element. [note: source text partially corrupted]
真: A compound ideograph of top-middle-bottom structure, combining several components to express its meaning. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眠: To close the eyes. [Shiming]: "Mian means 'to vanish'; knowing nothing, vanishing and gone." [Yupian] gives "to sleep." [Hou Hanshu, Biography of Diwu Lun]: "he did not sleep the whole night." [Sanguozhi, Biography of Zhao Yun]: "The former lord slept in the same bed as Yun." [Liezi, King Mu of Zhou]: "In the ancient country of Mang at the western extremity the people neither eat nor clothe themselves and sleep much, waking once in fifty days; in the country of Fulou at the eastern extremity the people are always awake and never sleep."
眢: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed with the signific 目 (eye) together with a phonetic element. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眥: The corner of the eye. [Shiji, Sima Xiangru's Rhapsody on Sir Fantasy]: "the bow was not shot in vain; whatever it struck must split the corner of the eye," the Hanshu writing the character 眦. [Liezi, Tangwen]: "wiping the eyes and raising the brows to look," glossed "zi is the edge of the eye." [Lingshu Jing, Diankuang]: "Where the corner of the eye splits toward the face it is the sharp canthus; where it lies inside, near the nose, it is the inner canthus," glossed "the zi is the corner of the eye outside the pupil."
眦: The corner of the eye. [Shiji, Sima Xiangru's Rhapsody on Sir Fantasy]: "the bow was not shot in vain; whatever it struck must split the corner of the eye," the Hanshu writing the character 眦. [Liezi, Tangwen]: "wiping the eyes and raising the brows to look," glossed "zi is the edge of the eye." [Lingshu Jing, Diankuang]: "Where the corner of the eye splits toward the face it is the sharp canthus; where it lies inside, near the nose, it is the inner canthus," glossed "the zi is the corner of the eye outside the pupil."
眨: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, built on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes the blinking of the eye. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眩: The eyes having no constant master; [Boya] gives "confused, disordered." [Zhongyong]: "If he respects the great ministers, he will not be dazzled." [Hanshu, Annals of Emperor Yuan]: "Vulgar scholars love to approve the ancient and condemn the modern, making men dizzy over name and reality," Yan Shigu glossing "xuan is disordered vision."
眬: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed with the signific 目 (eye) together with a phonetic element. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眭: A compound ideograph of left-right structure, combining several components to express its meaning; it is used as a surname. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眯: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, built on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes the eye narrowed or obscured. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眳: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
眵: A sore at the corner of the eye; another account gives meng-dou. [Guangyun]: "the congealing of the eye's fluid." [Han Yu, Song of the Short Lamp Stand]: "Both eyes gummed and dim, the head white as snow."
眶: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes the eye socket. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眷: A phono-semantic character of top-bottom structure, formed with the signific 目 (eye) together with a phonetic element; it denotes fond regard or family attachment. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眸: The pupil of the eye. [Shiming]: "Mou means 'to cover'; it is wrapped and covered over." [Mencius]: "Of what is preserved in a man, nothing is better than the pupil of the eye."
眺: The eyes not upright. [Pan Yue, Rhapsody on Shooting Pheasants]: "He glances askance and peers to the side," glossed as "the gaze not straight, ever startled and wary."
眼: The eye. [Lingshu Jing, Dalun]: "The essential qi of the five viscera and six bowels all ascends and pours into the eye, making its essence. The nest of this essence is the eye; the essence of the bones is the pupil; the essence of the sinews is the black of the eye; the essence of the qi is the white of the eye. Thus the pupil and the black of the eye take their model from yin, and the white of the eye and the red vessels from yang." [Shiming]: "Yan means 'to limit'; the pupil comes forth limited and bounded." [Yijing, Shuogua]: "Xun, as regards man, is the eye with much white." [Shiji, Hereditary House of Confucius]: "his eyes were like those of a gazing sheep." [Jinshu, Biography of Ruan Ji]: "Ji could make blue or white eyes." [Nanshi, Biography of Tao Hongjing]: "The immortal writings say that he whose eyes are square lives a thousand years; in his later years Hongjing's single eye was sometimes square."
眽: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes a sidelong or affectionate look. [note: source text partially corrupted]
眾: Many. Xu [Kai] says that in the Guoyu three men make a crowd, the number being completed in three. [Yijing, Shuogua]: "Kun is the crowd," the sub-commentary explaining that it takes the earth's carrying of things, which is not one. [Shangshu, Tangshi]: "Come, you multitudes"; [Shijing, Zhousong]: "he commanded our multitude." [Hongshanzi, Sunyi]: "The few are those who are above others; the many are those who are below others."
睁: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
睃: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, its semantic component conveying the meaning and its phonetic component conveying the sound. The source preserves no further gloss.
睇: A small look of the eye. [Yangzi, Fangyan]: "In southern Chu, to glance sideways is called di." [Liji, Neize]: "In the place of father and mother, and of father's brothers and their wives, one does not dare to look askance," glossed "an inclined look." [Chuci, Nine Songs]: "Now she holds a glance and is fit to smile," glossed "the appearance of a slight sideways look." [Jiyun]: "or written 眱."
睏: The surviving text is that of the character 困: "an old hut; composed of 木 (wood) inside 囗 (an enclosure)." Xu Kai says that it is an old dwelling-place, and so its wood in time becomes worn out. [Liushu Benyi]: "Wood inside an enclosure — the wood cannot stretch; it is borrowed for the meanings of poverty and distress, and of illness and exhaustion."
睐: The pupil of the eye not upright; [Liushu Gu] gives "a roaming gaze," and [Guangyun] "a sidelong look." The entry breaks off.
睑: The upper and lower eyelids of the eye. [Beishi, Biography of Yao Sengyuan]: "The eyelid drooped and covered the eye, so that he could not see." The quotation from [Wang Shuhe, Maijing] that follows breaks off.
睚: The corner of the eye; [Leipian] gives "to raise the eyes." [Hanshu, Biography of Du Qin]: "to repay a glance or a glare with resentment," glossed "ya is raising the eyes and zi is the socket of the eye; it means that whoever raises his eyes to offend one will certainly be repaid." [Zhengzi Tong]: "Ya-zi means to offend the eye; in offending the eye, when one looks straight the eye points upward, and when one looks sideways the eye points to the canthus."
睛: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, built on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it denotes the eyeball. [note: source text partially corrupted]
睜: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed with the signific 目 (eye) together with a phonetic element; it denotes the opening of the eyes. [note: source text partially corrupted]
睞: The pupil of the eye not upright; [Liushu Gu] gives "a roaming gaze," and [Guangyun] "a sidelong look." The entry breaks off.
睡: To sit and doze. [Shiji, Biography of Shang Jun]: "Wei Yang spoke of affairs for a long time; Duke Xiao from time to time dozed and did not listen." [Hanshu, Jia Yi's Plan for Ordering the Age]: "generals and officers dozed while wearing armour and helmets."
睢: To raise the eyes; [Shenglei] gives "to look greatly." [Hanshu, Wuxing Zhi]: "The ten thousand multitudes looked up, amazed and startled for days," glossed "the appearance of raising the eyes to look."
督: To scrutinize; [Guangyun] gives "to lead, to encourage," [Zengyun] "to urge and press on," and [Zhengyun] "to supervise."
睥: A phono-semantic character of left-right structure, formed on the signific 目 (eye) with a phonetic element; it occurs in the compound denoting a sidelong, disdainful look. [note: source text partially corrupted]
睦: The eye in accord; another account gives "respectful and harmonious." [Boya]: "trustworthy"; [Guangyun]: "affectionate." [Shangshu, Yaodian]: "The nine clans were at peace." [Liji, Liyun] speaks of cultivating trust and harmony.
睨: A sidelong look. [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Ai, 13th year]: "I and the old man in coarse cloth looked askance at him." [Shiji, Biography of Lin Xiangru]: "holding the jade, he looked askance at the pillar." [Qu Yuan, Lisao]: "Suddenly I looked back askance at my old home."
睪: A compound ideograph of top-bottom structure, combining several components to express its meaning; it denotes the watching of a suspect by an officer. [note: source text partially corrupted]
睫: The hair at the side of the eye; the eyelash. [Shiming]: "Jie means 'to insert and join'; it is inserted in the eye socket and joins on." [Liji, Neize]: "If a pig looks upward and has crossed lashes, its flesh is rank," glossed "the eyelashes cross." [Zhuangzi, Gengsang Chu]: "Just now I saw the space between your brows and lashes, and thereby I have got you." [Huangji Jingshi]: "In the walking kind the upper lashes join downward, and in the flying kind the lower lashes join upward — their kind makes it so."

示: Heaven suspends its images and reveals good and ill fortune, whereby it shows things to man. The character is composed of 二 with three pendants, which are the sun, moon, and stars; one observes the celestial patterns in order to examine the changes of the seasons, and thereby to show divine matters. Xu [Kai] says that 二 is the ancient form of 上, that the left stroke is the sun, the right the moon, and the middle one a star, and that the vertical strokes take the meaning of their light hanging down; 示 thus concerns divine matters, and hence all characters for ancestral temples, earth altars, and spirits follow 示. [Yupian]: "Shi means 'to speak'; to inform a person of a matter is shi." [Yijing, Xici]: "Qian, being firm, shows man what is easy; Kun, being yielding, shows man..."; the quotation breaks off.
礼: Li (ritual) means "to tread" — that whereby one serves the spirits and brings down blessings. [Shiming]: "Li means 'body'; one obtains its substance and body." [Yunhui]: "Mencius said that the substance of ritual consists in the regulation and adornment of these two things; it is to grade and order them according to the benevolence and righteousness of the human heart, so that each attains its proper sequence — this is what is meant by li."

福: Composed of 示 with 畐 as phonetic. In Jia Yi's Plan for Ordering the Age, "distant relatives may wield great power, whereby they press upon the Son of Heaven" — here 偪 was erroneously written 福, and it is not that 福 and 偪 are interchangeable. The various rhyme books mistakenly take 福 and 偪 to share both sound and meaning and merge them into one, not having examined carefully the Mao Odes, the Yili, the Song of the Peaceful Age, and Ban Gu's Hall poem, where 福 is in every case read 偪 and does not agree in meaning with 偪. The Yunhui, under the character 逼 in the Zhi rhyme, notes that it is interchangeable with 福, and the Zihui says flatly that 福 is the same as 逼 — which is still more wrong.

稍: [Shuowen]: 'The gradual issuing of goods.' The [Yili, Pinli]: 'only the 稍 is received,' the commentary glossing 稍 as the rations of the granary, and the sub-commentary explaining that because they are issued little by little (稍稍), the rice granary is called 稍.

[Chunqiu, Duke Xuan, fifteenth year]: 'for the first time the fields were taxed by the mu.' [Zhouli, Tianguan, Sishu]: 'in all levying of taxes, those in charge receive the rules.' [Qian Hanshu, Shihuozhi]: 'There are 賦 (levies) and 稅 (taxes). By 稅 is meant the tithe of the public fields together with the income of artisans, merchants, and the officers of mountains and marshes: the 賦 supplied chariots and horses, armor and weapons, the service of soldiers and laborers, and the filling of the treasuries for gifts and grants, while the 稅 provided for the sacrifices to the suburban altars, the ancestral temple, and the hundred spirits, for the support of the Son of Heaven, the stipends of the hundred officials, and the expenses of all affairs.'
稗: [Shuowen]: 'A separate kind of grain' — that is, one that resembles grain yet is distinct, namely the plant 稊稗 (barnyard millet). Xu says: 'it resembles grain but is of another kind.' [Guangyun]: 'a grass like grain whose seeds are small.' [Mengzi]: 'if it does not ripen, it is no better than tares and barnyard grass.' The [Hou Hanshu, Annals of Guangwu] continues 'in the thirty-first year of Jianwu ...', where the source text breaks off.

稷: [Shuowen]: 'The sacrificial grain (齋),' chief of the five grains. Xu says: 'according to the Bencao, 稷 is 穄, also called 粢; the people of Chu call it 稷, and those within the passes call it ...' — the source text breaks off here.

稼: [Shuowen]: 'When grain comes into ear and fills out it is called 稼; the stalk and nodes are called 禾.' [Shijing, Binfeng]: 'in the tenth month we bring in the grain and the crops.'
稽: Xu's commentary: '稽 is the bending and halting of grain, and 尤 means the exceptional; where something is exceptional it must be examined (稽考), which is to delay and detain.' 穫: [Shuowen]: 'To reap grain.' Cutting grass is called 刈 and cutting grain is called 穫. [Yijing, Wuwang]: 'not ploughing yet reaping, not clearing yet opening the fields.' [Shijing, Binfeng]: 'in the eighth month comes the harvest.'

竹: [Shuowen]: 'A green plant born in winter; pictographic, with drooping leaves (箁箬).' The [Zhu Pu] says 'among plants there is one called bamboo — neither hard nor soft, neither herb nor tree; in small things it differs, being hollow or solid, in great things it agrees, having joints,' and adds that though bamboo is fresh in winter its nature dreads severe cold, so it rarely flourishes in the Nine Rivers but is abundant in the Five Ranges. The [Shijing, Weifeng] has 'the green bamboo, so luxuriant,' and the [Liji, Yueling] records that 'when the day is shortest, they fell trees and take bamboo for arrows.' The [Zhouli, Xiaguan] notes that the southeast is called Yangzhou, 'whose resources are gold, tin, and bamboo arrows,' while the [Shiji, Huozhi zhuan] observes that 'a thousand mu of bamboo by the Wei makes a man the equal of a thousand-household marquis.' Finally, the [Shiming] says 'bamboo is called 个,' and the [Huainanzi, Chuzhen xun] states that 'bamboo lives by water.'

竽: [Shuowen]: 'The 竽 is a thirty-six-reed instrument.' The sub-commentary to the [Zhouli, Chunguan] gives its length as four feet two inches, and the commentary explains that it belongs to the class of pipes, made of bamboo, with pipes of uneven length like a bird's wing — the bird being a fire creature and fire's number seven; since it is blown at the winter solstice, when water governs with the number six, six times seven gives forty-two, the length of the 竽. [Shiben]: 'Sui made the 竽'; [Shiming]: '竽 (yú) is 汙 (hollow) — its interior is hollow'; [Boya]: 'the 竽 resembles the sheng, with thirty-six pipes, the palace pipe in the center.' The [Yueshu] notes that in recent times sheng and yu have nineteen reeds and that, though different instruments, they harmonize, which is why the Zhou Guan places both under the Master of Sheng; the [Zhouli, Chunguan] says 'the Master of Sheng teaches the blowing of the yu,' and the [Liji, Yueji] says 'when the gentleman hears the yu and sheng he thinks of ministers who gather and accumulate.' The [Yitong Guayan] says that at the winter solstice one blows the pitch of the Yellow Bell with the yu sounding between, while the [Laozi, Daodejing] speaks of 'wearing patterned silks, bearing sharp swords, satiated with food and drink, with goods and wealth in excess — this is called thieving 竽,' glossed that the 竽 is the leader of the five notes, and as when the 竽 leads all music harmonizes, so when a great villain leads, petty thieves follow. The [Jiyun] variant that follows breaks off in the source.
竿: [Shuowen]: 'A bamboo pole.' [Shijing, Weifeng]: 'slim and long, the bamboo rods.' [Shiji, Huozhi zhuan]: 'bamboo poles by the ten thousand.'

笙: [Shuowen]: 'The sheng has thirteen reeds and images the body of the phoenix; it is the note of the first month, when things are born, and so it is called 笙 (shēng).' [Shiming]: '笙 is 生, to be born — it images things piercing the earth and growing.' The [Boya, Shiyue] says it is made of a gourd with thirteen pipes, the palace pipe on the left, and the [Baihutong] says the sheng is the qi of the Great Cluster (大蔟), imaging the birth of all things, hence its name. [Erya, Shiyue]: 'the large sheng is called 巢 and the small one 和,' the commentary noting that the large has nineteen reeds and 和 thirteen. The [Qian Hanshu, Lüli zhi] says 'the gourd is called sheng,' the commentary explaining that 匏 is the gourd, with pipes set in it and reeds fixed at the pipe ends, while the [Shangshu, Yiji] has 'sheng and bells in alternation,' the [Shijing, Xiaoya] 'sheng and chime-stone sound together,' and the [Zhouli, Chunguan] says the Master of Sheng teaches the blowing of the yu and sheng.
笛: [Shuowen]: 'A musical pipe,' also written 篴. The [Fengsutong] says that in the time of Emperor Wu, Qiu Zhong made the flute: '笛 (dí) is 滌, to cleanse — to wash away wayward impulses and bring them into correctness; it is one foot four inches long with seven holes.' The [Tongya] distinguishes the elegant flute from the Qiang flute, and Ma Rong's [Changdi fu] relates how the double flute arose among the Qiang, who cut bamboo before the dragon's cry in the water had ceased and found the sound similar, sharpening the upper hole to make it through and trimming the piece to serve as a holder; Lord Ming of Yi, who understood pitch, added one hole to the original four, and this added hole, sounding later, gave the shang note and completed the five tones. The [Xijing Zaji] records that when Gaozu first entered the Xianyang palace he obtained a jade flute two feet three inches long with twenty-six holes, which when blown revealed chariots, horses, mountains, and forests in ordered succession, inscribed as the Zhaohua pipe, while the [Youyang Zazu] notes that an ape's arm can serve as a flute whose sound is rounder than bamboo, and the [Yunhui Xiaobu] describes a yizi flute fitted with a separate mouthpiece.

笱: [Shuowen]: 'A fish trap (笱) made of bent bamboo.' [Shijing, Beifeng]: 'do not open my trap.' [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi, fourth year]: 'the diviner said: yarrow divination is short and turtle divination is long; it is better to follow the long one.' The commentary explains that things are born and then have images, and having images they multiply, and multiplying they have numbers; the turtle gives images and the yarrow gives numbers, hence images are long and numbers short — the images being the shape of a thing at birth and numbers the condition of its increase, so that number arises from image: the turtle shows people the original images of metal, wood, water, fire, and earth and is therefore long, while the yarrow shows people the secondary numbers of the seven, eight, nine, and six stalks and is therefore short.

簉: The character 簉 properly belongs with the grass radical: the [Wujing wenzi], in its grass section, glosses 䔏 as 倅, an attendant or deputy, while the Chunqiu tradition writes it with 竹. Li Shan's commentary on the [Changdi fu] understands '簉弄' as the Shuowen's 簉倅, and his commentary on a poem of Jiang Yan understands '步櫩簉瓊弁' as the Shuowen's 簉襍; from this it follows that the bamboo-radical 簉 of the Zuo Zhuan and the Wenxuan are corruptions of the grass-radical 䔏. The Shuowen entry for the grass form originally contained the five characters '一曰䔏襍也,' one reading being that 䔏 means mixed; where people today say 集, the men of Han mostly said 襍, and 倅 is written 萃 or 倅 in the Zhouli, likewise carrying the sense of gathering together. The younger Xu's note on 䔏 says 'grass growing in order,' evidently recognizing this sense.
簋: [Shuowen]: 'A square vessel for millet and panicled millet.' [Guangyun]: 'a ritual vessel for grain holding two pecks; round within and square without it is called 簋.' [Zhouli, Dongguan Kaogongji]: 'the potter makes the kui, holding one 觳 and one chi in height,' the sub-commentary noting that ancestral temples used wooden kui while this passage uses an earthenware one, for sacrifices to heaven and earth and outer spirits value plainness, hence vessels of pottery and gourd. [Yijing, Sun]: 'two kui may be used for the offering,' the commentary explaining that 離 is the sun and the sun's body is round, while 巽 is wood and wooden vessels are round, so that the emblem implies the kui too was made of wood. [Shijing, Qinfeng]: 'for me, four kui at every meal,' the commentary listing the four as millet, panicled millet, rice, and fine millet. The [Zhouli, Diguan] says the She ren provides kui and fu at all sacrifices, the [Yili, Gongshi dafu li] describes the steward opening the kui lids at the east, and the [Shiji, preface of the Grand Historian] notes that the Mohists, honoring Yao and Shun and expounding their virtue, spoke of 'eating from earthen kui,' the commentary explaining that they used earthenware kui.

粟: [Shuowen]: 'The fruit of fine grain.' The [Yunhui xiaobu] says the millet is the chief of dry-land crops, rice that has a husk. The [Shangshu, Yugong] mentions 'four hundred li — millet'; the [Zhouli, Diguan] says the Lüshi has charge of gathering the wild 耡粟, 屋粟, and 閒粟 — the 耡粟 being what the people produce by mutual aid, the tax-grain of nine households from a single well-field, the 屋粟 the tax of three households levied on those who have fields and do not till them, and the 閒粟 the levy of one household from idlers without occupation. The [Erya, Shicao] commentary notes that 秫 denotes glutinous millet, like grain in appearance but glutinous in the grain, used by northerners to brew wine, its stalk like that of grain but thicker.
粢: [Shuowen]: 'A rice cake, the same as 餈.' [Liezi, Liming]: 'they ate coarse rice cakes,' the commentary noting that 粢 is a rice cake, in flavor like husked rice but not broken up. [Yangzi fangyan]: 'a dumpling (餌) is called 餻, or sometimes 粢.'
粥: [Shuowen]: 'Originally written 鬻; the popular form today is 粥.' [Qian Hanshu, Annals of Emperor Wen]: 'officials in charge of granaries who were to receive gruel, sometimes with stale millet'; the commentary notes that 鬻 is the same as 粥, and Yan Shigu adds that the Yellow Emperor first cooked grain into gruel, that the Zhou called it 饘, and that Song and Wei called it 餰.

粮: [Shuowen]: 'Grain for food.' [Zhouli, Diguan, Linren]: 'in all state affairs of assembly or of military service he provides the grain and the food,' the commentary distinguishing: 'grain for the road is called 糧, that is, parched rice; food for staying in place is called 食, that is, rice.' [Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi, fourth year]: 'the Marquis of Shen said: supply their provisions and straw sandals,' the sub-commentary explaining that 糧 means rice and millet, food for travel. [Shijing, Daya]: 'then they wrapped their dried provisions'; [Zhuangzi, Xiaoyaoyou]: 'one who goes a hundred li spends the night pounding grain; one who goes a thousand li gathers grain for three months.'
粱: [Shuowen]: 'The name of a grain.' [Pianhai]: 'it resembles millet but is larger; there are yellow, green, and white kinds, and also reddish-black ones.' The [Yunhui xiaobu] says that 粱 belongs to the millet class and is the finest of grains, chief of the five grains, but that people today mostly plant millet and seldom plant 粱, because it exhausts the soil and yields little. The [Erya, Shicao] commentary identifies 虋 as red 粱 millet and 芑 as white 粱 millet. [Zhouli, Tianguan]: 'dogs are suited to 粱,' the sub-commentary explaining that dog meat is sour and warming while 粱 rice is sweet and slightly cold, the flavors completing one another. The [Guangzhi] lists 具粱, 解粱, and Liaodong red 粱, while the [Bencao] says white 粱 is sweet, slightly cold, and non-toxic, dispelling heat and supplementing qi, the best coming from the bamboo roots of Xiangyang, and that yellow 粱 comes from Qing and Ji. Du Fu's poem for the recluse Wei VIII has 'night rain cuts the spring leeks; the new cooking mingles yellow 粱,' the note observing that the Bencao praises its fragrance as surpassing other millets and that it is popularly called bamboo-root yellow.

The [Shiji, Hereditary House of Yue] tells of a man who looked up to the gall when sitting or lying and tasted it in eating and drinking, the [Qian Hanshu, Memoirs of Zhang Er and Chen Yu] speaks of a general glaring and his gall swelling, the commentary explaining this as the height of courage, and the [Hou Hanshu, Annals of Guangwu] laments that men no longer share one heart and gall to raise a name and achievement together.

The [Gujin Zhu] describes it as having leaves like the lotus but larger, wrinkled on the surface as if boiling, with fruit bearing awns and prickles and an interior like rice, able to relieve hunger, and identifies it with what is now called weizi. 花: The source preserves modern lexicographic material rather than classical commentary. It defines 花 (hua) as the reproductive organ of a plant, typically made up of receptacle, calyx, corolla, gynoecium and androecium, of various shapes and colors, generally beautiful and sometimes fragrant, and ripening into fruit after it withers. It further covers ornamental plants, as in flowering tree, flowers and grasses, and flower gardener; things shaped like a flower, such as snowflake, wave-crest, steel-flower, spark and cotton-fluff; and decorative uses, as in wreath, flower basket, festive lantern and float.

荤: The commentary reads: 'Hun: pungent vegetables. It generally refers to rape, toon, leek and scallion, garlic, and asafoetida and the like, which practitioners of the arts forbid, holding their qi to be impure.' The [Tangshu, Wang Wei Zhuan] records that Wang Wei and his brothers were all devoted to Buddhism and did not eat pungent vegetables. 荥: This entry preserves a long philological discussion of the character. The source reads '濘: a cut-off small body of water,' with the fanqie 奴泠 (nu-ling), and argues that this can prove the error of the present edition, which nevertheless still omits the character 滎. It adduces the Ganquan Fu's phrase 'the weak waters of Liang are dingying (濎濙),' with Fu Qian's note that east of Kunlun lies the Weak Water and that crossing it is like dingying, and Li Shan's quotation of the Zilin that ying means a cut-off small water; it concludes that dingying and tingning both mean small water, that 濙 is precisely Xu Shen's 滎, one form being a contraction of 熒 and the other not, and that whereas Tang stelae and Song woodblock editions mostly wrote 熒 for Yingze and Yingyang without error, recent times have uniformly written 滎. It rejects the Qianqiu Zhaji's claim, drawn from the Erya's 'a cut-off flow is called luan,' as absurd, explaining that what is severed in the middle is called jue, that jue means 'exhausted' and by extension 'extreme,' and that in the six script types one must not let the original meaning annihilate an extended meaning. It closes by noting that 陘 in Xu's book means a mountain's cut-off pit, which is not of the same order, and by suggesting that the 火 (fire) element in the Yingze form reflects the unfathomable appearing and hiding of the phenomenon, like the flickering uncertainty of fire.

菏: The entry preserves an extended geographical and textual discussion. It opens with the reading 'the river issues south of Huling in Shanyang' and argues that this is not the He marsh, the present text of the Shuowen having been wrongly augmented with the word 澤 ('marsh') by a shallow hand. It then traces Huling through the Han: the former monograph of the Hanshu records it in Shanyang commandery, Wang Mang renamed it Hulü, Guangwu and later Emperor Zhang restored the name Hulü, and the old city lay sixty li southeast of Yu Tai district in Yanzhou, adjoining Pei district in Jiangnan. The former monograph records under Huling the Yugong's words 'floating on the Huai and Si, communicating with the He,' with 'the He water is in the south'; the entry stresses that the citation of this Yugong passage shows this He water is not the He marsh of Yuzhou and of the Dao-Yan water. It then quotes the Shujing on the course of the Ji water as it divides at Chengshi, runs past Changyi, Jinxiang, Dongmin and Fangyu to become the He water, and passes south of Huling into the Si, with Li Daoyuan's comment that the Shangshu's 'floating on the Huai and Si, reaching the He' refers to this; it concludes that the old course described in these records is now mostly silted up and cannot be traced in detail.

虫: 'It is also called the fu (蝮); it is three inches broad, its head as large as a thumb; the character depicts its coiled form. Creatures of the smallest size — some walking, some hairy, some shelled, some scaled — take the insect as their image, and all characters belonging to the 虫 radical are classified under it.' The [Yupian] identifies the graph as the ancient form of 虺, with a note referring to the three-stroke section, and the [Peixi Ji] states that the 虫 of 'snake' and 'insect' is properly 蟲豸, which is incorrect. A note observes that in the [Shuowen], [Yupian] and [Leipian] the three characters 虫, 䖵 and 蟲 are divided into three separate radical sections with three distinct readings and meanings, whereas the [Zihui] and [Zhengzi Tong] merged the 䖵 and 蟲 sections into the 虫 section; although this loses the ancients' purpose in dividing the sections, it makes consultation easier, and the old arrangement is therefore provisionally retained. The [Liu Shu Zheng E]'s view that 虫 is simply an abbreviated form of 蟲 is, however, a great error.

The sub-commentary explains that 螘 is the general name: the large ones are separately called 蚍蜉, popularly known as 馬蚍蜉 (horse-ant), while the small ones are simply called 螘; the people of Qi call them 螘蛘, and the [Fangyan] records that between Qi and Lu the 蚍蜉 is called 蚼蟓, between the southwestern regions of Liang and Yi it is called 元蚼, and in Yan it is called 蛾蛘. Their earthen mounds are called 坻 or 垤. The large, red, mottled kind is named 蠪, also called 朾螘, and those that have wings and fly are named — (the passage breaks off here).

The [Zhuangzi], 'Tian Yun' chapter: "When mosquitoes and gadflies sting the skin, one cannot sleep the whole night through."

Zuo Si's 'Rhapsody on the Capital of Wu': "The pearl-bearing womb of mussel and clam waxes and wanes with the moon." The [Shiyi Ji] records that by the shaded spring north of Cold Mountain there are black mussels that fly to and fro.

The [Bencao] records that the earthworm, also called 曲蟺 or 土龍, is used in medicine, and that a white neck marks an old one. The [Erya] calls it 螼螾, and the people of Ba call it 朐䏰. The [Xu Bowu Zhi] says the earthworm chants long within the ground, and in Jiangdong it is called the "singing girl." 蛄: The mole cricket. Yang Xiong's [Fangyan] states that 螻螲 is what is called the 螻蛄. The [Bencao] says it is also called 天螻 or 仙蛄; it dwells in burrows in the earth and has short wings and four legs. The male is a good singer and flies, while the female has a large belly and small wings and flies poorly; it feeds on wind and earth, and is fond of coming to lamplight. The sub-commentary to the [Erya] says that Cai Yong identified the 鼫鼠 with the mole cricket.
蛆: The brood of the fly, a worm found in meat. The [Bencao]: "The maggot is the offspring of the fly; it is generated wherever things rot and stink." The [Beishi], 'Biography of Zhen Chen': "When Zhen Chen had once received office, all his guests assembled, but Xing Luan arrived late. Chen said to Luan, 'Where have you been letting your maggots out, that you only show your face here tonight?'"
蛇: [Shuowen], under the head character 它 (the original form of 蛇): "它 is made from 虫 and lengthened, depicting a body bent and coiled with a drooping tail. In high antiquity, when people dwelt among the grass and dreaded 它, they therefore asked one another, 'Have you suffered no 它 (harm)?' All characters of the 它 class follow 它." Pronounced with the fanqie 託何切; your servant Xu Xuan and others note: "The popular reading now uses 食遮切." The [Peixi] remarks: "The character 蛇 is formed from 也; this is an error." Structurally a left-right phono-semantic compound (形声).

蛊: 蠱 means worms in the belly, referring to the working of insect poison. The five characters that follow are probably a silent gloss. Gu Yewang's [Yudi Zhi] says: "A host puts it into food and drink to kill a person, and the victim does not notice." The character is a compound ideograph: it places worms (蟲) in a vessel for food and drink (皿).

蛎: Written as 蠇; a kind of mussel. It resembles the 螊 but is slightly larger, comes from the sea, and people now eat it. The [Leipian] says that a certain carved creature turns into a 蠇 at a hundred years. The [Guangyun]: "It is the 牡蠣 (oyster)." The [Youyang Zazu] notes that the 牡 in 牡蠣 does not mean "male"; among shelled creatures only the oyster is formed from salt water. The [Bencao] says they are found everywhere along the seashore, growing attached to rocks and piled together like rooms, whence they are called 蠣房, while the people of Jin'an call them 蠔莆. 蛙: A kind of frog or toad. The [Bencao]: "They are now found everywhere; it resembles the toad but has a blue-green back, a pointed mouth, and a slender belly, and is popularly called the green frog. There are also those with yellow lines on the back, called the gold-line frog." The [Yinwenzi], 'Dadao' chapter, upper: "Meeting an angry frog on the road, he bowed from the carriage crossbar." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Wuxing Zhi': "In the autumn of the fifth year of Yuanding under Emperor Wu, frogs and toads fought in troops."
蛛: The spider; originally written 鼄. The [Tangyun]: "䵹鼄, the net-worm." The [Zishuo] says: "It spreads a net on one side, and only after a thing touches it does it put it to death (誅); it is one that understands the meaning of 誅." The modern form is 蛛. The sub-commentary to the [Erya]: "蟗 is another name for 䵹鼄, also called 鼄蝥; in Jiangdong it is now called 蝃蝥." The [Shuowen] calls it 鼄蝥, "the net-weaving 鼄蝥." Yang Xiong's [Fangyan]: "West of the pass, between Qin and Jin it is called 鼄蝥; east of the pass, in the region of Zhao and Wei it is called 䵹鼄, or else 蠾 — (the passage breaks off here)."
蛜: Written 蛜委; it is the 鼠婦 (woodlouse). It is interchangeable with 伊. The [Shijing], 'Bin Feng': "The 伊威 (woodlice) are in the room." Han Yu's poem: "The broken stove is covered with 蛜蝛."
蛞: Among the 附蠃, those that carry a shell on their backs are called 蝸牛 (snails), and those without a shell are the 蛞蝓 (slug). The [Bencao] gives as alternative names 陵蠡, 託胎蟲, and 鼻涕蟲 (snot-worm). Tao Hongjing says: "The 蛞蝓 has no shell and ought not to bear the name 蝸; the 附蝸 is simply the snail."
蛟: A creature of the dragon kind. Where there are three thousand six hundred pond fish, the jiao comes and becomes their leader, able to lead the fish in flight; when a fish-trap is set in the water, it departs. The [Piya]: "The jiao is shaped like a snake but has four feet and a slender neck bearing a white ring; the largest are several arm-spans around; it is born from eggs, and its eyebrows meet (交), whence the name 蛟." The [Shanhaijing]: "The largest jiao are a dozen arm-spans around, and their eggs are like one- or two-bushel jars; they can swallow people." The [Shuyi Ji]: "Tiger-fish that grow old become jiao." The [Youyang Zazu]: "A fish of two thousand catties becomes a jiao." The [Liji], 'Yueling': "In the last month of summer, the fishermen are ordered to attack the jiao." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Annals of Emperor Wu': "He sailed down the Yangtze from Xunyang and personally shot a jiao in the river, and captured it."

Xiahou Zhan's preface to the 'Eulogy-Portrait of Dongfang Shuo': "Sloughing like a cicada and transforming like a dragon, casting off the vulgar world and ascending as an immortal."

蜎: A worm of the well. It is to be feared that this gloss was altered on the basis of the [Erya] commentary; 肙 and 蜎 are probably ancient and modern forms of the same character. In the 'Shi Chong' chapter, 蜎 is explained as 蠉; 蠉 properly means the crawling of insects, and it was merely borrowed for the character 肙. Guo [Pu] says: "The small red worm of the well is called 蛣蟩, also known as 孑孑 (wriggler)." The [Guangya]: "孑孑 is 蜎." In the [Zhouli], "for a thrusting weapon one wants no 蜎," and the commentary says that 蜎 means "to shake," likening it to the way a worm in a well wriggles (蜎蜎). Mao's commentary to the [Shijing] says: "蜎蜎 is the appearance of a 蜀 (caterpillar)" — the 蜀 being the mulberry worm; this is the extended meaning. Nowadays such creatures breed abundantly in water jars, and popular speech calls them "water maggots"; their transformation is recorded in a character that is no longer legible.

蝇: A creature with a large belly. Lu Dian says: "The fly rubs its front legs together, with the appearance of one twisting a cord." The commentary: "The fly as a creature fouls what is white and makes it black, fouls what is black and makes it white — a figure for the flatterer who confounds good and evil." The [Shiliuguo Chunqiu]: "When Fu Jian was deliberating on a general amnesty, a great fly came in through the window and settled on the tip of his brush. 蝗: A kind of 螽 (locust). Lu Dian says: "The character 蝗 follows 皇; now on its head, belly, and back there are markings like the character 王 (king)." The [Liji], 'Yueling': "Locusts bring disaster." The [Wu Zhi], 'Biography of Zhao Da': "As a youth he studied under Shan Fu and mastered the art of the Nine Palaces and Single Calculation, so that he could reckon the flight of locusts and shoot at hidden things, never failing to hit."

蝤: The 蝤蠐 (a wood-boring grub). The [Erya], 'Shi Chong': "The 蝤蠐 is the 蝎," glossed as living in wood. The sub-commentary, citing the [Fangyan]: "East of the pass it is called 蝤蠐; between Liang and Yi it is called 蝎. The kind in wood is white and long, and so the poets used it as a comparison for a woman's neck." The [Shijing], 'Wei Feng': "Her neck is like the 蝤蠐." The [Piya]: "The body of the 蝤蠐 is plump, clean, and white"; the [Qibian] says, "The neck of the 蝤蠐, so graceful, fit to turn and look" — this is the reference.
蝥: Also written 蟊. It eats the roots of grain, and it appears when officials falsely seize the people's wealth. The [Shijing], 'Xiaoya': "And the 蝥 and the 賊." The commentary: "Those that eat the roots are called 蝥, those that eat the joints are called 賊." The [Zuo Zhuan], thirteenth year of Duke Cheng: "They led on our 蝥 and 賊 (vermin)."

蝮: A snake. The [Erya], 'Shi Yu': "The 蝮虺 is three inches broad, with a head as big as a thumb." The commentary: "Its body is three inches wide and its head as large as a man's thumb; this is a species of snake in itself, named 蝮虺." The [Chuci], 'Zhao Hun': "The 蝮 snakes are thick." The commentary: "蝮 is a great snake." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Biography of Tian Dan': "If a 蝮 stings the hand, cut off the hand; if it stings the foot, cut off the foot." Shigu's commentary: "The 蝮 comes from the south." The [Bowu Zhi]: "The poison of the 蝮 snake is most severe in the autumn moon; having nothing to sting, it bites grass and trees to release its qi, and the grass and trees die at once. If a woodcutter is wounded or pricked by such grass or trees, it likewise kills him." The [Bencao]: "The 蝮 snake is not long of body, with a flat head and pointed mouth and a red body with mottled markings; there are also blue-black ones. If a person offends it, it fastens head and feet upon him." Han Yu's poem: "When the 蝮 snake gives birth, its belly splits and there is no liver."

螟: A borer worm; it appears when officials secretly (冥冥) break the law. The [Shijing], 'Xiaoya': "Remove the 螟 and the 螣, and the 蟊 and the 賊." 蟲: Formed from three 虫 (insects), a pictograph; all characters of the 蟲 class follow 蟲. The [Da Dai Liji]: "Of feathered creatures there are three hundred and sixty, and the phoenix is their chief; of hairy creatures there are three hundred and sixty, and the qilin is their chief; of shelled creatures there are three hundred and sixty, and the divine tortoise is their chief; of scaled creatures there are three hundred and sixty, and the jiao dragon is their chief; of naked creatures there are three hundred and sixty, and the sage is their chief." The [Erya], 'Shi Chong': "Those with feet are called 蟲; those without feet are called 豸." The [Zhouli], 'Dongguan, Kaogong Ji, Ziren': "Those with armor outside or bones inside, those that walk backwards or sideways, those that move in files or in curves, those that sound with the neck, with the mouth, with the sides, with the wings, with the thighs, with the chest — these are called the small creatures, and are used for carving and polishing." The [Da Dai Liji]: "Twice nine is eighteen; eight governs wind, and wind governs insects; therefore insects transform in the eighth month." The [Xunzi], 'Quan Xue': "When flesh rots, worms come forth."

蟻: Written as 螘, it denotes the 蚍蜉, the large ant. In the [Erya], 'Shi Chong' (Explaining Insects): "The 蚍蜉 is the great ant." The sub-commentary explains that 螘 is the general name: the large ones are separately called 蚍蜉, popularly known as 馬蚍蜉 (horse-ant), while the small ones are simply called 螘; the people of Qi call them 螘蛘, and the [Fangyan] records that between Qi and Lu the 蚍蜉 is called 蚼蟓, between the southwestern regions of Liang and Yi it is called 元蚼, and in Yan it is called 蛾蛘. Their earthen mounds are called 坻 or 垤. The large, red, mottled kind is named 蠪, also called 朾螘, and those that have wings and fly are named — (the passage breaks off here).

The commentary: "The fly as a creature fouls what is white and makes it black, fouls what is black and makes it white — a figure for the flatterer who confounds good and evil." The [Hou Hanshu], 'Biography of Wei Xiao': "The flight of a gray fly goes but a few paces, yet if it entrusts itself to the tail of a thoroughbred it can outstrip the flock." Yang Xiong's [Fangyan]: "The fly is called 羊 in eastern Qi." The [Shiliuguo Chunqiu]: "When Fu Jian was deliberating on a general amnesty, a great fly came in through the window and settled on the tip of his brush. Presently a little man in black cried out, 'An amnesty is proclaimed today!' — it was that gray fly."

蠕: A fragment of commentary, apparently taken from a note on 臑 rather than on 蠕: "None of these readings can be made to work, and they are now corrected. Xu's book is strict about the distinction between things human and animal: the human limb is called 臂, that of sheep and pigs is called 臑, and this is the distinction. Among birds and beasts there are those that borrow the name 臂, as in the [Zhouli] and the 'Nei Ze,' where 'the horse's foreleg is 般臂' is meant. In Xu's book the wording was originally 'X says Y,' and transcribers have often altered it, so that the text has long been corrupted. Why does he not say 'the foreleg of sheep and pigs is called 臑,' but first speaks of the arm? It is to honor man: what in man is the arm is in sheep and pigs called 臑. In the ritual classics 臂 and 臑 are two terms, though in general the forelimb is 臂 in both man and beast, while above it man has 厷 and beasts have 臑. 臑 means 濡, and 濡 means yielding."

蠣: Written as 蠇; a kind of mussel. It resembles the 螊 but is slightly larger, comes from the sea, and people now eat it. The [Leipian] says that a certain carved creature turns into a 蠇 at a hundred years. The [Guangyun]: "It is the 牡蠣 (oyster)." The [Youyang Zazu] notes that the 牡 in 牡蠣 does not mean "male"; among shelled creatures only the oyster is formed from salt water. The [Bencao] says they are found everywhere along the seashore, growing attached to rocks and piled together like rooms, whence they are called 蠣房, while the people of Jin'an call them 蠔莆. 蠱: Worms in the belly. The [Tongzhi], 'Liushu Lue': "The method of making 蠱 is to place a hundred insects in a vessel and let them devour one another; the survivor is the 蠱." The [Zuo Zhuan], first year of Duke Zhao: "In the writing, 皿 and 蟲 make 蠱." The commentary: "皿 is a vessel; a vessel that has suffered harm from insects is 蠱." The [Zhouli], 'Qiuguan', office of the 庶氏: "He is in charge of removing poisonous 蠱." The [Shiji], 'Annals of Qin': "In the second year of Duke De, at the first fu, dogs were used to ward off 蠱."
蠲: The 馬蠲 is an insect. The 'Mingtang Yueling' says: "Rotten grass becomes 蠲."
蠵: A great tortoise; it makes sound with its stomach. The [Yupian]: "蟕蠵 resembles the hawksbill turtle but is patterned." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Liyue Zhi': "Leaning on the 蠵, it cuts harmony and spreads levelness." The 'Biography of Yang Xiong': "Seizing the spiritual 蠵." See also the entry for 蟕.
蠶: The creature that produces silk. The [Shijing], 'Bin Feng': "In the silkworm month they strip the mulberry." The [Shujing], 'Yugong': "The mulberry land was already given to silkworms." The [Huainanzi], 'Tianwen Xun': "The silkworm hangs silk, and the shang string breaks." The [Bowu Zhi]: "The silkworm transforms three times; it conceives before it mates, and those that do not mate still lay eggs." The [Erya Yi]: "As to the appearance of the silkworm, its snout is broad like a horse's and its color is mottled like a tiger's. The first brushing is called 蚝; it is swept with a feather, for the silkworm is still small and should not see the dew. Mulberry leaves are put in the bosom to warm them and then cut, and when they take in the qi, all noxious things are removed." The [Youyang Zazu]: "That which eats but does not drink is the silkworm."
蠹: A worm in wood. The [Zhuangzi], 'Renjian Shi': "Used for door or window it oozes sap, used for a pillar it is worm-eaten (蠹) — it is a tree of no use." The commentary: "A worm in wood is called 蠹."

衆: A modern dictionary entry: 衆 means "the multitudes, a crowd," citing the [Guangyun], 'Song' rhyme: "衆, many; three men make 衆," and the [Zhengzitong], 'Mu radical': "眾 is formed from a horizontal 目 together with 乑, meaning that the number of people is great; the transmitted classics and commentaries now erroneously write it 衆." It further records the sense of the agricultural slaves of the Yin and Zhou or of those who managed slaves, citing the [Shujing], 'Tang Shi': "Come, all you multitudes, hearken all of you to my words," and the senses "numerous, abundant" and "many," citing the [Shangjun Shu], 'Ruo Min,' and the [Zhuangzi], 'Qiwu Lun,' with its tale of the monkey-keeper. The [Tangshu], 'Biography of Huan Yanfan': "Li Chaoyin memorialized: 'Yanfan and the others fear being slandered and smeared by enemies; we beg to send a censor to verify the facts.'"
行: The walking and hastening of a person. The [Leipian]: "It is composed of 彳 and 亍." The [Yunhui]: "彳 is the left step, 亍 is the right step; only when left and right steps are both taken is there walking." The [Erya], 'Shi Gong': "What is on the hall is called 行; what is below the hall is called 步." The [Shiming]: "行 (to walk) is 伉, to advance with raised feet."

衔: The bit in a horse's mouth. It is composed of 金 and 行; 銜 is what keeps the horse going. Xu [Kai] says: "The horse's bit is what controls its going" — hence a compound ideograph. The [Zhanguo Ce]: "Leaning on the crossbar and curbing the bit, they traversed the world." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Biography of Zhang Chang': "To sharpen its bit and whip."

衹: A commentary passage: "There is no character 衹 [in the [Shuowen]]. The [Wujing Wenzi] inherited an error from the [Yupian], and so slipped once in a thousand considerations. 衹 was corrupted into 祇, and popular usage further made it 秖. Tang poets and writers used it, reading it like 支; nowadays it has been replaced by 只 and is read like 質 — this is the shift from ancient to modern. As for the [Shiji], 'Biography of Han Anguo,' which says '禔取辱耳,' this uses a homophone of 衹. Similarly the [Zhouyi]'s '衹旣平' is written 禔 in other editions with a different sense, but they are surely homophones. ○ Yan Yuansun's [Ganlu Zishu], stone edition, glosses 祇 and 秖: 'The upper, 神祇, has the fanqie 巨移反; the lower, 適秖, has the fanqie 章移反.' Thus the character 秖 arose in the early Tang and is presumably a Six Dynasties vulgar character."

裔: The commentary says: "裔 is the skirt of a garment; in the phrase 苗裔 (descendants) it takes the sense of hanging down. Note that a cape is called 裠 and the lower garment 下裠; here 衣裠 means the lower skirt. Hence the [Fangyan] and the commentary to the [Lisao] both say that 裔 means 'end' or 'last.' The [Fangyan] further says 裔 means 'ancestor,' which likewise refers to its remoteness; and again that 裔 is the general name for the Yi and Di barbarians, on which Guo notes that frontier land is called 裔. In the [Zuo Zhuan], the Marquis of Wei's divination text says '裔焉大國,' meaning that he bordered on a great state. Such is the meaning of 裔; to speak of a garment's skirt allows the sense to be extended, whereas if one said 衣裾 (the hem of a robe) how could it be explained? Xiao Xu says that 裾 is the edge of a garment; it would seem that in Xiao Xu's time the text read 裙."

襞: A garment folded or pleated. Xu Xuan says: "It is the division in the middle of a hide; a garment's pleats pile up like such a division." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Biography of Sima Xiangru': "Pleated and gathered, tucked up." Shigu says: "襞積 is what is now called a skirt pleat." Yang Xiong's 'Fan Sao': "When fragrant scents are fierce and none hears them, one might as well fold them away and seclude them in a separate chamber."
襟: The crossed lapel. The [Guangyun]: "The front lapel of a robe or jacket." The [Erya], 'Shi Qi': "The corner of a garment is called 襟." Qu Yuan's [Lisao]: "My lapels were drenched and streaming." 襦: A short jacket. The [Shiming]: "襦 is 耎 (soft), meaning warm and soft." The commentary to the [Jijiu Pian]: "What is short and fitted at the waist is called 襦." The [Liji], 'Nei Ze': "Clothing is not to be of silk, whether jacket or trousers."
襪: A modern dictionary gloss: 襪 denotes an article of clothing worn on the feet, citing the [Shiming], 'Shi Yifu': "襪 is 末 (the end), for it is at the end of the foot," and the [Jiyun], 'Yue' rhyme: "韤 — the [Shuowen] says 'a foot garment,' sometimes written with 衣." 西: A bird upon its nest. When the sun is in the west the birds perch, and hence this graph was used for 西, the west of east-and-west. The seal-script form is written 㢴, a pictograph. The [Qian Hanshu], 'Lüli Zhi': "The Lesser Yin is the west; 西 means to move west, the yin qi moving and dropping things, the season being autumn." The [Shangshu Da Zhuan]: "What is the west? It is the fresh region (鮮方); some say it is the region of inquiry, the region of questioning — the questioner being one who questions people's appearance."

覆: To cover over. The [Shijing], 'Daya': "The bird covered it with its wings." The [Liji], 'Tangong': "He saw something like a roof covering a summer house."
见: To see. It is composed of 目 (eye) and 儿 (person). The [Yijing], 'Qian' hexagram: "The flying dragon is in the sky; it is favorable to see the great man." The sub-commentary: "His virtue covers the world, and he is looked up to by all things." The [Shujing], 'Lizheng': "He clearly saw that the three had fine minds." The [Liji], 'Wangzhi': "One who asks about a centenarian goes to see him in person." The [Zhouli], 'Chunguan': "The Grand Master of Rites, by the rites of guests, brings the states into kinship: the spring audience is called 朝, the summer 宗, the autumn 覲, the winter 遇, the occasional 會, and the grand 同." The commentary: "These six rites take as their meaning the seeing of the king by the feudal lords." The [Shiji], 'Wudi Ji': "Shun chose an auspicious month and day, and saw the four mountains and the various herdsmen, and distributed the jade tokens." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Biography of Dongfang Shuo': "He had not yet obtained an audience." The commentary: "It means he was not recognized and promoted."
观: To examine closely. The [Yunhui]: "What is observed; also to display." The [Yijing], 'Guan' hexagram: "The great observation is above; compliant and penetrating, he observes the world through central correctness." Zhu's commentary: "觀 means that one displays something to others with central correctness and is looked up to by them." The [Shujing], 'Yi and Ji': "I wish to observe the emblems of the ancients." The commentary: "He wished to observe and display the regulations of ceremonial dress that serve as models." 觀 was anciently read 官; Lu reads it with the fanqie 工喚切. The [Zhouli], 'Dongguan, Kaogong Ji': "The officer of grain made a measure; when the fine measure was completed, it was shown to the four quarters." The commentary: "He displayed it to the four quarters so that they might imitate and copy it." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Annals of Emperor Xuan': "Displayed with precious treasures." Shigu says: "觀 means to display."
规: That which has rule and measure. The [Yupian]: "It is the instrument for making a circle true." The [Liji], 'Jingjie': "When the compass and square are truly set, one cannot deceive them with squareness or roundness." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Lüli Zhi': "The balance in motion produces the compass; the compass's roundness produces the square." The [Zhuangzi], 'Mati' chapter: "The round ones match the compass; the square ones match the square." The [Huainanzi], 'Shize Xun': "The compass is what makes all things round."

视: To gaze at, to look up at. The [Guangya]: "It means clear, bright." The [Yijing], 'Lü' hexagram: "Observing his tread, he examines the omens." The [Shujing], 'Tai Jia': "In seeing far off, one is clear-sighted."
觇: To spy, to peer. The [Zuo Zhuan], seventeenth year of Duke Cheng: "The duke sent a man to spy on him, and it was true." The [Liji], 'Tangong': "Excellent — how he spied out the state!"
览: To survey, to view. Kong Anguo's preface to the [Shangshu]: "Seeing the cumbrous text of the historical records, he feared that those who surveyed it would not be of one mind." The [Shiji], 'Annals of the First Emperor of Qin': "Climbing this Mount Tai, he surveyed the eastern extremity all around."
觋: One able to serve the spirits with fasting and reverence; a male is called 覡, a female 巫. Xu Kai says: "One able to see the spirits." The [Zhouli], 'Chunguan', sub-commentary on the office of the Shenshi: "The male, being yang, has two designations, 巫 and 覡; the female, being yin and unchanging, is simply called 巫 and has no title 覡." The [Hou Hanshu], 'Biography of Zhang Heng': "Some examine the words of the witches and wizards." The [Beishi], 'Annals of the Young Sovereign of Qi': "He trusted wizards and witches, and his prayers and exorcisms were without method."
觌: To see, to have an audience. The [Yijing], 'Kun' hexagram: "For three years he did not appear." The [Chunqiu], twenty-fourth year of Duke Zhuang: "The wives of the great officers had an audience and used silk offerings." The [Gongyang Zhuan]: "What is 覿? It means to see." The [Liji], 'Jiaotesheng': "One does not presume to have a private audience." The commentary to the [Zhouli], 'Qiuguan, Siyi': "A private audience is a private meeting." The [Yunhui Xiaobu]: "Towards a ruler it is called 覿; towards a minister it is called 面; 覿 is a face-to-face meeting. In loose prose 面 is also 覿."

觚: A wine cup used at the village drinking ceremony; another account says that a 觴 holding three pints is called 觚. The [Zhouli], 'Dongguan, Kaogong Ji': "The Ziren makes drinking vessels; the 觚 holds three pints." The commentary: "觚 should be 觶." The sub-commentary, on the regulations for ritual vessels: "The 觚 is two pints, the 觶 is three pints" — hence Zheng takes two pints for 觚 and three for 觶. The [Hanshi Waizhuan]: "Two pints is called 觚; 觚 means few (寡), for one should drink sparingly." The [Lunyu]: "A 觚 that is not a 觚." The sub-commentary: "The 觚 is a ritual vessel holding two pints of wine."

觞: When a 觶 is full it is called 觴; when empty, 觶. The [Yunhui]: "It is the general name for a wine vessel." The [Sanli Tu]: "All 觴 are alike in form, though they differ in capacity." The sub-commentary to the [Shijing], 'Zhou Nan, Juan Er': "One pint is called 爵, two pints 觚, three pints 觶, four pints 角, five pints 散; the general name is 爵, and what it contains is called 觴. 觴 is 餉 (to present)." The [Zuo Zhuan], second year of Duke Cheng: "He presented the cup of wine with a jade disk and advanced." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Waiqi Zhuan': "Pour the feathered cup to dispel sorrow." Meng Kang says: "The feathered cup is a 爵 made in the shape of a living sparrow, with head, tail, and wings."
解: To divide, to discriminate. It is composed of 刀 (knife) dividing the horn of an ox (牛角). The [Zhuangzi], 'Yangsheng Zhu': "Cook Ding carved up an ox." The [Zuo Zhuan], fourth year of Duke Xuan: "The cook cut up a turtle." The [Qian Hanshu] — (the passage breaks off here).
觥: Originally written 觵: it is a drinking vessel made from the horn of a 兕 rhinoceros, and its shape is curved and rising (觵觵), whence the name 觵. Xu says: "觵 describes a curving, rising appearance." The [Shijing], 'Zhou Nan': "I will pour from that 兕觥." The commentary: "It is a horn cup." The sub-commentary: "The [Litu] says the 觥 holds seven pints and is made from a 兕 horn; one account says it is carved from wood in the shape of a 兕 horn, so that where no 兕 exists wood is used. The [Hanshi] says the 觥 holds five pints and is used to punish disrespect: 觥 is 廓, for when a gentleman has a fault it becomes broadly (廓然) manifest." The [Zhouli], 'Chunguan, Xiaoxu': "He fines with the 觵 those who are disrespectful." The commentary: "觵 is a punitive cup; some editions write 觥." ○ Note that the Shigu says: "The 兕觥 is a horn cup," which describes its substance, while the commentary's "觥, a punitive cup" explains its use. Yet where the 'Juan Er' and 'Qi Yue' odes speak of the 兕觥, it is never for punishment; so the 觥 is a large cup that may sometimes be used for a fine, not one made solely for fining."
触: To butt, to collide. The [Yijing], 'Dazhuang': "A ram butts against a hedge." The [Qian Hanshu], 'Annals of Emperor Yuan': "Casting off ritual and rightness, colliding — (the passage breaks off here)."
