赓: This entry preserves a philological discussion rather than a dictionary gloss. Xu Xuan notes that current usage reads the character with the fanqie 古行切 (gǔ xíng); the writer argues that the Shuowen is not in error here, since Xu Shen treated the character as a compound ideograph composed of 庚 and 貝, the sense being that cowries alternate and are linked in succession. From the Tangyun onward it has been treated as phono-semantic with 庚 as phonetic, hence the reading 皆行反; but the writer observes that if the character really took 庚 as phonetic, Xu Shen would necessarily have placed it under the 貝 or the 庚 radical. The error begins with Kong's commentary, which explains 賡 by 續 (continuation) and so abandoned Xu's account, though the writer notes that explaining an old graph by a modern one is an established practice and that Mao's Shijing commentary in fact glosses 庚 as continuation, which is precisely why the ancient graph for 'continue' took it as a signific. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic by the later classification.

赖: To profit by, to rely on. Xu Shen defines it as to profit; the Leipian adds, 'one says, to rely on.' The [Shangshu, Dayu Mo] has 'for ten thousand ages ever to rely on him,' the subcommentary explaining it as what ten thousand generations constantly depend upon. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
赘: To pledge a thing for money; the Shuowen explains it as composed of 敖 and 貝, 敖 meaning, as it were, lending out cowries, which ought later to be reclaimed. Upper-lower in form, compound ideograph.
赙: To contribute to funeral expenses, that is, to help. [Yupian] defines it as to help with wealth at a funeral. The [Yili, Jixi] distinguishes gifts to those who knew the dead from 賻 to those who knew him in life; the [Gongyang Zhuan], Duke Yin, year 1, says that goods and wealth given for a death are 賻, the note adding that 賻 is like 助, to help, and referring to the note under 賵. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
赚: No annotation survives in the source for this entry. The character is left-right in form and phono-semantic in structure.
赛: To repay, to requite, used of thank-offerings and of competition. The Changjian notes that the vulgar call a sacrifice of thanks 賽神, and that the word is borrowed for competing in boastfulness; Han Yu's Chengnan Lianju has 'the sacrificial offerings are heaped upon wooden trays.' Upper-lower in form, phono-semantic.
赜: This entry sets out and discriminates the errors of vulgar writings that do not conform to the structure of the six scripts, treating 賾 as a loan character which should in general be used interchangeably with 嘖. The Jiyun notes an alternative form, cut off in the source. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
赝: Half-enclosing in form and phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
赞: To present, to assist; the Shuowen glosses it as to see, composed of 貝 and 兟. Xu Xuan's note explains that 兟 is pronounced 詵 (shēn) and means to advance: holding gifts and advancing, the officers assist him. Upper-lower in form, compound ideograph.
赠: To present, to give as a parting gift. Xu Shen defines it as sending off with things of play and delight; the Shijing (Zhengfeng) has 'with mixed girdle-ornaments she presented them to him,' the tradition glossing 贈 as to escort, to send. The [Yili, Pinli] records that the duke sent a minister to present gifts in the manner of the ceremonial gifts of the first audience, and the [Liji, Tangong] asks with what one will present another. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
赢: Profit, gain; the profit of a merchant who has a surplus. The [Zuo Zhuan], Duke Zhao, year 1, asks how one can be a merchant and wish for profit yet hate the clamour of the market, the note explaining that a merchant seeking profit cannot dislike the noise. The Hanshu (Shihuo Zhi) describes men who held their rare profits and daily wandered the capital, Yan Shigu explaining rare profits as surplus wealth and the gathering of rare things. Upper-middle-lower in form, phono-semantic.
赣: Left-right in form and phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
赤: Red, the colour of the south. [Yupian] gives 'vermilion.' [Yijing, Shuogua] says 'Qian is great red,' the subcommentary explaining that it takes the colour of full yang; [Shangshu, Yugong] mentions the tribute of earth of five colours, the subcommentary describing the altar of the Son of Heaven, five zhang square, with blue-green to the east, red to the south, white to the west and black to the north, covered above with yellow earth; and the [Liji, Quli] states that the men of Zhou honoured red, the note explaining that they took the month of the first earthly branch as the first month, when things sprout and their colour is red. Compound ideograph in structure.
赦: Left-right in form and phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
赧: To blush; the face red with shame. The Mengzi observes of a man that, looking at his countenance, he was all blushing, Zhao Qi's note explaining this as a red face, the look of a mind not upright. The Shuowen is cited for a variant, cut off in the source. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
赫: The appearance of fire-red; scarlet. [Boya] gives 'red.' The Shijing (Beifeng) has 'red as if thickly smeared with red earth,' the tradition glossing 赫 as the look of red. Left-right in form, compound ideograph.
赭: Red earth, ochre. The Hanshu (Sima Xiangru) describes a land of cinnabar, blue, ochre and white earth, the note explaining 赭 as what is now called red earth. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
走: Upper-lower in form and a compound ideograph (会意) in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
赳: Light and strong, of martial vigour. Xu Shen defines it as light and strong, having ability and strength; [Erya, Shixun] gives '赳赳, martial,' the note adding the look of resolute bravery. The Shijing (Zhounan) has 'the martial warrior,' which Zhu Xi glosses as the appearance of martiality. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.
赴: To hasten toward, to go to. Xu Shen defines it as to hasten. Xu Xuan's note observes that the Chunqiu Zhuan used this character for announcing a death, and that the vulgar writing 訃 for that sense is incorrect; the [Zuo Zhuan], Duke Yin, year 3, records an announcement made on the day 庚戌. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.

起: To rise, to stand up, to begin. The Shiming explains 起 as 舉, to raise, that is, to raise the body upright. The [Liji, Quli] prescribes rising when asking about one's studies and when asking for further instruction, and the Mengzi has 'rising at cockcrow.' Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.

超: To leap over, to surpass, to transcend. The Yangzi Fangyan gives '超, far'; [Boya] 'to ford, to cross'; the Shiming derives it from 卓, eminent, that is, raising the foot and having something to surpass; [Yupian] gives 'to go beyond.' The [Zuo Zhuan], Duke Xi, year 33, records three hundred chariots' worth of men who leapt up into the carriages; the Mengzi speaks of tucking Mount Tai under the arm and leaping over the North Sea; and the Chuci (Buju) asks whether one should rather soar aloft in transcendence and preserve one's purity. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.
越: To cross over, to exceed, to overstep. [Yupian] gives 'to overstep.' [Yijing, Xici Zhuan] says the things of the world are mixed yet not overstepping, the note explaining that each obtains its order and does not transgress another's; the [Liji, Quli] warns 'be careful not to overstep,' the subcommentary adding, be careful not to exceed. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.
趋: To walk quickly, to hasten forward. [Boya] gives 'to walk'; the Shiming explains that swift walking is 趨, deriving it from 赴, to hasten toward, that is, hastening to the place one is bound for. The Shijing (Qifeng) has 'how deftly he hastens and steps,' the subcommentary noting that 趨 is what is now a quick pace; the [Liji, Quli] rules that outside a curtain or screen one does not scurry, the note explaining that to walk stretching out the feet is 趨; and the [Erya, Shigong] states that the space outside the gate is called 趨. The Gujin Zhu and Lu Ji's Wu Qu Xing are also cited for a song in which the men of Wu sang of their land, 趨 there meaning a step. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.
趑: To walk haltingly; it appears in the compound 趑趄. Xu Shen defines it as 趑趄, to walk without advancing; [Guangya] as 趑趄, difficult to walk. The Jiyun notes a variant form, cut off in the source. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.

趕: The source for this entry is a modern dictionary extract rather than a classical annotation: 趕 (gǎn), the traditional form of 赶, means to pursue, to chase, the Zhengzitong (Zou radical) giving '趕, to chase.' It further means to hurry so as not to lose time, as in the Sanguo Yanyi, chapter 1, 'bring the wine quickly; I must hurry into the city to join the army'; to catch a conveyance, as in 'catch a train'; to take advantage of or coincide with, as in a Ming play's 'today I have this free moment'; to wait until, as in the Hongloumeng's 'a reply will come by evening'; and to encounter or run into. An enclosing compound, phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]

趣: Swift, urgent; also inclination, direction. Xu Shen defines it as swift; [Boya] gives hurried; [Guangyun] inclination. [Yijing, Xici] says that what changes and adapts is what follows the time, and the Shijing (Daya) has 'those on left and right hasten to him,' where the phonetic note gives the reading 七喻反, the tradition glossing 趣 as 趍, to hasten, and the commentary explaining that the ministers on either side all press eagerly at the business; Zhu Xi takes 趣 as inclination. Half-enclosing in form, phono-semantic.

趨: To walk quickly, to hasten forward; the traditional form of 趋. [Boya] gives 'to walk'; the Shiming explains that swift walking is 趨, deriving it from 赴, to hasten toward, that is, hastening to the place one is bound for. The Shijing (Qifeng) has 'how deftly he hastens and steps,' the subcommentary noting that 趨 is what is now a quick pace; the [Liji, Quli] rules that outside a curtain or screen one does not scurry, the note explaining that to walk stretching out the feet is 趨; and the [Erya, Shigong] states that the space outside the gate is called 趨. The Gujin Zhu and Lu Ji's Wu Qu Xing are also cited for a song in which the men of Wu sang of their land, 趨 there meaning a step. An enclosing compound, classified as a loan character (假借).
趯: To leap, to spring up. Xu Shen defines it as to leap. The Hanshu (Li Xun) has 'surging and leaping over the dark yin,' Yan Shigu noting that 趯 is the same as 躍; the Hou Hanshu (Ban Gu) has 'southward leaping to the vermilion bounds,' the note glossing it as to leap. Enclosing in structure, phono-semantic.

足: The human foot, described in the Shuowen as being below and composed of 止 and 口, Xu Kai's note explaining that the 口 depicts the shape of the thigh and shin. The Shiming derives it from 續, continuation, the foot continuing the shin. [Yijing, Shuogua] has 'Zhen is the foot,' the subcommentary explaining that the foot can move and act and so is the foot; the [Liji, Yuzao] requires the bearing of the feet to be grave, the note explaining that one should raise them slowly. Upper-lower in form, compound ideograph.

趺: The source for this entry is a modern dictionary extract: 趺 (fū) is the same as 跗 — the instep, the foot, or the foot of a mountain; also the calyx of a flower, the base of an inscribed stele, the posture of sitting with the feet crossed, and a footprint; it is further used for 俯, to bow down or lie prone. Left-right in form, phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
趼: A callus, a hardened foot; the Shuowen defines it as a beast's foot standing on tiptoe. The [Erya, Shixu] describes the 騉蹄 horse whose hooves are like 趼 and which is strong and good at climbing mountains, the note explaining that its hooves are like 趼 and sturdy, and the subcommentary glossing 趼 as level, the hooves being level and correct and so good for climbing. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

跂: To have extra toes on the foot; also to stand on tiptoe. Xu Shen defines it as a foot with many toes. The Zhuangzi (Pianmu) argues that what is joined is not for that a fusion, nor what branches for that a 跂. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
跃: To leap, to spring. Xu Shen defines it as swift; [Boya] gives to rise, to advance; the Liushu Gu distinguishes a great spring as 躍 and a small one as 踊, a 躍 leaving its place while a 踊 does not leave its place; [Yupian] gives to jump. [Yijing, Qian] has 'or leaping in the abyss,' and the Shijing (Beifeng) 'leaping and springing, they took up arms.' Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
跄: To move, to step briskly. [Erya, Shixun] gives '蹌蹌, to move,' the note explaining movement in awed haste. The Shijing (Qifeng) has 'how deftly he steps,' the tradition glossing 蹌 as the look of deft stepping. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

跎: To stumble; it appears in the compound 蹉跎, to miss one's footing. The Jinshu (Zhou Chu) tells of a man who went to Wu to seek the two Lu brothers and, finding Lu Yun, told him all his circumstances, saying he wished to cultivate himself but the years had already slipped away; the Chuci (Jiuhuai) has 'the steed lets down both ears as it stumbles on the mid-slope,' the note explaining 蹉跎 as to lose one's footing. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

跚: Left-right in form and phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
跛: Lame, walking unevenly. Xu Shen defines it as walking not straight, with the alternative 'the foot pushes it aside'; the Pianhai glosses it as the foot partially crippled. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
距: The spur of a cock. The [Zuo Zhuan], Duke Zhao, year 25, tells how the Ji family armed their cocks and the Hou family made metal spurs for theirs. The Jiyun notes a variant form, cut off in the source. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

跣: Barefoot, the foot touching the ground. The [Shangshu, Yue Ming] warns that if one goes barefoot without looking at the ground, his feet will be hurt; the [Liji, Wensang] mentions the mourning rites performed barefoot; and the Shiji (Xiao Xiangguo Shijia) records a man entering barefoot to make apology. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
跤: Left-right in form and phono-semantic in structure. [note: source text partially corrupted]
跨: To straddle, to step across, to ford. Xu Shen defines it as to ford; [Yupian] as to overstep. The [Zuo Zhuan], Duke Zhao, year 13, records that King Kang straddled it, the note explaining that he passed over the top of it. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
跪: To kneel, to bow. Xu Shen gives 'to bow'; the Shiming derives it from 危, peril, since with both knees resting on the ground the body is perilously poised; [Yupian] cites the Shenglei for 'to kneel upright.' The [Liji, Quli] rules that when handing something to a standing man one does not kneel. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

路: A road, a path. Xu Shen gives 'a way,' Xu Xuan's note explaining that on the road each man goes his own way. The Shiming derives 路 from 露, to be exposed, the road being the place men tread and where they are exposed to view. The [Zhouli, Xiaguan, Hefangshi] has charge of opening up the roads of the world, and the [Erya, Shigong] gives 路 as a highway, the note explaining a highway as a way and adding that a single-track thoroughfare is called 道路, a long way. Xu Shen gives 'to stumble, to fall,' with the alternative 'to leap'; [Boya] gives to rise; the Shiming derives it from 條, a branch, since as a tree's branches strive upward so does the leaper. The Zhuangzi (Xiaoyaoyou) has 'leaping and bounding east and west,' the Shiji (Sima Xiangru) 'the waves race and the foam leaps,' and Wang Bao's Dongxiao Fu 'leaping forth again.' The Leipian notes a variant, cut off in the source. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
践: To tread, to fulfil, to put into practice. Xu Shen gives 'to tread.' The [Liji, Quli] has 'cultivating the person and putting his words into practice,' the note glossing 踐 as to tread. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

踏: To tread, to stamp. Xu Shen notes that the character was originally written 蹋, is written 踏 in modern texts, and is also written 蹹. Guo Maoqian's Yuefu contains treading-song lyrics and treading-song ballads. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

踝: The ankle. Xu Shen gives 'the ankle of the foot'; the Shiming derives 踝 from 踊, since it sits at the two sides of the foot, hard and knobby, and is likewise named from its own shape. The Jijiu Pian commentary glosses it as the outside of the foot; the [Liji, Shenyi] prescribes that the sash and its hanging ends reach the ankle so as to answer to uprightness, the note explaining 踝 as the heel. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
踞: To squat. Xu Shen gives 'to squat.' The Da Dai Liji has 'dwelling alone and squatting,' the note glossing 踞 as to squat. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

踶: To trample, to kick. Xu Shen gives 'to kick'; [Yupian] gives to trample. 踽: Walking alone, solitary. Xu Shen gives 'the look of walking apart'; [Yupian] 'the look of walking alone'; [Boya] '踽踽, to walk.' The Shijing (Tangfeng) has 'walking alone, 踽踽,' the tradition explaining it as having none to be close to, and the Mengzi asks why one should walk so solitarily and coldly. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

蹂: Of a beast's foot, to trample the ground; the seal-script form is 厹, composed of 足 with 柔 as phonetic. [Boya] gives swift and to tread; [Yupian] gives to tread. 蹇: Lame, halting; also trouble, difficulty. Xu Shen gives 'lame'; the Shiming explains 蹇 as lameness, the infirmity that prevents a man from carrying out service. The Shiji (Jin Shijia) records that Xi Ke was hunchbacked while Lu sent a lame envoy and Wei a one-eyed one; the Hanshu (Xuzhuan) has a jaded, lame team; and the Zhuangzi (Dasheng) speaks of the deaf, the blind and the lame. Upper-lower in form, compound ideograph.
蹈: To tread, to dance. Xu Shen gives 'to tread'; [Boya] gives to tread; the Shiming derives it from 道, a way, treading with the feet as if along a road. 蹌: To move, to step briskly. Xu Shen gives 'to move'; [Erya, Shixun] gives '蹌蹌, to move,' the note explaining movement in awed haste. The Shijing (Qifeng) has 'how deftly he steps,' the tradition glossing 蹌 as the look of deft stepping. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.
蹑: To tread, to walk on; to mount. Xu Shen gives 'to tread'; the Yangzi Fangyan gives to mount; the Shiming derives 躡 from 攝, to subdue, that is, to mount upon it and make it submit; [Boya] gives to tread. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

蹯: The pad of a beast's foot; the Shuowen writes it as 番, a beast's foot. The [Zuo Zhuan], Duke Wen, year 1, records the eating of a bear's 蹯, the note explaining it as a bear's paw. The Leipian notes a variant, cut off in the source. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

蹲: To squat, to crouch. Xu Shen gives 'to squat.' The Hou Hanshu (Lu Gong) has 'squatting and lolling at ease,' and the Zhuangzi (Waiwu) 'squatting on Mount Kuaiji.' Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

蹶: To fall prostrate; one account gives to leap. [Guangyun] gives to lose one's footing. The Mengzi has 'those who stumble and those who hurry,' and the Zhuangzi (Renjianshi) 'to collapse, to fall.' Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

The 轀 was closed and the 輬 open at the sides, each a separate vehicle named after its function; later men used it only for carrying the dead and, doing away with one of the pair, made of the two a single screened carriage, calling it by both names together. 辛: Pungent, bitter; the eighth of the ten stems. Xu Shen writes that in autumn all things ripen and mature, that metal is hard and its flavour pungent, and that pungency brings pain so that tears come; Xu [Kai] explains this as a figure for things first meeting with cutting and regulation and so feeling pain. The [Shangshu, Hongfan] says that metal is said to follow change and that following change produces pungency, and the Baihu Tong explains why metal's flavour is pungent: in the west it kills and completes things, and pungency is what kills and completes them, just as among the five flavours it is pungency that brings about the harvest. 送: To send off, to escort a departing person. [Shijing, Beifeng] has: “Far away I escort him to the open country.” [Liji, Quli] states: “When an envoy returns, one must bow and escort him beyond the gate.”
适: To proceed to, to go towards. [Guangyun] glosses it “to go”; [Zhengyun] gives “to go to, to arrive at.” [Shijing, Zhengfeng] has: “She went to your lodging.” [Liji, Quli] says: “When about to go to a lodging, do not insist on fixed arrangements.”
逃: To flee, to go into hiding. [Shujing, Mushi] says: “Thus it was that throughout the four quarters there were many criminals who fled.” The commentary explains that these were men who had committed crimes and run away.
逄: The character is read páng and is used interchangeably with 逢 (féng), meaning “to encounter.” [Ganlu Zishu, Pingsheng] notes that 逄 is a vulgar variant of 逢, and [Jiyun, Jiangyun] glosses it as “to block, to stop up.” The entry then breaks off into an HTML fragment. [note: source text partially corrupted]
逅: In the compound 邂逅 (xièhòu), it means to meet or come upon someone. [Zengyun] explains: “To meet without prior appointment is called xièhòu.” [Shijing, Zhengfeng] has: “We met by chance.”
逆: To receive, to go out to meet someone. [Zhouli, Chunguan] says: “In mid-spring they played the Bin poems on the flute in order to receive the summer heat.” The entry goes on to cite the [Shujing, Lü…], but the text breaks off there.
选: An ancient character of semi-enclosing structure, a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) in the six-book classification. The source text for this entry is corrupted and no gloss can be recovered. [note: source text partially corrupted]
逊: To withdraw, to flee. [Shujing, Weizi] says: “The aged men of our house have withdrawn into the wilderness,” the commentary explaining this as fleeing into the wilds. The character is interchangeable with 孫 (sūn), so that [Shijing, Binfeng] has “the Duke's son, large and fair,” [Liji, Xueji] has “to yield in one's studies,” and the [Chunqiu, Duke Zhuang, first year] records that “the Lady withdrew to Qi.” [Jiyun] also records the variant 愻.
逋: To flee, to abscond. [Shujing, Dagao] speaks of “the ministers of Yin who fled and wandered,” explained as ministers who had fled and been scattered abroad. [Yijing, Song] says: “He returns and hides, with the people of his town, three hundred households,” and the Image text adds: “He cannot carry on the dispute, and returns to hide.”
逍: In the compound 逍遙 (xiāoyáo), it means to roam at ease, as if soaring. [Shijing, Zhengfeng] has: “By the river he roams at liberty.”

途: The source preserves a fragment of commentary on the waterways associated with this character. It discusses how the records say a river “enters the Sheng” while the [Shuijing Zhu] says it enters the Ruo, tracing the courses of the Sheng and Ruo rivers and their confluence, and concludes that the Jinsha River is the ancient Sheng River while the Yalong River is the ancient Ruo. The commentator observes that the Jinsha rises far away and after receiving dozens of large tributaries and countless small ones is unquestionably the upper source of the Great River, yet notes that this does not accord with the [Yugong] account of the source of the Jiang. He ends by admitting uncertainty as to which present-day county and river correspond to Mumi and to the Tu water.

逖: The source preserves a commentarial discussion of this character. It notes that a quoted poem reads 介逖 where the [Shijing] text of the Daya has 介狄, and that Mao's commentary explains the word as “far,” taking 狄 as a phonetic loan for 逖; it further observes that the use of 逷 for “distant” elsewhere is a case of semantic transfer (zhuǎnzhù). The discussion concludes that the reading preserved in the [Jiyun] is not to be trusted.
逗: To stop, to halt. [Yupian] glosses it “to stay, to dwell.” [Hou Hanshu, biography of Zhang Heng] has: “He halted at the rushing islet of Huayin.”
通: To penetrate, to reach through. [Zhengyun] glosses it “to pervade.” [Yijing, Xici] says: “He first made the eight trigrams in order to penetrate the virtues of the divine and luminous.” [Liji, Xueji] speaks of “understanding the categories and penetrating to full comprehension.”

逝: To go away, to depart. [Zengyun] gives “to walk, to leave.” [Shijing, Weifeng] has: “I will go away and leave you.” [Chuci, Jiuge] has: “We shall mount the chariot and depart together.”
逞: To carry through, to gratify. [Yupian] glosses it “pleased, gratified.” [Zuozhuan, Duke Yin, 11th year] says: “The spirits and ghosts have in truth found no gratification in the Lord of Xu.”

造: To accomplish, to bring to completion. [Shijing, Daya] has: “The young men have accomplished their work.” [Liji, Wangzhi] says: “Those promoted to study are not levied for service by the Minister of Education, and are called accomplished scholars (zàoshì).”
逡: To retire, to fall back. [Yupian] gives “to withdraw, to yield,” and [Jiyun] explains the compound 逡巡 (qūnxún) as advancing hesitantly and holding back from going forward. [Hanshu, biography of Gongsun Hong] says: “If the meritorious are raised and the unmeritorious lowered, the assembled ministers will give way in order,” the commentary explaining this as proper sequence. [Chuci, Jiuzhang] has: “I move on hesitantly, in order, and do not press the horses.”
逢: To encounter, to meet. It is composed of 辵 (chuò, motion) with an abbreviated form of 峯 as phonetic. [Zhengyun] glosses it “to come upon.” [Zuozhuan, Duke Xuan, 3rd year] has: “He did not meet with anything inauspicious.” [Shujing, Hongfan] says: “His sons and grandsons will meet with good fortune.”

逵: A road where nine paths meet. [Erya, Shigong] states: “Where nine roads meet it is called kuí,” the commentary explaining this as four roads crossing with further side paths. 逼: To press close upon, to approach. [Guangyun] glosses it “to press, to compel,” and [Zhengyun] “to drive.” [Jiyun] notes that it is sometimes written 偪, for which see the note under the 偪 entry in the human radical.

邙: A settlement on the northern hills of Luoyang in Henan. [Zhengzitong] notes that the tombs of the noble are mostly on Mount Beimang.
邛: The source preserves an extended commentarial discussion of this place name. It argues that the [Shuowen] and the Han geographical tables agree, and that a change of administrative assignment in the Former Han accounts for the discrepancy between the records; it then traces how the name Qiongcheng came to be wrongly written as Gaocheng, owing to Wang Mang's renaming of the place as Gaocheng. Citing the [Shuijing Zhu], the discussion shows that the Han [Dili Zhi] originally read 邛 and that a corrupt edition introduced the character 卬, leading Dai's collation astray. It concludes that the characters 成 and 城 are frequently confused in geographical texts and that the readings are hard to settle.

邰: The name of a state, enfeoffed to descendants of the Yan Emperor of the Jiang lineage. The primary consort of Emperor Ku was a daughter of the Tai clan, who bore Qi, the Lord of Millet, and he was enfeoffed at Tai. [Shijing, Daya] has: “Then he had his home at Tai.” It is also written 斄; [Hanshu, Jiaosi Zhi] says “the Lord of Millet was enfeoffed at Tai,” the commentary noting that 斄 is read like 邰. Its territory is identified with Wuzhangyuan in Wugong county, Xi'an prefecture, Shaanxi, though some say there is also a Wuzhangyuan with a Tai pavilion in Mei county, Fengxiang prefecture.

邸: A lodging for dependent states. [Xu's commentary] explains that the lodging where feudal lords stayed when coming to court was called di, the term implying a root or base, a place to which one returns. [Hanshu, Wendi Benji] says: “They proceeded to the residence and deliberated there,” the commentary explaining that the court lodgings of the commanderies and states, when in the capital, were generally called di; di means “to arrive,” referring to the place where one comes to rest. Hence people now call all inns di lodgings.

邺: A county name in Wei commandery. [Zhengzitong] notes that the present Ye city in Xiangzhou was built by Duke Huan of Qi.

郊: The countryside a hundred li from the capital. [Erya, Shidi] says: “Beyond the settlement is called the jiao.” [Zhouli, Diguan, Zaishi] distinguishes the near jiao and the far jiao, the commentary explaining that fifty li is the near jiao and a hundred li the far jiao. [Shujing, Feishi] speaks of “the men of Lu's three jiao and three sui,” the commentary explaining that beyond the capital is the jiao and beyond the jiao the sui; the Son of Heaven having six armies, there were six townships and six sui, while a great state had three armies, hence Lu's three jiao and three sui.

郡: The source preserves a note on the history of the commandery as an administrative unit. Under the Zhou system, according to the passage, the Son of Heaven's domain of a thousand li was divided into a hundred counties, each county having four commanderies, so that the county was large and the commandery small. When Qin united the realm it established thirty-six commanderies to govern the counties, and the Han followed this arrangement. From Sui and Tang times onward the institution was abolished and restored at different times, and under the Song, Yuan and Ming the name of commandery gradually fell out of use.
郢: The capital of Chu, ten li north of Jiangling in Nan commandery. [Gongyang Zhuan, Duke Xuan, 12th year] records that at the battle of Bi, Zi Zhong remonstrated: “Southern Ying and Zheng are several thousand li apart.” A note cites the [Liushu Gu] stating that Ying was the Chu capital and is now Jiangling county in Jiangling prefecture, that Zi Xi moved the capital from Ying to Ruo, and that King Kaolie of Chu moved it from there, at which point the text breaks off.

郯: A state enfeoffed to descendants of Shaohao. [Chunqiu, Duke Xuan, 4th year] records: “The Duke and the Marquis of Qi made peace between Ju and Tan.”
郴: A county name in Guiyang. The [Yitongzhi] records that the Han established Guiyang county and the Sui established Chenzhou. [Shiji, biography of Qing Bu] says: “Xiang Yu sent Qing Bu, King of Jiujiang, and others to attack Emperor Yi, pursuing and killing him at Chen county.”
郵: A relay station for carrying documents within the borders. [Guangyun] glosses 郵 as a post station. [Fengsu Tong] says that the Han changed the term you to zhi, a zhi also being a post station, established according to the distances involved. [Zengyun] explains that transmission by horse was called zhi and transmission on foot you. [Erya, Shiyan] gives 郵 as “to pass,” the commentary explaining it as what the road passes through.

都: The entry defines 都 (dū) as a great city or metropolis, as the seat of a state's highest administrative organs, that is, the capital, as “fine, elegant,” and as “all, altogether,” with illustrative phrases for each sense. 郾: A county name in Yingchuan. [Zhengzitong] notes that it is the old territory of the ancient state of Yanzi, now Yancheng county in Xuzhou, Kaifeng prefecture.

鄋: A state of the long Di of the north. In Xia times it was the Fangfeng clan and in Yin times the Wangmang clan. [Zuozhuan, Duke Wen, 11th year] says: “Souman invaded Qi,” the commentary explaining that Souman was the name of a Di state, whose people were descendants of the Fangfeng clan and bore the surname Qi.
鄒: A county of Lu, the ancient state of Zhulou, enfeoffed to descendants of Emperor Zhuanxu. [Xu's commentary] cites the Preface to the Mencius: “By the time of Mencius, Duke Mu of Lu had changed the name of the state of Zhu to Zou.”

鄞: A county name in Kuaiji. [Hou Hanshu, Jun Guo Zhi] states: “Yin was the former administrative seat of Zhang'an, in Minyue territory, and Guangwu changed its name,” the commentary noting that it was originally Huipu township south of Yin county and was established in the first year of Zhanghe under Emperor Zhang.
鄢: An ancient character written in a left-right structure, a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) by traditional analysis. Its transmitted gloss is corrupted and unreadable. [note: source text partially corrupted]
鄣: A settlement of Ji. [Chunqiu, Duke Zhuang, 13th year] records: “The men of Qi brought Zhang to submission,” the commentary noting that Zhang was a dependent state of Ji and that there is a Zhang city northeast of Wuyan county in Dongping.
鄦: The source preserves a commentarial discussion of this character, an old form of the name Xu. Tracing the [Shuowen] postface, which says that Lü Shu acted as a bulwark and was enfeoffed as marquis at Xu, the passage argues that the one enfeoffed at Xu was Wen Shu and not Fu Hou. Citing Zheng's commentary to the [Lü Xing] chapter and the [Shangshu], along with the [Guoyu], Mao's commentary, the [Shiji] and the [Qianfu Lun], it concludes that the states of Lü, Fu and Xu were all fiefs of the Jiang lineage, and that Fu Hou, Lü Shu and Wen Shu are one and the same person rather than two.
鄧: A state of the Man lineage. [Chunqiu, Duke Huan, 7th year] records: “The Marquis of Deng, Wu Li, came to court,” the sub-commentary noting that Deng lay in the southern region and belonged to Mount Heng.

鄯: Shanshan, a state name in the Western Regions. [Hanshu, Xiyu Zhuan] states: “Shanshan was originally named Loulan and was renamed in the fourth year of the Yuanfeng era.”

酉: “To come to completion”: in the eighth month the millet ripens and can be made into zhou wine. [Xu's commentary] explains 就 as “to ripen to maturity,” noting that mao (卯) is the gate of spring, when all things have come forth, while you (酉) is the gate of autumn, when all things have entered in, the single horizontal stroke depicting a closed door. [Guangyun] gives “satiated” and “old,” and [Erya, Shitian] states that when the Great Year is in you it is called Zuoe. [Shiji, Lüshu] places the eighth month under the pitch Nanlü and assigns it to you among the twelve branches, since you means that all things have grown old; [Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun] likewise says that the handle points to you, you meaning “satiated,” its pitch being Nanlü.
酊: In the compound 酩酊 (mǐngdǐng), it means drunk. [Jiyun] explains 酩酊 as “greatly intoxicated.” The Xiangyang Children's Song has: “At dusk he comes home sprawled in the cart, so drunk he knows nothing.”
酋: “To draw off wine”; the character is composed of 酉 (wine) with the water component appearing only halfway above, since when wine is kept long the liquid rises to the surface and the lees diminish. In the [Zhouli, Tianguan, Jiu Zheng] note on the second kind of wine, “former wine” is explained as what is now called you, a long-kept white wine, the sub-commentary explaining 酋 as also carrying the sense of “long enduring.”
酌: To pour wine and pass the cup. [Shijing, Zhounan] has: “I will pour out that golden jar of wine.” [Liji, Jiaotesheng] says “to strain and pour, using cogongrass,” the commentary explaining 酌 as “to ladle,” that is, when the wine has been strained it is ladled out to fill the sacrificial vessels. [Hanshu, biography of Gai Kuanshao] has: “Do not pour much for me, for I am a wine-madman.” [Ban Gu, Xidu Fu] has: “The wine carts speed along, pouring and ladling.”
配: An ancient character written in a left-right structure and classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). The source text for this entry is corrupted, so no definition can be recovered. [note: source text partially corrupted]
酎: A thrice-brewed rich wine. [Yupian] glosses it “rich” and “brewed.” [Zuozhuan, Duke Xiang, 22nd year] says: “He appeared at the autumn zhou offering and took part in the burnt sacrifice,” the commentary explaining that doubly brewed new wine was called zhou. [Liji, Yueling] says that in the first month of summer the Son of Heaven drinks zhou, the commentary explaining that 酎 implies richness and refers to wine brewed over again, the spring wine being ready only at this time. [Shiji, Xiaowen Benji] records the zhou offering at the temple of the exalted ancestors with the dances Wu De, Wen Shi and Wu Xing performed, the commentary citing Zhang Yan: “Wine made on the first morning of the first month and completed in the eighth month is called zhou; zhou implies purity.”
酏: A wine made from millet, or alternatively “sweet.” An editorial note observes that the [Shuowen] glosses it as millet wine and the [Yupian] as rice wine, both referring to what is now called congee, and that a careful examination of the [Neize] chapter and the [Zhouli] shows no case in which it is glossed simply as “wine.”
酐: An ancient character written with a left-right structure and classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) in the six-book system. No gloss for it survives in the transmitted source text.
酒: “To bring to completion,” since wine brings human nature's good and evil to full expression; alternatively “to make,” as that by which good and ill fortune are made. [Shiming] explains 酒 as 酉, since it is brewed from rice and yeast and its liquid grows mellow and its flavor fine with age; it is also explained as 踧 (“to urge”), because whether able or not, people press one another to drink.
酕: An ancient character of left-right structure, classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). The transmitted source text preserves no gloss for it.
酖: To take pleasure in wine. [Xu's commentary] explains it as the appearance of being at ease and happy in drinking. [Guangyun] glosses it as “addicted to wine.”

酝: To brew, to ferment. [Yupian] glosses it “to brew wine.” [Zhang Heng, Nandu Fu] says: “Of wines there are the nine-times brewed and the sweet mead, the ten-day vintage and the doubly clear,” the commentary explaining that “nine-times brewed” and “ten-day” are names of wines taken from their brewing methods. [Wang Sengda, replying to Yan Yannian] has: “The spring brew is at times offered and poured.”

酢: Sour, a synonym of 醶. [Xu's commentary] notes that people nowadays use this character for the “toast and reply” word in zǔchóu and conversely use 醋 for the sour-wine character, a change handed down by vulgar usage. [Yupian] glosses it “sour.” The [Jijiu Pian] has: “Sour, salty, tart and insipid are distinguished, the turbid and the clear.” [Ma Dibo, Fengshan Ji] mentions “tart pears and sour jujubes,” and the [Suishu, Ku Li Zhuan] records a Chang'an saying: “Better to drink three pints of vinegar than to meet Cui Hongdu.”
酣: The pleasure of wine. [Xu's commentary] explains it as drinking to satisfaction, and [Yupian] as enjoying wine without becoming drunk. [Shujing, Yixun] says: “To sing songs of revelry in the chamber,” the commentary explaining that delighting in wine is called han. The [Zhanguo Ce] records that Lord Pingyuan set out wine, and when the drinking was at its height he rose and stepped forward to offer a thousand pieces of gold as a birthday gift for Lu Lian. The [Yunhui] notes that the popular reading han (呼甘切) is incorrect.
酤: A wine made overnight. [Xu's commentary] explains it as wine made in a single night and ready the next day, like what is now called “cock-crow wine.”

酪: A milk drink. [Yupian] explains it as a liquid made from milk, and [Shiming] explains 酪 as 澤 (“moistening”), since milk made into liquid makes people plump and glossy. [Liji, Liyun] mentions “making li and luo,” the commentary explaining that these were steamed and fermented and that luo was a sour fermented preparation. [Hanshu, Shihuo Zhi] records that officials were sent out to teach the people to boil milk into luo, Ru Chun's commentary explaining this as making things like apricot luo. [Li Ling, reply to Su Wu] speaks of “rank meat and luo milk, to fill…,” at which point the passage breaks off.

酲: Suffering from wine; alternatively, to awake from drunkenness. [Yupian] glosses it as “drunk but not yet sober.” [Shijing, Xiaoya] has: “My sorrowful heart is as if sick with wine,” the commentary explaining that being ill from wine is called cheng. [Hanshu, Liyue Zhi] speaks of “a great goblet of sugarcane juice to resolve the morning's cheng,” the commentary citing Ying Shao: “Cheng means illness, xi means to dispel; the sugarcane juice can dispel the morning-after sickness.” [Zhang Heng, Nandu Fu] has: “Its sweetness is not cloying; one is tipsy but not sick.”

酸: Sour. East of the Pass people call sour wine suan. [Guangyun] glosses it as vinegar. [Shujing, Hongfan] says: “The crooked and the straight produce sourness,” and [Liji, Yueling] says that in the first month of spring the flavor is sour. [Zhouli, Tianguan, Yangyi] states: “In all medicines, the sour nourishes the bones,” the commentary explaining that sourness is the flavor of wood and that a tree's root standing in the earth resembles bone. [Hanshu, Baiguan Gongqing Biao] records that Ren Yueren, Marquis of Guang'an, was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies and was condemned because the wine in the temple had turned sour.
酹: A libation poured out in sacrifice. [Yupian] explains it as offering wine to the earth, and [Guangyun] as pouring wine onto the ground. The entry goes on to cite the [Hou Hanshu] biography of Qiao…, where the text breaks off.
酽: Originally written 醶; a sour drink. [Guangyun] explains it as the rich flavor of wine or vinegar, and [Zengyun] as “strong, thick.”
酾: To strain wine. [Xu's commentary] explains it as straining out, like sifting. [Shijing, Xiaoya] has: “The strained wine is fine,” the commentary explaining that straining with a basket is called shi and with a marsh-grass filter is called xu; the [Shiwen] explains it as using a bamboo basket, at which point the text breaks off.
酿: To ferment; making wine is called niang. [Guangyun] glosses it as “to brew wine.” [Shiji, biography of Lord Mengchang] says: “He then brewed much wine and bought fat cattle,” and the [Huozhi Zhuan] says that in a large city a wine seller might brew a thousand batches in a year. [Hanshu, Shihuo Zhi] states that one brewing used two hu of coarse rice and one hu of yeast, yielding six hu six dou of finished wine.
醃: The entry gives the reading yān and states that the character is used for 腌 (yān), to salt or pickle. The remainder of the text is scraper residue. [note: source text partially corrupted]
醄: An ancient character of left-right structure, classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). No gloss for it survives in the transmitted source text.
醅: A left-right structure character and a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) by traditional analysis. The source entry is corrupted and yields no readable definition. [note: source text partially corrupted]
醇: Unwatered wine. [Hanshu, biography of Cao Shen] says: “Those who came all wished to speak, and when they arrived Shen would give them rich wine to drink,” the commentary explaining that unwatered wine means thick, full-bodied wine. [Hou Hanshu, biography of Liu Penzi] says: “He then brewed more rich wine.”
醉: “Drunk”: the word is explained by 卒, meaning to finish one's measure without going so far as disorder; an alternative explanation is 潰 (“to break down”). [Zhengzitong] objects that drunkenness invariably damages virtue and ruins deportment, as the [Jiugao] and [Binyan] chapters set out in detail, and that no one who is drunk can finish his measure without disorder. It therefore concludes that the [Shuowen] explanation built on 卒 is mistaken.
醋: For a guest to pour wine for his host. [Xu's commentary] notes that the popular reading cānggùqiè and the confusion with 酢 are incorrect. [Yupian] explains it as “to requite”: offering wine to a guest is called xian, and the guest's reply to the host is called zuo, now pronounced cuò. [Yili, Shisheng Kuishi Li] says: “The invocator poured and received the impersonator of the dead, and the impersonator poured for the host,” the commentary noting that in the modern text this zuo is written 酢.
醌: An ancient character written in a left-right structure and a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) by traditional analysis. No gloss for it survives in the transmitted source text.
醍: Clear wine. [Yupian] explains it as the red color of wine. [Liji, Liyun] says: “The millet and the ti wine are in the hall,” the commentary explaining that the wine when finished has a reddish-crimson color.
醐: In the compound 醍醐 (tíhú), the finest part of milk products. [Guangyun] explains it as a kind of butter, and [Jiyun] as the essence of butter. For related details see the note under 醍. The [Leipian] gives a variant form, at which point the text breaks off.
醑: An ancient character of left-right structure, classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). The transmitted source text preserves no gloss for it.
醒: To sober up, to shake off drunkenness. [Zuozhuan, Duke Xi, 23rd year] records: “Sobering up, he drove off Zi Fan with a spear.” [Hanshu, biography of Gai Kuanshao] says: “Cigong was mad even when sober; why must it have been the wine?” [Chuci, Yufu] has: “The crowd are all drunk; I alone am sober.”
醚: An ancient character written with a left-right structure and classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) in the six-book system. No gloss for it survives in the transmitted source text.
醛: An ancient character written with a left-right structure, classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). No gloss for it survives in the transmitted source text.
醞: To brew, to ferment wine. [Yupian] glosses it as brewing wine. [Zhang Heng, Nandu Fu] has: “Of wines there are the nine-times brewed and the sweet mead, the ten-day vintage and the doubly clear,” the commentary explaining that these are names taken from the brewing methods. [Wang Sengda, answering Yan Yannian] has: “The spring brew is at times offered and poured.”
醢: An ancient character of left-right structure recorded as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). The entry text in the source is corrupted and yields no readable definition. [note: source text partially corrupted]
醣: An ancient character written with a left-right structure, a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) by traditional analysis. No gloss for it survives in the transmitted source text.
醪: Wine with its lees, an unfiltered drink. [Guangyun] glosses it as cloudy wine. [Shiji, biography of Yuan Ang] says: “He then took all his goods and baggage and set out two piculs of rich unfiltered wine.” [Zhang Hua, Qingbao Pian] has: “The floating lees turn with the cup, and the white ants dance on the waves.”
醫: One who heals illness, a physician. [Liji, Quli] says: “If a physician is not of three generations' standing, do not take his medicine.” [Shiji, biography of Bian Que] says: “He practiced medicine sometimes in Qi, sometimes in Zhao.”
醬: An ancient character written in a top-bottom structure and classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). The source entry is corrupted, so no definition survives. [note: source text partially corrupted]
醭: A left-right structure character classified as a phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng). The transmitted source text preserves no gloss for it.
醮: A rite of libation performed at capping, marriage or sacrifice. [Liji, Guanyi] says: “He received the libation at the guest's place,” the sub-commentary explaining that pouring wine without the exchange of toasts is called jiao.
醯: Vinegar, something sour. [Yupian] glosses it as sour flavor and [Guangyun] as the taste of vinegar. [Liji, Quli] says: “Vinegar and sauce are placed within.” [Shiji, Huozhi Zhuan] mentions “a thousand jars of vinegar and sauce,” at which point the text breaks off.
醴: A phono-semantic compound (xíngshēng) written in a left-right structure. The entry text in the source is corrupted and contains no recoverable gloss. [note: source text partially corrupted]
醵: To drink together by common contribution, to club together for a drinking party. [Guangyun] explains it as pooling money to drink wine. [Liji, Liqi] records Zengzi saying: “The rites of Zhou — are they not like a ju?” the commentary explaining that collecting money together to drink is called ju. [Shiji, Huozhi Zhuan] says: “At the seasons they had nothing with which to sacrifice, so they contributed to eating and drinking together,” Xu Guang's commentary explaining it as gathering to eat in common.
醺: Mellow with wine, drunk. [Xu's commentary] explains it as drinking until the warm aura of wine rises about one. [Yupian] glosses it “drunk,” and describes 醺醺 as the appearance of being genial and pleased.
釀: To ferment; the making of wine is called niang. [Guangyun] glosses it as brewing wine. [Shiji, biography of Lord Mengchang] says: “He then brewed much wine and bought fat cattle,” and the [Huozhi Zhuan] notes that in a great city a wine seller might brew a thousand batches in a year. [Hanshu, Shihuo Zhi] records that one brewing took two hu of coarse rice and one hu of yeast and yielded six hu six dou of finished wine.
釆: To distinguish, to discriminate; the character depicts the parted claws of a beast. [Liu Shu Zheng E] explains that it originally depicted a beast's claws and was borrowed for the word meaning “to distinguish,” and that characters such as 審, 釋, 悉 and 番 all take their form from it.
采: To pluck, to gather with the hand. [Shijing, Zhounan] has: “Pluck, pluck the cocklebur,” Zhu's commentary explaining that 采采 means not plucking once only, that is, gathering repeatedly.
釉: The entry defines 釉 (yòu) as the thin glassy layer covering the surface of ceramics and enamelware, with illustrative words such as glaze, glaze material and glaze color. The remainder of the text is scraper residue and HTML. [note: source text partially corrupted]
释: To untie, to release. It is composed of 釆, that component being taken in the sense of distinguishing things. [Zuozhuan, Duke Xiang, 29th year] says: “In spring, the king's first month, the Duke was in Chu, which released him from appearing in person at the temple for the new-year court,” the commentary explaining 釋 as “to release” and the sub-commentary setting out why he could not appear in person. The [Wuyu] says: “He then sent the messenger Xi Si to explain himself in Qi,” the commentary explaining 釋 as “to untie,” that is, to clear oneself by speech.
釋: To loosen, to set free. Formed from 釆, the component being taken in the sense of separating out things. [Zuozhuan, Duke Xiang, 29th year] records that the Duke, being in Chu, was released from the obligation to appear at the temple, and the [Wuyu] tells of a messenger sent to explain matters in Qi, the commentary in each case glossing 釋 as “to untie” or “to release.” The character is classified as a loan usage in the traditional analysis.
里: An ancient character written in a top-bottom structure and classified as a compound ideograph (huìyì) in the six-book system. Its transmitted gloss is corrupted and no definition can be recovered. [note: source text partially corrupted]
重: Heavy, weighty. [Zengyun] explains it as the opposite of light. [Yijing, Xici] says: “Now the mat-grass is a thin thing, yet its use may be weighty.” [Liji, Wangzhi] says: “Light duties are combined, heavy duties are divided.”
野: Open country beyond the suburbs. [Yijing, Tongren] says: “Fellowship with men in the open country: success,” the sub-commentary explaining that the wilds are a broad and far-reaching place. [Shijing, Lusong] has: “Fat and strong are the stallions, in the far-off wilds,” the commentary explaining that beyond the settlement is the jiao and beyond the jiao is the ye.
量: To weigh, to measure the lightness or heaviness of a thing. [Feng Yan, Suizhi Fu] has: “He discarded the balance and the stone weights and measured by his own judgment.”
釐: Blessing upon a house, good fortune. [Yang Xiong, Ganquan Fu] has: “He welcomed the blessings of the three deities,” the commentary explaining 釐 as “blessing.”
金: Metal of the five colors, of which the yellow is chief: buried long it does not grow a covering, refined a hundred times it does not become light, and though it be worked it does not disobey; it is the agent of the west and is born from earth. [Erya, Shiqi] states: “Yellow metal is called dang and its finest kind liu; white metal is called silver and its finest kind liao.” [Shujing, Yugong] says: “Its tribute was the three grades of metal,” the commentary explaining these as gold, silver and copper. [Hanshu, Shihuo Zhi] says: “Metal has three grades: yellow metal is the highest, white metal the middle, red metal the lowest,” the commentary explaining that white metal is silver and red metal the copper of Danyang, and that, as Shigu says, metal has five colors — yellow gold, white silver, red copper, green lead and black iron.

銎: The socket of an axe or adze, the hole in which the handle is fitted. [Guangyun] explains it as the place where an axe head receives its shaft. [Taigong, Liutao] says: “The large-hafted axe has a socket eight inches long.”
銜: A bit held in a horse's mouth. It is composed of 金 and 行; the bit is what governs the horse's going. [Xu's commentary] explains that the bit controls the horse's movement, and that the character is a compound ideograph. [Zhanguo Ce] has: “Leaning on the crossbar and reining in the bit, he traversed the world.” [Hanshu, biography of Zhang Chang] speaks of “the profit of bit and whip.”
銮: The chariot bells of a ruler. When the ruler rides with four horses there are eight bells on the bridles, the bells imitating the cry of the luan bird, and when they sound in harmony the ruler is reverent.
鋈: “White metal,” composed of 金 with 沃 as phonetic. [Shijing, Qinfeng] contains the phrase rendered as “the hidden trace and the wu-joined rein.” The [Yunhui], reviewing the commentators, notes that Mao glossed the word as white metal while Zheng explained it as white-metal plating on the ring that joins the rein, and that Kong's sub-commentary observes that white metal is silver and its finest kind liao. The discussion concludes that wu is not itself the name of white metal but denotes the melting of white metal to pour over and plate a rein ring, and that the terms in the poem refer to an iron base plated with another metal — much as people today speak of gold-plating — the same technique by which iron door-rings are now coated with tin.

鍪: The source preserves a commentarial note on this character. The Changjian says that soldiers used their helmets as cooking vessels, whence the name dou, so that dou is the name of a helmet while mou is the name of a cauldron, one object carrying both senses. The passage objects that army units had their own cooking pots, used by day for cooking and by night for signalling, and that no soldier ever cooked in his helmet. The cases of besieged troops boiling crossbows and armor or eating sinew and hide arose from desperate straits, not from ordinary practice; the note in the Changjian is therefore mistaken.

[Zuozhuan, Duke Huan, 2nd year] says: “The luan-bells, the harmony-bells and the ling make manifest their sound,” the commentary noting that the ling is on the banner and gives forth a ringing tone, the [Shiwen] giving its pronunciation as ling. 铅: “Green metal,” that is, lead. [Yupian] glosses it as black tin, and [Zhengzitong] classes it with tin, noting that it occurs in the flat marshes of Shu commandery and is now found wherever there are silver mines, being also called black tin because tin is white and lead therefore black. Li Shizhen says that lead is so named because it readily flows along. [Shujing, Yugong] lists lead among the tribute together with pine and strange stones, and the [Baozang Lun] enumerates several kinds: Persian lead, hard and white, is the best; grass-joint lead from Qianwei is the essence of silver; the lead that accompanies silver in silver mines contains five colors; the lead of Shangrao and Leping is inferior, and “negative-slab lead” is an iron ore. Dugu Tao describes the fishing-foot lead of Yazhou as shaped like a honey-locust pod, as large as a tadpole, black and growing in sand, and says it can also be used to dry mercury.
