镯: "A zhēng (signal bell)." Composed of 金 with the phonetic 蜀. By military law the Minister of War held two zhuó. In [Zhouli, Diguan, Guren]: "with the metal zhuó he marks the drum-beat"; the note says that the zhuó is a zhēng shaped like a small bell, sounded on the march to mark the drum's rhythm. The [Shiwen] gives the fanqie zhi-jiao.
镰: A dictionary gloss defines it as "a farming implement for harvesting grain and cutting grass," as in 镰刀 (sickle). It is left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
镲: A character of left-right structure, phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. No source text is preserved for this entry.
镳: "A horse's bit." [Zhengyun]: "also called shàn hàn, also called pái mò." [Erya, Shiqi]: "A biāo is called a niè"; the note calls it the iron at the side of the bridle. [Shiming]: "Biāo means bāo (to wrap); it wraps and gathers the mouth at the sides." The citation from [Cao Zhi, Poem in Response to the Imperial Command] then breaks off.
镴: An ancient character, left-right in structure and a compound ideograph (huìyì 会意) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
镶: "To make a mould; the 'middle intestine.'" [Zhengzitong]: "Some say that the xíng (mould) is the method of casting vessels. In making a mould one first uses cord to form the matrix; once the mould has set, the ends of the cord are drawn out through an opening; when the cord is gone the mould remains — this resembles an intestine."
長: An ancient character, pictographic (xiàngxíng 象形) in both structure and six-books classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
长: An ancient character, pictographic (xiàngxíng 象形) in both structure and six-books classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
门: "Wén (hearing)." Composed of two 户 (door) graphs, a pictograph. [Yupian]: "that by which people go in and out; within a hall or room it is called hù (a single door), in a region it is called mén (a gate)." [Guangya]: "Mén means to guard." [Shiming]: "it means to touch (mén); it is what people outside push and touch." In [Yijing, Tongren]: "Fellowship with men at the gate," the commentary explaining that with no selfish impediment in the heart one is in accord with the great unity, and all who go out of the gate are the same — hence the phrase; and in [Shujing, Shundian]: "the guests were received at the four gates..." — the citation then breaks off.
闩: A character of semi-enclosing structure, classified as zhǐshì (指事, indicative). No source text is preserved for this entry.
闪: "Peeping one's head through a gate." Composed of 人 (a person) within 門 (a gate), a compound ideograph. [Guangyun]: "the appearance of going out of a gate."
闫: A dictionary gloss records that it was formerly used as a simplified form of 阎 (yán) and was later withdrawn from use. It is enclosing in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
闭: "To shut the gate." Composed of 門 and 才; 才 is what props the gate shut — a compound ideograph, and also pictographic. The popular form with 下 beneath is not correct. In [Liji, Yueling]: "they repair the bolts and locks," the note explaining that the bolt is male and the closed part female, and the sub-commentary that the bolt is the door leaf, two wooden posts being set up behind with holes in their upper ends, through which the lock is pushed into the doorway. In [Zuozhuan, Huan 5]: "when the hibernating insects are shut in, the winter sacrifice is held," the note explaining that in the month of the tenth earthly branch the insects close their doors; the [Shiwen] gives the fanqie bi-ji.
问: "To interrogate." In [Shujing, Zhonghui zhi Gao]: "One who loves to ask becomes rich [in knowledge]." In [Shijing, Bei Feng]: "She asked after my aunts, and then reached my elder sisters."
闯: "The appearance of a horse going out of a gate." Composed of 馬 (horse) within 門 (gate) — a compound ideograph, and also pictographic. Read as 郴 (chēn).
闰: "The month of the surplus fraction: in five years there are two intercalary months." In the ceremony of announcing the new moon the Son of Heaven resides in the ancestral temple, and in an intercalary month at the gate. Composed of 王 (king) within 門 (gate); the Zhouli says that in an intercalary month the king stays in the middle of the gate for the whole month. In [Shiji, Wudi ji]: "The Yellow Emperor regulated the intercalary surplus"; in [Yijing, Xici]: "The odd stalks are laid aside to image the intercalary month; in five years there are two intercalations," the commentary explaining that nineteen years contain seven intercalary months, forming one zhang, and the sub-commentary that the remaining stalks are gathered to make up the intercalary month. In [Shujing, Yaodian]: "the year has three hundred and sixty-six days, and by the intercalary month the four seasons are fixed and the year completed"; [Guliang Zhuan, Wen 6] adds that an intercalary month consists of the surplus days attached to a month, accumulated from fractions to form a month.
闱: "A gate within the palace." In [Liji, Zaji]: "When the lady arrived, she entered by the palace gate (wéi mén)"; the [Shiwen] glosses wéi as a gate within the palace. The commentary to [Zuozhuan, Min 2] says that a small gate in the palace is called wéi. In [Shiji, Qi Tai Gong shijia]: "he attacked the palace gate and the great gate," the note giving "a gate within the palace" as the meaning; in [Qian Hanshu, Xuzhuan] we read of "the gates of the ruler's gate."
闲: "A railing, a barrier." Composed of 門 with wood in the middle. Xu says that xián is like a lán, using wood to bar the gate — a compound ideograph. [Guangyun]: "to guard against, to resist, a rule." In [Yijing, Qian]: "he guards against depravity and preserves his sincerity," the sub-commentary explaining that one should fence off evil and keep one's sincerity intact.
闳: "A lane gate." Composed of 門 and 厷, the latter serving for both sense and sound. [Erya, Shigong]: "A lane gate is called hóng"; the note calls it "the gate at the head of the lane." In [Zuozhuan, Cheng 17]: "he rode in a carriage and entered the lane gate," the note giving "a lane gate."
间: "A crevice." Composed of 門 and 月 — a compound ideograph, and also (phonetic). Xu Kai says that the gate is shut at night, and that when it is shut one sees the moonlight, which is "having a gap" ... — the citation then breaks off.
闵: "Autumn." Citing the Yu Shu: "when it compassionately (mǐn) covers all below, it is called the autumnal heaven (mín tiān)"; sometimes it is written 閔, and it is interchangeable with ... — the text breaks off at this point.
闶: "Kāng làng: a high gate." In [Qian Hanshu, Biography of Yang Xiong]: "Kang-lang-lang, how vast and empty!"; the note says this describes the appearance of a high gate.
闸: An ancient character, semi-enclosing in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
闹: An ancient character, semi-enclosing in structure and a compound ideograph (huìyì 会意) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
闺: "A door standing alone, round above and square below, resembling a guī (jade tablet)." In [Zuozhuan, Xiang 10]: "people of wicker gates and small doors," the note explaining that the guī door and the dòu are small doors made by piercing the wall. [Guangyun] gives "a boudoir"; in [Qian Hanshu, Xunli zhuan]: "the instructions were passed in and out of the inner apartments," the note explaining that guī gé are the small gates within. [Yupian] says that the small gate in a palace is called guī. In [Du Fu, Poem Given to Li Bai]: "Lord Li is a talent of the golden guī," the note explaining that Dongfang Shuo and Gongsun Hong waited for their summons at the Golden Horse Gate, whence "golden guī"; and in [Xie Tiao's poem]: "at last he passed through the roll of the golden guī," that is, his name was listed on the register of officials.
闻: "To hear and know." In [Shujing, Yaodian]: "The Emperor said: Yes; what have you heard?" In [Liji, Shaoyi]: "I have heard that one who first meets a gentleman..."; the sub-commentary explains that the author of the record did not presume to institute the ceremony himself but passed on what he had heard of the old accounts, and so speaks thus.
闼: "A door." [Guangya]: "A tà is called a mén." In [Shijing, Qi Feng]: "That lovely lady is in my doorway"; the commentary explains tà as "inside the door." The [Shiwen] gives the fanqie ta-da, and the Han version of the Odes says that the space between the door and the screen is called tà.
闽: "A southeastern branch of the Yue." [Guangyun]: "Min Yue." In [Zhouli, Xiaguan]: "the Officer of Regions distinguishes the states, the capital districts, the four Yi, the eight Man and the seven Min." In [Shiji, Dong Yue zhuan]: "Wu Zhu, king of Min Yue," the note explaining that this is another name for Dong Yue, and adding that according to the Shuowen the Min are the eastern Yue, of serpent stock, so that the character is composed of 虫 with the phonetic 門. In [Shanhaijing]: "Min is in the sea," the note identifying Min Yue with the Western Ou, which is present-day Jian'an commandery.
阀: "Fá yuè: the record of one's own merits." [Yunhui]: "fá yuè, the register of merit." In [Shiji, Table of Meritorious Officials]: "The merit of a minister is of five grades; to make clear his rank is called fá, and accumulated days are called yuè."
阁: "That by which a door leaf is stopped." Composed of 門 and 各, the latter serving for both sense and sound. Xu says that a long peg is called gé and serves to stop the door leaf — what is today called the door jamb, to which the leaf is attached. [Zhengzitong], citing the [Erya, Shigong]: "a peg is called yì; one in a wall is called huī, one in the ground is called niè; the large one is called gǒng, the long one is called gé."
阂: "Shut from outside." Composed of 門 and 亥, the latter serving for both sense and sound. [Yupian]: "to stop." The commentary on [Yijing, Meng]: "retreating, one is hemmed in by danger; advancing, one is blocked by the mountain"; the sub-commentary explains that Kan lying below Gen means danger beneath the mountain, so that one fears neither advance nor retreat is possible, and hence all is obscure.
阃: An ancient character, semi-enclosing in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
阆: "A wǎng liǎng (spectre)." In [Shiji, Confucius shijia]: "the monsters of wood and stone are the kui and the wang-liang"; the note gives their pronunciations and observes that the Jiayu writes 魍魎.
阈: "The wooden threshold of a door." The Analects says: "In walking, one does not tread on the threshold." Xu says that it is the door sill; [Erya, Shigong]: "A zhì is called yù," the sub-commentary explaining that it is the crossbar beneath the door marking the limit between outside and inside. In [Liji, Yuzao]: "a guest does not stand in the middle of the gateway nor tread on the threshold," the note glossing yù as the door sill. In [Zuozhuan, Xi 22]: "women did not go out of the gate to see off or welcome, and did not cross the threshold to meet their brothers"; the note to [Qian Hanshu, Wang Mang zhuan] explains the word as "door post."
阉: "A eunuch attendant" — the palace eunuch who shuts the gates. Composed of 門 and 奄, the latter serving for both sense and sound. [Guangyun]: "a male without potency, whose essence is shut in." In [Qian Hanshu, Xuzhuan]: "the fault of the eunuch director," the note explaining that palace men are called yān because their vital essence is covered and shut in and does not escape; another account says it denotes one in charge of shutting the gate.
阊: "The gate of heaven." Another account has it that the people of Chu call a gate chāng hé. In [Qian Hanshu, Liyue zhi]: "roaming at the Changhe," the note explaining that Changhe is the gate of heaven. In [Hou Hanshu, Du Du zhuan]: "he pushed open the Changhe and entered the dark valley"; in [Huainanzi, Yuandao xun]: "he pushed open the Changhe and unlocked the gate of heaven," the note saying that Changhe is the gate through which one first ascends to heaven.
阋: "Constant litigation." Composed of 鬥 (strife) and 兒, a child being fond of quarrelling. In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "Brothers quarrel within the walls," the commentary glossing xì as "stubborn." [Erya, Shiyan]: "xì is resentment," the note adding "mutual resentment." In [Yangzi, Fangyan]: "xié xì means fear"; among the people of Song and Wei, any anger that chokes the voice is called xié xì.
阍: "A servant who regularly shuts the gate at dusk." In [Liji, Jiyi]: "The gatekeeper (hūn) is the lowliest of those who guard the gate." In [Zhouli, Tianguan]: "the gatekeeper is in charge of guarding the prohibitions of the palace's inner gates," the note explaining that the gatekeeper is made to guard the middle gate of the royal palace. [Zhengzitong] adds that when officials or commoners, suffering injustice, come to the palace gate to state their case, it is called "knocking at the gate" (kòu hūn).
阎: "A gate within a lane." In [Hou Hanshu, Biography of Ban Gu]: "the lanes and lane-gates numbered nearly a thousand," the note, citing the Zilin, glossing yán as the gate of a lane. In [Shiji, Yue shijia]: "Though Zhuang Sheng lived in a poor lane, he was known throughout the state for his integrity."
阏: "To block and dam up." [Guangyun]: "to stop, to obstruct." In [Qian Hanshu, Biographies of the Thirteen Princes of Jing]: "Now your servant is blocked and cannot be heard," the note giving the fanqie wu-he and the sense "to stop." In [Chuci, Jiusi]: "My aims are cut off — where shall I go?" the note explaining that his hopes are at an end and he knows not where to turn. In [Liezi, Yang Zhu]: "Guan Yiwu said: Let them be, and nothing more; neither dam nor block them." In [Cai Yong, Song of the Fanhui Canal]: "I have a long stream, and none blocks it." The [Shiwen] gloss then breaks off.
阐: "To open." [Zengyun]: "to open up." In [Hou Hanshu, Ban Gu zhuan]: "those who, having clan names, continued heaven and opened out [its meaning]"; the note glosses chǎn as "to open."
阑: "A screen or barrier at the gate." In [Zhanguoce]: "Jin lies more than a thousand li from Liang, with rivers and mountains barring it." In [Shiji, Chu shijia]: "Even as a menial at the gate-barrier, which is what Yi greatly desires, he would not precede the great king." In [Hou Hanshu, Mingdi ji]: "he rewarded the county officials and the gate-runners," the note, from the Xu Han zhi, describing the gate-barrier with its attendants and street wardens.
阒: "Quiet." [Yupian]: "still and without people." In [Yijing, Feng]: "Peering in, there is no one there"; the sub-commentary: "he looks into the house and finds it silent, with no one in it."
阔: "Spaced apart"; another account gives "far." [Erya, Shigu]: "Kuò means far."
阕: "When a matter is finished, the gate is shut." [Yupian]: "to stop." [Guangya]: "Què means to conclude."
阖: "A door leaf." [Erya, Shigong]: "A hé is called a fēi (leaf)," the sub-commentary glossing it as a leaf. In [Liji, Yueling]: "In the second month of spring they repair the door leaves," the note saying that one made of wood is called hé. In [Zuozhuan, Xiang 18]: "they counted the door leaves with sticks," the note glossing hé as a door leaf; and in [Shiji, Song Weizi shijia]: "the shepherd's teeth were fixed in the door leaf."
阙: "The watchtower-gate (què)." Xu says that the centre is left open (quē) as a passage, and hence it is called què. [Yupian]: "the xiangwei què." [Guangyun]: "the què stand on either side of the gate, with the centre left open as a passageway." [Zhengyun]: "the pair of què at a palace gate." [Yunhui] explains that two terraces were built outside the gate with towers upon them, round above and square below, and that because the laws were hung there they were called xiangwei — xiang being the published ordinances and wei describing their towering height; the people were made to look up at them, and so they were called "lookouts" (guān), the two lookouts being set up in a pair with no gate between them.
阚: An ancient character, semi-enclosing in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
阞: "The natural grain of the ground." In [Zhouli, Dongguan, Kaogongji, Craftsman]: "Whenever a ditch goes against the grain of the ground (lè), it is said not to work"; the note explains that lè means the veining, and that "not to work" means that the water breaks out and overflows.
队: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
阡: "A path running north and south is a qiān." In [Shiji, Qin benji]: "he opened the field paths (qiān mò)." The note, citing the Fengsutong, says that north-south is called qiān and east-west mò, while in Hedong east-west is called qiān and north-south mò; Zhu Xi holds that the two accounts differ and that the latter is correct, mò meaning "hundred" and qiān meaning "thousand," the names being derived from the hundreds of mu and thousands of men lying between the irrigation channels. A further note observes that Lu Ji's poem "the winding channel skirts the crooked path, the flowing wave follows the straight qiān" takes north-south as qiān, whereas Liu Zongyuan's line "driving the cart toward the eastern qiān" takes east-west as qiān.
阢: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
阪: "A slope is called bǎn"; another account gives "a marsh dyke," and another "the flank of a mountain." [Yupian]: "steep." [Guangyun]: "a large, uneven bank." In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "Look at that sloping field," the commentary explaining it as rugged, stony ground. In [Liji, Yueling]: "skill in assessing hills, slopes, steeps, plains and marshes"; in [Zhanguoce]: "lingering on the outer slope," the note glossing bǎn as a slope; in [Shiji, Fan Sui zhuan]: "with Long and Shu on the right and the passes and slopes on the left." A note further observes that the Guangyun places both 阪 and 遠 in the Ruan rhyme, and that the later dictionaries record a further reading xiǎn.
阮: "The Wuyuan Pass in Daijun." The [Qian Hanshu, Dili zhi] writes it 五原. [Zhengyun]: "Ruǎn is the ancient form of 原."
阱: "Jǐng is a variant character for 穽." A textual note: in the current edition of the Jingdian Shiwen the word 爲 has been wrongly added after 或. Ancient editions of the Shuowen often say "X or Y," and this is frequently the case in the Jingdian Shiwen, which is what the Zhouli commentary means by "ancient characters often have variants." The present text of the Shuowen ... — the note then breaks off.
防: "A dyke." [Yupian]: "a barrier." [Guangyun]: "to defend against." [Erya, Shidi]: "A fén is a great dyke," the sub-commentary explaining that a fén is a bank shaped like a grave and therefore called a great dyke. In [Zhouli, Dongguan, Kaogongji]: "every ditch must follow the lie of the water, and every dyke the lie of the ground." In [Zuozhuan, Xiang 25]: "the plains were bounded by dykes," the note glossing fáng as a dyke. In [Guliang Zhuan, Zhao 8]: "they mowed the orchids to make a dyke," the note saying that a dyke is the great boundary of a field. The [Mengzi] has "no crooked dykes," and the [Zhanguoce] speaks of "the Long Wall and the great dyke, enough to serve as a frontier."
阳: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
阴: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
阵: A character of left-right structure, a compound ideograph (huìyì 会意) in classification. No source text is preserved for this entry.
阶: "The steps (bì)." [Yupian]: "the way up into a hall; a rank or step." In [Shujing, Dayumo]: "they danced the shield-and-feather dance on the two flights of steps."
阻: "Difficult, steep." [Guangyun]: "to separate." In [Yijing, Xici]: "his virtue and conduct are constant ..." — the quotation then breaks off.
阼: "The master's steps." [Yupian]: "the zuò steps are the eastern steps, used when responding to and toasting guests." In [Liji, Quli]: "he ascends the master's steps to conduct the sacrifice," the sub-commentary explaining that the zuò is the host's stair and that in sacrifice the Son of Heaven ascends the zuò stair. In [Yili, Gongshi Dafu li]: "there is no zuò mat."
阿: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陀: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陂: "A slope"; another account gives "a pond." [Yupian]: "a marsh dyke." [Fengsutongyi]: "Bēi means 'to multiply'; it means that water collects in the low ground so as to multiply benefits for the myriad things; nowadays all bēi are used for irrigation." In [Shujing, Yugong]: "the nine marshes were banked"; in [Liji, Yueling]: "do not dry up the streams and marshes, do not drain the ponds," the note saying that stored water is called bēi.
附: A note by Duan Yucai: 坿 (from 土, earth) serves as the character for "to add to"; this 附 is given the fanqie bu-kou and means "a small earthen mound." Yucai holds that 坿 in the earth section means "to increase," and that this sense, as well as the sense "to be near to," should be written with it; but nowadays 附 is used for all of them, and the original sense of 附 has fallen out of use.
际: "The junction of walls." [Yupian]: "to join." [Guangyun]: "a meeting." In [Yijing, Tai]: "the junction of heaven and earth"; in the Kan hexagram: "the junction of the firm and the yielding." In [Qian Hanshu, Biography of Yi Feng]: "the Odes have five junctions (jì)," the note, citing the Neizhuan, explaining that the five junctions are the years mao, you, wu, xu and hai, the years in which yin and yang meet at their beginning and end, when there are reforms in government.
陆: An ancient character, left-right in structure and a compound ideograph (huìyì 会意) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陇: "The great slope of Tianshui." The [Qian Hanshu, Dili zhi] has Long county in Tianshui commandery; the note says that this is what is now called Longcheng county.
陈: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陉: "A broken gap in a mountain." [Yupian]: "a boundary." [Erya, Shishan]: "A mountain cut off is a xíng"; the sub-commentary explains that where a mountain ridge runs on and is suddenly cut through, it is called xíng.
陋: "Narrow and confined." The Analects has "in a mean lane," the sub-commentary glossing it as a narrow, mean lane. In [Zuozhuan, Cheng 9]: "Ju relied on its remoteness and made no preparations."
陌: A character of left-right structure, phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. No source text is preserved for this entry.
限: "To obstruct." [Yupian]: "a boundary, a measure, to make equal." In [Yijing, Gen]: "Nine in the third place: he stops at his waist," the note explaining that the limit (xiàn) is the middle of the body. In [Zhanguoce]: "to the south are the barriers of Wu Mountain and Qianzhong." In [Shiji, Pingzhun shu]: "in dwellings, carriages and dress they overstepped their superiors without limit."
陔: "The order of steps." [Yupian]: "steps; a ridge." In [Qian Hanshu, Jiaosi zhi]: "the altar for sacrifice was modelled on Bo Ji's Tai altar, one altar with three steps (gāi)"; the note explains that gāi means a layer, and that three gāi make a three-tiered altar.
陘: "A broken gap in a mountain." [Yupian]: "a boundary." [Erya, Shishan]: "A mountain cut off is a xíng"; the sub-commentary explains that where a mountain ridge runs on and is suddenly cut through, it is called xíng.
陛: "Steps for ascending." [Yupian]: "the steps of the Son of Heaven." In [Zhanguoce]: "Qin Wuyang, bearing the box with the map, advanced in order to the steps." In [Qian Hanshu, Biography of Dongfang Shuo]: "at that time Shuo stood with a halberd on the steps below the hall."
陜: A fragmentary citation from the Shuowen Jiezi, "Fu" section: "陜 means narrow (ài)." Left-right in structure, a compound ideograph in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陞: An ancient character, left-right in structure and pictographic (xiàngxíng 象形) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陟: An ancient character, left-right in structure and a compound ideograph (huìyì 会意) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陡: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
院: "Firm." [Yupian]: "a surrounding wall," also written 寏. [Zengyun]: "that which has a wall around it is called a yuàn." In [Tangshu, Xuanzong ji]: "he built a Court of the Five Princes to house the young imperial princes."
除: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陧: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陨: "To fall from a height." [Erya, Shigu]: "Yǔn means to fall"; and again: "yǔn means to fall down," the note explaining that the two words are the same and differ only in dialectal weight. In [Shujing, Tanggao]: "trembling with fear, as if about to fall into a deep abyss." In [Yijing, Gou]: "there falls from heaven"; and in the [Chunqiu, Zhuang 7]: "in the middle of the night the stars fell like rain," which the Gongyang commentary writes with 霣.
险: "A difficult obstacle." [Yupian]: "high; perilous." In [Yijing, Zhun]: "moving amid danger"; in the Kan hexagram: "the doubled danger of Kan." And again: "the dangers of heaven cannot be ascended; the dangers of earth are its rivers, mountains and hills; princes and dukes set up defences to guard their states — great indeed is the timely use of danger."
陪: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陬: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
陰: "Dark." [Shiming]: "Yīn means shade; the vital force within is hidden in deep shade." [Yupian]: "hidden and formless, deep and unfathomable — this is called yīn." In [Yijing, Kun]: "Though the yin has beauty, it keeps it hidden; in serving the king's affairs it does not presume to complete them — this is the way of earth, the way of a wife, the way of a minister." In [Liji, Yueling]: "the hundred officials keep their affairs quiet and do not ..." — the citation then breaks off.

[Erya, Shigong]: "A dī is called a liáng (bridge)," the note explaining that this means a bridge. In [Zuozhuan, Xi 25]: "the men of Qin passed Xi and the bend," the note identifying Xi as a Chu town and the wēi as a hidden, marshy spot. In [Guanzi, Xingshi]: "In the bend of the great mountain, how deep can it be?" In [Chuci, Tianwen]: "Corners and bends are many — who knows their number?" In [Huainanzi, Yuandao xun]: "Shun fished on the riverbank for a full year, and the fishermen vied to yield the rapids and the deep pools at the winding bends to him."

隗: "Duǐ wěi (lofty)." [Yupian]: "high." In [Yang Xiong, Ganquan fu]: "㟎 ..." — the citation then breaks off.

隰: "Low, damp ground below a slope." [Shiming]: "Xí means zhé (to hide); zhé carries the sense of dampness." In [Shujing, Yugong]: "the plains and lowlands were brought to order." 隱: "To conceal." [Yupian]: "to hide." The Analects: "When a matter is spoken of and one does not speak of it, this is called concealing." In [Liji, Tangong]: "In serving one's parents there may be concealment, but not offence." The citation from the [Lu Yu] then breaks off.
隳: A dictionary gloss defines it as "to ruin; to collapse," as in "to ruin another's city walls." It is also read duò. Upper-lower in structure, phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]

隸: "To attach to." In [Hou Hanshu, Biography of Feng Yi]: "he assigned the various generals, each with his own subordinates," the note glossing lì as "to be attached to."

隻: "A single bird." Composed of 又 (the hand) holding 隹 (a bird): holding one bird is zhī, holding two is shuāng. [Yupian]: "an odd one." [Zengyun]: "a single item is called zhī." In [Hou Hanshu, Fangshu zhuan]: "he obtained one shoe."
隼: "A zhù jiū (a kind of falcon)." [Erya, Shiniao]: "the hawk-and-falcon kind"; the sub-commentary, citing Lu Ji, says it belongs to the kite family, and that the people of Qi call it jī zhēng, or tí jiān, or sparrow-hawk, the bird that transforms into the cuckoo in spring. [Piya] observes that a hawk in seizing prey cannot always be sure, while the falcon alone is accurate, so that every strike hits; the ancients made the character accordingly, and the [Yijing, Xie] has "the prince shoots the falcon on the high wall," the sub-commentary describing the falcon as a greedy, cruel bird of the zhān and yào kind. In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "Swiftly flies the falcon, its flight reaches heaven," the commentary explaining it as a swift bird whose flight reaches the sky, a figure for strong and brave soldiers who can drive deep into the enemy; and [Liji, Yueling] says that "hawks and falcons seize their prey early."
隽: A textual note: "... yet it must be a good text of the Shuowen. If it does not speak of a bird, how then is the character composed with 隹? Kuai Tong wrote a book entitled Juàn Yǒng ('lasting flavour'), meaning that what he set out was delicious and long-lasting in flavour. Only wild birds' flavour can be called juàn, hence the composition with 弓."

雛: "A chick." Composed of 隹 and 芻. [Erya, Shiniao]: "a fledgling that pecks for itself," the note explaining that it can feed itself from birth. The [Shiwen] gives chú as the fanqie shi-ju. In [Liji, Yueling]: "the Son of Heaven tastes the new millet with a chick," the [Shiwen] giving a further fanqie for that passage; and in [Mengzi]: "whose strength cannot overcome a single chick."

In [Yijing, Shuogua]: "Xun is the fowl." In [Shujing, Taishi]: "a hen has no dawn-crow." In [Zhouli, Chunguan, Dazongbo], among the six gifts, "the artisan and the merchant hold a fowl"; and in [Liji, Quli]: "a fowl is called hàn yīn (a 'feathered sound')."

[Yuanmingbao]: "when yin and yang are in harmony there is rain"; [Dadai Liji]: "when the vital forces of heaven and earth are in harmony, it rains." [Shiming]: "Yǔ means to assist, meaning that it assists the season in producing and nourishing." In [Yijing, Qian]: "the clouds move and the rain is spread, and the various things take form"; and in [Shujing, Hongfan], among the eight verifications, "rain" and "sunshine."

[Erya, Shixun]: "to dance and cry out is the yú [sacrifice]"; the note explaining that in the yú sacrifice the dancers sigh and call out to seek rain. In [Liji, Yueling]: "in mid-summer the great yú [is held]," the note adding that the yú is the sacrifice in which one sighs and calls for rain. In [Zuozhuan, Huan 5]: "when the dragon appears, the yú is held," the note explaining that it prays far in advance for the fattening rain of the hundred grains, the sub-commentary adding that yú means "far," since one makes ready beforehand for the autumn harvest, and the sense is deep and far-reaching.
雪: "Originally written 䨮: congealed rain." [Yuanmingbao]: "when yin congeals it becomes snow." [Shiming]: "Xuě means suí (to fall gently); water below, meeting cold air, congeals and comes down softly and slowly." [Piya]: "Snow forms blossoms in six rays; the flowers of plants and trees are five-rayed, but the snow-flower alone is six-rayed, the completing number of yin." In [Shijing, Bei Feng]: "the snow falls thickly."

雲: "In the ancient script the form depicts the revolving shape of a cloud." 雲 is a compound ideograph, composed of 雨 (rain) and 云 (cloud); its original meaning is "cloud," a sense later written with this character. [note: source text partially corrupted]

雷: "Originally written 靁: yin and yang strike and move, and the thunder-rain gives life to things." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 畾; it depicts a revolving form. In [Yijing, Shuogua]: "Zhen is thunder." In [Liji, Yueling]: "in mid-spring the thunder begins to sound."
雹: "Rain in the form of ice." [Dadai Liji]: "The concentrated qi of yang becomes graupel and the concentrated qi of yin becomes hail; graupel and hail are transformations of a single qi," the note explaining that yang qi within the rain is warm like yang, and that when yin qi presses on it the two do not enter each other but wrestle and become hail, whence the Guliang commentary of the Chunqiu says that hail is the image of yin coercing yang. [Piya] says that yin wrapping up yang makes hail, and Shen Feng held that the ancients stored ice to strengthen yin so that the cold was sealed and there was no hail, for when yang has no outlet it produces hail. The hailstone resembles a half-pearl of today and its grains are three-rayed; snow forms blossoms in six rays and hail forms fruit in three, hail being the surplus of ice, and it is likewise said that hail is the ice of rain.
電: "Yin and yang clash and blaze." Composed of 雨 and 申. [Piya]: "Lightning and thunder share the same qi; thunder is written with 回 (revolving) and lightning with 申 (extending), because yin and yang, revolving and pressing, make thunder, and by extending and releasing make lightning." Another account says that thunder issues from the qi of heaven and lightning from the qi of earth, so that lightning is composed of an abbreviated 坤; the Shuogua says that Li is lightning, and lightning belongs to fire. For when yin and yang violently oppose each other and, dividing and contending, shoot forth, fire is produced: its light is lightning and its sound thunder. Today, when iron and stone strike each other, fire is produced, and when heated stone is thrown into a well, thunder arises.
雾: A dictionary gloss defines it as "water vapour near the ground which, on meeting cold, condenses into tiny droplets that float in the air," as in 雾气 (mist) and 迷雾 (fog), and also as "something resembling mist." 霁: "The ceasing of rain." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 齊. [Erya, Shitian]: "Jì is called jì (clearing)," the note observing that the people of Nanyang today call the stopping of rain jì, and the sub-commentary glossing jì as "to stop." In [Shujing, Hongfan]: "rain and clearing," the commentary explaining that some crack patterns resemble rain and some the stopping of rain. In [Qian Hanshu, Biography of Wei Xiang]: "he relaxed (jì) his sternness," the note glossing jì as "to stop."
霂: "Mài mù (a fine drizzle)." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 沐. [Erya, Shitian]: "light rain is called mài mù." In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "it was increased by the fine drizzle." For further detail see the note under 霡 below.
霄: "Rain with graupel makes xiāo snow." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 肖; this is a Qi dialect usage. [Erya, Shitian]: "rain with graupel is xiāo," the note quoting the Odes — "like that falling snow, first gathered as graupel" — and explaining that graupel is snow and ice falling mixed, which is called xiāo snow; the sub-commentary says that xiāo is the same as 消, to melt away. [Yunhui]: "Xiāo snow is what people today call wet snow; it melts as soon as it touches an object."
霆: "The lingering sound of thunder — the ringing by which things are brought forth." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 廷. [Yupian]: "a peal of thunder." [Erya, Shitian]: "a swift thunder is tíng ní." In [Yijing, Xici]: "they are stirred by thunder and lightning." In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "like a peal of thunder, like thunder." In [Liji, Kongzi xianju]: "the spirit-qi, wind and thunder; wind and thunder give form to things."
震: "That which crashes and shakes things." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 辰. Xu Xuan's note: "The popular separate characters 霹靂 are not correct." In [Yijing, Shuogua]: "Zhen is thunder." In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "there is a flashing of thunder and lightning," the commentary glossing zhèn as thunder. In the [Chunqiu, Xi 15]: "thunder shook the temple of Yi Bo"; the sub-commentary says that an extreme thunder is a zhèn. [Shiming]: "Zhèn means zhàn (battle); what it strikes is always broken, as in attack and battle."

霏: "The appearance of falling snow." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 非. [Jiyun]: "a fall of snow." In [Shijing, Bei Feng]: "the snow falls in flakes," the commentary explaining fēi as "in abundance."

霓: "A bent rainbow, blue and red; or, a white vapour of yin." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 兒. [Yupian]: "a cloud colour resembling a dragon." [Piya]: "The male is called hóng (虹) and the female ní (霓); the old account has it that rainbows usually appear in pairs, the bright and full one being male and the dim one female." Another account says that the red-and-white one is called hóng and the blue-and-white one ní. The [Erya, Shitian] says that ní is qiè èr, èr meaning two, and the [Huainanzi, Shuoshan xun] likewise states that when heaven has two qi a rainbow is formed. In [Mengzi]: "like one gazing at clouds and rainbow in a great drought." [Jiyun] notes that it is interchangeable with 蜺.
霖: "Rain lasting three days or more." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 林. [Yupian]: "rain that does not stop." [Erya, Shitian]: "prolonged rain is called yín, and yín is called lín." In [Shujing, Yue Ming]: "I shall use you as the soaking rain," the commentary explaining that the lín rain relieves drought. In [Zuozhuan, Yin 9]: "In spring, the royal first month, there was great rain together with thunder — this is where the record begins; all rain lasting from three days onward is lín."

霢: "The original form of 霡. Mài mù means light rain." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 脈. [Jiyun]: sometimes written 䨫.
霪: An ancient character, upper-lower in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
霰: "Grain snow (graupel)." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 散. In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "like that falling snow, first gathered as graupel"; the commentary explains that when heavy snow is about to fall it is at first slightly warm, and the snow coming down from above meets the warm air and wrestles with it, which is called xiàn. [Dadai Liji]: "the concentrated qi of yang becomes graupel," the note explaining that yin qi in the rain congeals into snow, and when yang qi presses on it the two do not enter each other but scatter and become graupel, whence the Guliang commentary of the Chunqiu says that graupel is the token of yang coercing yin. [Shiming]: "Xiàn means xīng (star); water and snow wrestle together and scatter like stars." [Piya]: "In Fujian popular usage it is called rice-snow, meaning that its grains are like rice — which is the sense of 'grain snow'; today it is also called astringent snow or wet snow."
露: "Moistening moisture." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 路. [Yupian]: "the juices of heaven, by which all things below are moistened." [Shiming]: "Lù means lǜ (to consider); it covers and considers things." [Dadai Liji]: "when yang qi prevails it scatters as rain and dew"; the [Wujing Tongyi]: "the harmonious qi condenses its juices as dew." Cai Yong's [Yueling] says that dew is the fluid of yin, and the [Baihutong] that dew is the beginning of frost. In [Liji, Yueling]: "in the first month of autumn the white dew descends"; in [Shijing, Zhaonan]: "wet lies the dew upon the path," the commentary explaining it as the middle of the second month, the season of marriages, when the dew first lies on the road.
霸: "The first appearing of the moon, its bà brightness; on the second day after a long month and the third after a short one." Composed of 月 with the phonetic 䨣. [Zengyun]: "the dark part of the moon's body is called bà (pò)." [Yupian]: "now written 魄," the [Shujing, Wucheng] phonetic notes giving pò for 魄 and pi-ge for the Shuowen's 霸. In [Qian Hanshu, Lüli zhi]: "in the fourth month, on the day ji-chou, the first day, the dead pò" — the dead pò being the new moon and the growing pò the full moon. Yan Shigu notes that bà was anciently the same as pò, and the [Yunhui bu] cites Ouyang's remark that the popular form 覇 written with 西 is wrong.
霹: "The Shuowen says that zhèn is 'that which crashes and shakes things.'" A swift thunder is also called tíng ní or zhèn; the Chunqiu's "thunder shook the temple of Yi Bo" means that it crashed and broke it. 霹靂 is a popular form. [Piya]: "Zhèn is also called pì lì; pì means to break, for wherever it passes all is broken." [Jiyun]: sometimes written 礔.
霾: "Wind, rain and dust." Composed of 雨 with the phonetic 貍. [Shiming]: "Mái means huì (darkened); it speaks of a dusty, dimmed colour like that of things." [Piya] glosses mái as "to descend," and [Erya, Shitian] says that wind with falling dust is mái; the sub-commentary, citing Sun Yan, explains that a great wind raises the dust so that earth falls from above. In [Shijing, Bei Feng]: "the wind blows and the dust falls," the commentary glossing mái as "earth raining down." [Jiyun]: sometimes written 䨪.

非: "To go against." It is formed from 飛 with the wings (翄) lowered, taking the sense of the two turning away from each other. [Yupian]: "it is not so." In [Shujing, Yue Ming]: "to feel no shame for one's errors and so make them wrong"; in [Yijing, Xici]: "to distinguish right from wrong."

靡: "To fall away (pī mǐ)." [Guangyun]: "to bend down, to lie down." In [Zuozhuan, Zhuang 10]: "looking at their banners, they had fallen." In [Shiji, Annals of Xiang Yu]: "Xiang the King shouted and charged down, and the Han troops all scattered like grass before the wind," the Zhengyi commentary explaining mǐ as the substance drooping and hanging low.
面: An ancient character, pictographic (xiàngxíng 象形) in both structure and six-books classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
靥: "Comeliness." Composed of 面 with the phonetic 厭. The [Yupian] cites the [Huainanzi, Shuolin xun]: "when the dimples are in front of the cheeks the face is beautiful"; a note observes that the present text of the Huainanzi writes it ... — the citation then breaks off.
革: "An animal's hide dressed by removing its hair; gé also means 'to change.'" Xu Kai's note: "A hide with the hair removed, dyed and polished, is called gé." [Yunhui]: "A dressed hide is wéi and a raw one gé"; Master Lü adds that gé is a hide with the hair removed but not yet made into wéi. In [Shujing, Yugong]: "ivory, hides, feathers and hair," the commentary glossing gé as rhinoceros hide; in [Shijing, Zhaonan]: "the lamb's hide," the commentary explaining gé as simply a hide, and the sub-commentary that a hide with the hair dressed off is gé, the distinction being made only in paired usage, while in ordinary prose leather and hide are interchangeable. In [Zhouli, Tianguan], the Officer of Hides collects hides in autumn and gé in winter, the sub-commentary explaining that gé requires deeper dressing work and is therefore collected in winter.
靳: "The strap that lies over the chest [of the horse]." Xu Kai's note: "Jìn means to make firm; it controls the horse's going." In [Zuozhuan, Ding 9]: "I follow you as the outer horse follows the jìn," the note explaining jìn as the middle horse of a team; the sub-commentary says that the jìn is the leather lying over the chest, the head of the outer horse being at the chest of the pole horse, upon which chest lies the jìn.
靴: "A kind of leather shoe." [Yupian]: "a slipper; also a shoe." In [Suishu, Yili zhi]: "only the pleated uniform is worn with boots; the boot is a shoe, chosen for convenience in action and used with military dress." [Guangyun]: "originally written 鞾"; [Jiyun]: "also written ..." — the citation then breaks off.
靶: "The leather of the bridle." [Erya, Shiqi]: "the head of the reins is called gé"; the note gives it as the leather of the bridle. The sub-commentary, citing the Zilin: "bà is the leather of the reins."

鞅: "A band about the neck." [Guangyun]: "the halter of an ox." In [Zuozhuan, Xiang 18]: "he drew his sword and cut the yoke-strap." [Shiming]: "Yāng means yīng; that below the throat is called yīng, meaning that it is wound round like a collar. The ornament below it is the fán collar, whose shape spreads out and connects upward to the collar."
鞋: A dictionary gloss defines it as "a thing worn on the foot to make walking easier," as in 皮鞋 (leather shoes), 鞋袜 (shoes and socks) and 鞋底 (sole). Left-right in structure, phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]

鞘: "A scabbard." In the [Xijing zaji]: "he opened the box and put it into its sheath." [Guangyun]: "the same as 韒"; [Jiyun]: "originally written 韒, also 削 ..." — the citation then breaks off.
鞠: "To kick a ball (tà jū)." In [Zhanguoce]: "the games of liu bo and kicking the ball"; the note, citing Liu Xiang's Bielu, says that the ball-kicking game was invented by the Yellow Emperor as a pastime to train warriors. In [Yangzi, Fayan]: "they worked leather into a ball."

In [Liji, Quli]: "the dī shoe"; the note calling it a sandal without the qú ornament, and the sub-commentary explaining that shoes are ornamented with the qú, and since this was worn in mourning the ornament was omitted. In [Zhanguoce]: "armour, shields, leather shoes and helmets," the note glossing dī as leather shoes.

韧: "Soft yet firm." Composed of 韋 with the phonetic 刃. [Guangyun]: "supple and tough." [Jiyun]: "originally written 肕, sometimes 忍."
韪: "Right, correct." Composed of 是 with the phonetic 韋. In [Zuozhuan, Yin 11]: "he offended against the five rights." In [Qian Hanshu, Xuzhuan]: "he made plain what was right and showed the warning"; the note, citing Zhang Yan, explains wěi as "right," so that making plain what is right warns against what is not. In [Hou Hanshu, Biography of Xun Shuang]: "the five rights were all complete." [Jiyun]: interchangeable with 愇.

韬: "A bow-case." Composed of 韋 with the phonetic 舀. [Yupian]: "a sword-case." [Guangyun]: "to conceal." The commentary on the [Shijing, Xiaoya, Tonggong] glosses gāo as tāo.
韭: "A vegetable; because it is planted once and lasts long, it is called jiǔ" (a pun on 久, "long-lasting"). It is a pictograph, [the plant] above the stroke 一, where 一 stands for the ground. [Yunhui], citing the Tongzhi: "The chive is warm in nature and is called the stalactite of plants." In [Liji, Quli]: "the chive is called the 'abundant root.'"

韱: "Mountain chives." Composed of 韭 with the phonetic 㦰. [Yupian]: sometimes written 韯; [Jiyun]: sometimes written ... — the citation then breaks off.
音: "...is called yīn (a musical tone). The notes gong, shang, jiao, zhi and yu are shēng (sounds); silk, bamboo, metal, stone, gourd, clay, leather and wood are the eight kinds of yīn." Composed of 言 with 一 contained within it. In [Shujing, Shundian]: "the eight tones can be harmonized"; in [Liji, Yueji]: "when a sound becomes patterned it is called yīn," the sub-commentary explaining that when sounds are transformed and blended and their order is accomplished as a pattern it is called yīn, which is what we now call song. In the [Zhouli, Chunguan, Dashi] tones are made by the six pitch-pipes, the sub-commentary describing how the music master blew the pipes while singers matched them, and what matched was called yīn; the [Shi Xu] says that feeling issues in sound and that when sound becomes patterned it is called yīn, the sub-commentary noting that shēng and yīn are thereby distinguished — the Yueji commentary stating that "mixed and matched is yīn, single-issued is shēng." In paired usage the three — sound, tone and music — are distinguished, while in loose usage they may be interchanged.

韶: "The music of Shun of Yu." [Yupian]: "to continue, to carry on." In [Shujing, Yiji]: "the flute music of Shao in nine movements." In [Liji, Yueji]: "Sháo means to continue," the note explaining that sháo means shào (to carry on) and that Shun was able to carry on the virtue of Yao.

项: "The back of the head." [Shiming]: "Xiàng means què (firm); it is the firm place that receives the pillow." In [Yili, Shiguan li]: "the black cloth cap with the xiàng band"; the note explains that the black cloth cap has no hairpin, so a band is put round the hairline and tied at the back of the neck, with cords at the four corners to fasten the cap.
顺: "Order, reason." Composed of 頁 and 巛, a compound ideograph, 巛 being a flowing stream. [Yupian]: "to follow." In [Shijing, Daya]: "having upright virtue and conduct, the four quarters of the state follow him"; the commentary explaining that one who has great virtue and conduct is followed in government by all under heaven. [Shiming]: "Shùn means xún (to follow along); it is to follow along with the principle of things."
须: "The hair of the face." In [Yijing, Bi]: "adorned in his beard"; the note explaining that the beard is a thing that attaches upward, and the sub-commentary that it attaches upward to the face. [Shiming]: "that below the chin is called xū; xū means to flourish." It was separately written 䰅 and popularly 鬚.
顽: "A head that cannot be turned." Composed of 頁 with the phonetic 元. [Yupian]: "blunt, dull"; [Guangyun]: "stupid"; [Yunhui]: "foolish." In [Shujing, Yaodian]: "his father was obstinate and his mother quarrelsome"; in [Zuozhuan, Xi 24]: "a mind that does not conform to the norm of virtue and righteousness is wán (obstinate)."
顾: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
顿: A textual note: "At the beginning of the Shuowen Jiezi it is said: 'Your servant Chong, of the eighth rank, of Wansui lane in Zhaoling, bows his head and twice salutes, submitting a memorial to His Majesty the Emperor.' At the end it says: 'Your servant Chong, in sincere fear and trembling, bows his head again and again, guilty of death, guilty of death, bows his head and twice salutes, to make it known to His Majesty the Emperor.' In both places dùn shǒu is distinguished from qǐ shǒu, qǐ shǒu being the phrase used in replying and setting forth."
颀: A dictionary gloss defines it as "tall of body," as in 颀长 (tall and slender). Left-right in structure, phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
颁: "The hair of the temples." [Zhengyun]: "the two sides of the forehead are called bān." In [Mengzi]: "those with grizzled hair"; the note explaining bān as 班 (patterned), the hair being half white and speckled.

领: "The neck." Composed of 頁 with the phonetic 令. [Shiming]: "Lǐng means jǐng (neck), so called because it encloses the neck; it also means gathering up the body of a garment, being its head and beginning." In [Shijing, Xiaoya]: "the twittering greenfinches, with their patterned necks," the commentary explaining that their necks are brightly patterned and glossing lǐng as neck. In [Xunzi, Quanxue]: "as when one lifts a fur robe by the collar."
颇: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
颈: "The stalk of the head." [Shiming]: "Jǐng means jìng (straight); it is straight and long." [Guangyun]: "the jǐng is in front and the xiàng behind." In [Liji, Yuzao]: "head and neck must be straight."
颉: A textual note: "... the original sense of xié is 'a straight neck,' as in the Bei Feng poem 'the swallows fly, now dipping, now rising'; the commentary says that flying down is xié and flying up is háng, which is an extended sense. Since a straight neck is xié háng, by extension going straight down and straight up is also called xié háng." [note: source text partially corrupted]
颊: "The sides of the face." [Guangya]: "the cheekbones are called jiá." [Shiming]: "Jié means jiā (to press between); it is the name for the two sides, and also takes its sense from pressing and gathering food." In [Yijing, Xian]: "he moves his cheeks, jaw and tongue"; the sub-commentary explaining that cheeks, jaw and tongue are the instruments of speech.
颌: An ancient character, left-right in structure and phono-semantic (xíngshēng 形声) in classification. [note: source text partially corrupted]
颍: A geographical and textual note on the Yingshui and Yingchuan commandery: it observes that the commandery name in the Han treatise and in the ancient text of the Shuowen ought perhaps to be written with 禾, and that the counties of Yiyang, Wuyang and Wuyin take their names from rivers without writing the characters 汝 or 潕. According to the [Qian Hanshu, Dili zhi], in Yangcheng there is Mount Yangqian, from which the Yingshui issues, flowing east to Xiacai where it enters the Huai, passing through three commanderies over a course of fifteen hundred li and counted as a marsh of Jingzhou; the [Shuijing] and the [Shuidao Tigang] then trace its source on Mount Shaoshi below Mount Song, its division into two branches, their reunion, and its final junction with the Huai, the mouth being called Yingkou.

颐: "The chin." In [Liji, Yuzao]: "the chin like a roof-eave, the hands folded"; the sub-commentary explaining that the eave is the roof-edge, and that when the body bows the head comes forward so that the chin hangs like an eave; and again: "in upright walking the chin is like an eave, straight as an arrow." The [Shiwen] gives yí as the pronunciation. In [Qian Hanshu, Biography of Jia Yi]: "he had things done as he wished by pointing with his chin," the note explaining that a mere movement of the chin in command obtained whatever he desired.

颔: "A yellow face." In [Qu Yuan, Lisao]: "long hungry-faced, what harm?" the note explaining kǎn hàn as the look of one who has not eaten his fill.
颖: A textual note: "[this character] belongs to the 禾 (grain) section; the Zihui and the Zhengzitong wrongly enter it under the 頁 section, which is here corrected."

饥: A textual note: "The two characters 飢 and 饑: 飢 glosses as 'hungry,' with the fanqie ju-yi, while 饑 glosses as 'the grain not ripening,' with the fanqie ju-yi (居衣). Wang Laiyu the provincial governor says that the 饑 of 饑饉 (famine) is written with 幾 and the 飢 of 飢渴 (hunger and thirst) with 几; the rhyme dictionaries all list them separately under the Zhi and Wei rhymes, and only the Jiyun glosses 飢 as sometimes written with 幾, the two being largely used interchangeably in the classics and their commentaries. The [Changjian] says that in recent times those who love fullness of form write 饑 for both ..." — the note then breaks off.

馁: A textual note: "'Fish gone bad is called něi,' originally also written 餧, and the dictionaries agree; the Erya phonetic gloss likewise gives něi with the fanqie nu-zui. The Shuowen reads 'fish gone bad is něi' while the dictionaries write 餧, and since the dictionaries distinguish it from the Shuowen, it is clear that the Shuowen used by Lu [Deming] was composed with 妥. For the sound of 妥 is close to the fanqie nu-zui, just as 挼 must be composed with 妥 to be close to the fanqie nü-he, and 綏 must be composed with 妥 for 妥 and 綏 to be ancient and modern forms of one another. The Wujing Wenzi says that 餧 means 'hungry,' and in the transmission of the classics 餒 was distinguished for hunger and 餧 for provisions; presumably by Zhang's time the Shuowen had already been altered to the phonetic 委, differing from the text Lu relied on, which is why the characters differ."
馂: "The leftovers of food." In [Liji, Neize]: "While the parents live, at the morning and evening meals the sons and their wives assist at the jùn; when the meal is over they always eat the remainder. When the father is dead and the mother lives, the eldest son attends at the meal, and the other sons and their wives assist as before; sweet and delicate things are eaten by the children." The note explains that assisting at the jùn means urging the parents to eat again before the sons and wives begin, and that jùn means "finished," that is, finishing what is left. The eldest son attends the meal because he fears his mother would be grieved to eat alone; and sweet things such as dates, chestnuts, syrup and honey, which can harmonize all flavours, are given as the children's jùn, to nourish and comfort the aged.

马: "Angry, and martial." It depicts the form of a horse's head, mane, tail and four legs. [Yupian] says that Xiang, a minister of the Yellow Emperor, rode a horse; the horse is a martial beast, and an angry one. [Zhengyun]: "a domestic animal; it is born in the wu branch, receiving the qi of fire, and because fire cannot produce wood the horse has a liver but no gall-bladder, the gall-bladder being the essence of wood; since the wood viscus is deficient, one who eats its liver dies." 髂: A philological discussion rather than the Shuowen gloss itself. The writer notes that 骼 is also written 胳 and that in man the corresponding part is the 髖 (hip); that the foreleg of a domestic animal has three parts, the shoulder, upper arm and arm, the 臑 being in man the upper arm, and the hind leg three, the 骼, 髀 and 腨; and that because the thigh was accounted base and not served at table the classics mostly name the shoulder, arm, 臑, 膞 and 骼, the order of naming being explained by the greater honour attaching to the parts below the limbs. 骼, he holds, is the original graph, replaced by 髂 in the Pi Cang and altered to 䯊 in the Guangya and Zilin, a shift he attributes to the interchange of the 魚, 虞, 歌 and 麻 rhyme groups. He argues further that the distinction between 骼 and 骴 marks only a difference of naming between men and beasts, and that Xu Shen, following the seventeen chapters [of the Yili], did not venture to call 骼 a human bone: the Yueling's "in early spring cover the bones and bury the flesh" is glossed by Zheng as dried bone and rotting flesh respectively, by Cai as exposed bone and fleshed bone, while Gao's note to the Lüshi Chunqiu and the Huainanzi commentary agree in not restricting 骼 to the bones of birds and beasts, so that the terms may after all be used interchangeably. Left-right in form, phono-semantic.

鬼: What a man returns to is the ghost. It is formed from 人 (man) and depicts the head of a ghost, and because a ghost is a baleful yin influence it also takes 厶. 麃: A kind of 麠. 麇: The river deer, like a deer. Because the river deer is by nature timorous and yet gathers and disperses readily, it is also named 麇 (jūn, "to flock") — one creature with two names. The Zuo Zhuan (Ai 14) records a great 麇 at Feng Marsh. Phono-semantic in form and phono-semantic in structure.

麝: The musk deer, like a small 麋, with musk in its navel; also called 射父. [Erya, Shishou] gives 麝父 with deer's feet, the [Zilin] explaining that it is a small deer bearing musk whose feet are like a river deer's, whence the gloss. The [Zihui] says the creature resembles a small 麋 with leopard-like markings on its body and musk in its navel, and that when pressed by men it throws itself down from a high cliff and tears out the musk with its claws; even when bound and near death it still folds its four feet to guard its navel — just as the elephant gives up its tusks and the rhinoceros its horn, each covering and hiding what it knows to be precious. 麟: A great 麚: deer's body, ox's tail, wolf's brow and horse's hooves, five-coloured with a yellow belly, standing twelve feet tall. [Yupian] calls it a benevolent beast. [Shijing, Zhounan] has "the unicorn's hoof," the commentary saying that the 麟 is trustworthy and answers to ritual, coming by foot, and the [Zheng] note explaining that the tip of its horn has flesh, showing that it has martial power but does not use it. 黍: A kind of millet, the glutinous one, sown at the time of great heat and hence called 黍 (shǔ); it is composed of 禾 with the abbreviated 雨 as phonetic. The [Zihui] classes it with the panicled millets: its shoots resemble reeds, over ten feet high, its ears black, its grains round and heavy, the soil it wants high and dry; the [Shijing Ji] says there are two kinds, the glutinous being 秫, used for brewing, and the non-glutinous 黍, as rice has its 秔 and 糯. 黼: A pattern of white and black alternating. The [Zhouli, Dongguan, Kaogong Ji] says that white and black together are called 黼, and [Erya, Shiqi] says an axe is called 黼, the subcommentary explaining that the 黼 is half white and half black, like an axe whose blade is white and body black, taking the sense of the power to cut. Another account holds that white is the colour of the west and black of the north; where northwest, the meeting of black and white, is the position of Qian's yang, firm and strong and able to cut, hence the painting of 黼 in black and white. The [Liji, Yueling] records that in late summer the women officials were ordered to dye colours, the 黼, 黻 and ornamental patterns always according to rule; Jia Yi's "Policy of Peace and Order" speaks of the fine wearing 黼 embroidery, and Han Yu's "Prayer to the Weaving Girl" of 黼 and 黻 on the emperor's person. 鼎: The tripod: three legs and two ears, the precious vessel in which the five flavours are blended. Of old Yu gathered the metal of the nine provinces and cast tripods at the foot of Mount Jing; [Yupian] says the tripod is the vessel for cooking food. The Zuo Zhuan (Xuan 3) recalls that when Xia was still virtuous the distant regions sent pictures of their creatures and the nine herdsmen presented metal, wherewith tripods were cast bearing images of the creatures, so that the people should know the divine and the malignant and, entering marshes, mountains and forests, should meet nothing uncanny, the mountain sprites and spectres being unable to come upon them. The [Zhouli, Tianguan, Shanfu] records that the king each day set out one set of tripods with twelve kinds of food, all with their stands, Zheng's note explaining that there were twelve tripods, nine for the flesh and three supplementary. 鼓: The drum: 鼓 (gǔ) is 郭 (guō, "to enclose"). It is the sound of the spring equinox, when all things push out through enclosing skin and shell, and so it is called 鼓, Xu Kai explaining 郭 as "to cover over." [Yupian] says that with earthenware for the body and hide for the face it may be struck, and the Yueshu says the drum regulates music and is chief of all sounds. The [Zhouli, Diguan, Guren] has charge of teaching the six drums, the note listing them: the thunder drum with eight faces, the numinous drum with six, the road drum with four, and the 鼖, 皋 and 晉 drums with two faces each.
